en: Regarding the preface to the *Continued Compilation of the Record of Sages and Worthies of the Pure Land*:

the structural conventions of this record follow those of the previous compilation entirely. For instance, members of the two monastic orders (bhikṣu and bhikṣuṇī) are recorded by their single names, whereas lay practitioners are recorded by their two names.
The sole exception is for Layman Er-lin; apart from his primary biography, all cited evidence regarding him is recorded using only his courtesy name.
The term "Zun" (Venerable) refers to those who preside over [the teachings].

Since the previous record was established by a layperson (*upāsaka*), it headed the list with the Founder of the Teaching, followed by the holy assembly who expounded the teaching; this was intended to explore the root and exhaust the source.
Now, as this is titled a "Continued Compilation," the first two strata need not be elaborated upon further, as they are already clear from the preceding works.

The citations in the preceding record are largely complete. Therefore, in this classification by category and division, I have placed the *bhikṣu* first, recording events by month and by year, beginning from the inception of our dynasty.
I have merely arranged the narrative according to chronological sequence, regardless of the status or rank of the subjects.
However, as the materials I have been able to collect are limited, omissions and errors are inevitably many. I pray that all you gentlemen will favor me with whatever remains.
[This] pearl awaits inclusion in the third compilation.
As for the *Ranxiang ji* (Anthology of Fragrant Incense) and other texts, anyone who maintains right mindfulness at the time of death shall be registered therein.

Although the auspicious signs of rebirth may sometimes be hidden and sometimes manifest, they cannot be taken as certain; nevertheless, they must be verified by one's prior conduct in accordance with their vows.
One's power is not yet deep and one's practice is not yet matured; to wait until the moment of death to recite the Buddha’s name makes it difficult to guarantee a definitive rebirth.

In the *Huixin lu* (Record of Turning the Mind), those such as Wang Zhen-sheng and Shi Jing-yan, though their sincerity in ten recitations was perhaps a hundredfold more courageous than others, were surely such individuals for whom rebirth in the West could be predicted.
Otherwise, there would be a discrepancy between name and reality, and I fear that [the practitioner] will fall short.
Fearing the confusion of fish eyes with pearls, I have slightly edited and refined the text to ensure consistency.
Recently, those who have been recorded as having attained rebirth have been added incrementally through citations from various scriptures. Layman Er-lin deeply lamented this practice;
therefore, in his previous compilation, he appended the original source texts following each biography to serve as verification.
I have maintained this same structural format, merely slightly altering some of the colloquial and vulgar phrases.

As for matters that are somewhat recent, I ensured they necessarily originated from the mouths of those who do not speak falsely; furthermore, I consulted with the elders repeatedly before daring to commit them to writing.
However, if a person’s pure conduct was worthy of transmission but they lacked right mindfulness at the time of death, such cases were generally omitted.

I have included them in the *Wanshi Wangsheng Ji* (Collection on Rebirth at Yunqi). Although there were occasional eulogies (*zan*) in later editions that clarified their hidden meanings, the previous record contained only general discussions and eulogies, which were treated with overall brevity. Herein, for those whose meanings were not clear, I have likewise employed eulogies.
These words are set forth not out of any presumptuous claim to knowledge or insight, but merely to guide those at the beginning of their practice.
Composed by the disciple of Pure Land cultivation, Hu Ting, as a supplement to the *Jingtu Shengxian Lu* (Records of the Holy and Sages of the Pure Land) in verse form.
I contemplate the ocean of true nature, Profoundly clear and fundamentally unmoving. Of the mundane and supramundane dharmas, there is not one that is not fully present.
Above, it is equal to all Buddhas; Below, it is equal to all classes of sentient beings.
It is impartial and beyond thought, Free from all marks of conceptual discrimination, Unimpeded in both the ultimate and the conventional.
Principle and phenomena are entirely interfused, yet in a single instant one fails to realize this.

Like pressing upon the eyes so that flowers suddenly appear, ignorance acts as a fetter, obscuring the sun of wisdom. Thus, within the state of a single mark, one falsely gives rise to views of purity and defilement;
forgetting the source, one pursues only external objects, entering the cycle of saṃsāra moment by moment.
Due to this inverted mind, one sinks and is difficult to liberate; Driven by karma, one wanders through transmigration, and from this point on, the holy and the mundane are separated.
How could one know that the lands of the ten directions are all but a single mind?
Great Awakening is like space, and worlds are like floating clouds— their gathering and dispersal leave no trace at all.
Arising empty and ceasing empty, it follows only the purity or defilement of the mind.

In every land, the turbidity of various karmic actions manifests as the five corruptions; oppressed by manifold sufferings, yet when the mind is pure, it perceives a pure land adorned with the seven treasures.
Deluded people grasp only at external objects, so that east and west appear to them as different.
Just as one who has experienced a dream Still undergoes the suffering and joy within that dream, Upon awakening, knowing the dream was not real, The suffering and joy naturally vanish.
So too does our Buddha of Great Compassion Reveal this extraordinary expedient:
The single phrase "Amitābha," Which can sever the stream of birth and death Without ever leaving the Sahā world.
Sitting steadily upon the purple-gold lotus, Amitābha and the mind-ground are neither one nor two;
if one can understand it thus, one will certainly enter the state of non-arising.
I now compile this record to universally exhort all sentient beings: may all who see or hear it resolve to attain Bodhicitta.
Cultivating all meritorious and virtuous deeds, I dedicate them toward supreme enlightenment.
I look up and pray for the power of the Triple Gem to provide secret perfuming and protection, so that I and all sentient beings may together be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Continued Compilation of the Record of Sages and Worthies of the Pure Land, Volume One:

Xingxiu. It is unclear where she originated from. During the Shunzhi era of the Great Qing dynasty, she resided at Yuanzhao Hermitage in Changde Prefecture.
Wearing simple clothes and subsisting on vegetarian fare, she recited the name of Amitābha Buddha ten thousand times daily without ceasing through cold or heat.

When the harvest failed, she gave away all her money, grain, cloth, and silk to those who were hungry, cold, orphaned, or suffering. Her disciples collectively rebuked her for this, but Xiuxiu could only weep.

He did nothing but recite the Buddha’s name. At the age of seventy, one month prior [to his passing], he knew for himself that the time had arrived. When the appointed day came, he sat and passed away with a smile on his face.
Celestial music was heard in the sky by those far and near, and a wondrous fragrance filled the room, lingering for a month without dispersing.

(From *Shenshi Jinlian*). Master Xishi said: "If one does not begrudge giving in alms, the karma of greed is exhausted; if one recites the Buddha’s name while shedding tears, the karma of hatred is exhausted."
If one practices frugality and moderation for oneself, then the karma of delusion will be exhausted and the three karmas will be purified; thus, one’s rank upon rebirth will surely be high.
Is it not the case that the extraordinary fragrances and celestial music are brought about by the fragrance of one's pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) and the resonant clarity of one's mental voice?
Xing Xiu-xing, surnamed Chen, was a native of Shacun Village in Taizhou. He worked as a farmer and was illiterate, unable to support himself by any other means.
One day, he went into the water seeking death, but a person dressed in white rescued him. At the age of thirty-one, he left the household life to become a monk.
Wearing a single robe through both winter and summer, he practiced asceticism for several years. While traveling toward Mount Putuo, his path was cut off;

he encountered an old man who led him to a house where he stayed overnight. When dawn broke, he saw nothing but a desolate ruin. After returning, he sat in meditation within a stone niche in a deserted tomb outside the South Gate.
He frequently went without food for five or seven days while investigating the supreme matter. One night, deep in the darkness, someone struck at his niche.
He said: "Regarding the dharma that can be received, while practicing in a secluded cell, he saw beneath a bridge a large boat passing by with lamps, fire, drums, and blowing instruments.

Thereupon, he attained great enlightenment. Later, he moved to reside at Jueyin Temple, where he practiced the Pure Land teachings diligently for six years. In the spring of the fourth year of the Kangxi era..."
He said to the people, "On the second day of the sixth month next year, I shall depart. Early the following summer, everyone came to inquire after him.

Fearing he might delude the masses, the Governor of the Prefecture dispatched soldiers to guard him, saying, "If the appointed time does not come to pass, you shall certainly be subjected to legal punishment.

On the first day of the sixth month, [Huiyuan] was still in good health, which caused people to feel anxious and terrified. Rising at dawn the following day, he wrote a verse: "The Sun of Wisdom is in the midst of heaven..."

Illuminating the great trichiliocosm. During the day I perform prostrations; at night I engage in Zen meditation. A "blow-off" sword slants across my brow; hell and heaven are left for me to traverse as I please.
He then sat upright within his coffin and ordered people to carry it to a bridge. He said, "This is not right; the people here all possess animal forms.
They carried it to Dongba Bridge, where he said, "Turn me southward. Holding a fish in his hand, he recited the Buddha’s name.
A single wisp of light smoke rose from the tip of his nose; in an instant, it burst into a blazing fire. The sounds of the *yu* and *fo* mantras resounded clearly, reaching beyond the clouds.

Suddenly, a loud crash was heard from within the shrine; the top of the shrine flew down a hundred paces. Among the remains of the fire, one object was left behind, shaped like a lotus flower, firm and white, and indestructible.

(The *Yangzhou Fu Zhi* records this as the "Lotus Treasury" [Lianzang]. The *Yangzhou Fu Zhi* account of his nirvana on the first day of the eleventh month differs from the account of the Lotus Treasury.)

Master Xi Shi said: "Emerging from fire to burn one's body is not a matter of forced contrivance or artificial adornment. Those who have fallen under demonic influence while pursuing the Way should examine this closely.
Endure life."
Ren was born into the Li clan in Pingyang Prefecture, Shanxi. A scion of an established family, he felt a sense of weary detachment from worldly life from his youth.
At the age of forty-four, he left the household life to practice Chan meditation, attaining profound realization and insight. He held the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation in high esteem.

While traveling on pilgrimage, he arrived at Taizhou, where he met the lay practitioner Yang of Xiaye, who built a hermitage for him and provided offerings. Ren then closed himself within the gate to cultivate pure karma in quietude, leading and transforming the inhabitants of various villages.
The virtuous practitioner later traveled downriver due to flooding and again went to his home province to exhort others to practice; every household there recited the Buddha’s name.
In the first month of the eighth year of the Kangxi era, he knew in advance that the time had come and took leave of his patrons. On the nineteenth day, he bathed and changed his robes.
He exhorted the assembly that mindfulness of the Buddha was of vital importance, whereupon he sat in the lotus posture and passed away. A wondrous fragrance filled the room.
On the twenty-sixth day, his coffin was carried to the outskirts of the city, where it ignited spontaneously and consumed itself (from the *Lianzang*).
Renfai, whose secular surname was Pei, was a native of Beiguo in Changzhou. His parents died early, and his family estate fell into ruin.

He worked as a hired laborer until he was over thirty years old, when he heard of the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land. Thereupon, he resolved to leave the household life and solicited donations to carve woodblocks for the Pure Land scriptures.
He wrote: "I shall extensively bestow [this teaching] upon the fourfold assembly. Later, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*) on Mount Hua and practiced meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Every night, he would invariably sit in meditation for several incense sticks' worth of time. In the seventh month of the nineteenth year of the Kangxi era, he suddenly manifested illness. On the twenty-first day, he bid farewell to his friends.
At the fifth watch of the following night, he said to his disciples, "I am going. He then adjusted his robes and sat in the lotus posture. A monk standing nearby was chanting the Buddha’s name;
Ba said, "The Buddha's name must be recited clearly," and then he called out the name of the Buddha loudly once before passing away (into the Lotus Treasury).

Shi Wangyong, style name Zhenhui, was surnamed Chen and was a native of Huoqiu County in Fengyang Prefecture. At the time of his birth, auspicious light illuminated the neighboring houses and a rare fragrance filled the room.
From childhood, he possessed extraordinary features; his skin never retained impurities. He was compassionate and forgiving by nature and delighted in hearing monks recite the scriptures.
At the school, he mastered his lessons as they passed before his eyes like flowing water. His teacher was deeply impressed by him and said to his parents, "This boy is truly not of the mundane world;
he is a vessel for the Buddha-dharma. Do not let such a talent go to waste. His parents gave their consent.
He was then sent to Daibi-ān in his native district, where he received the tonsure from Master Sincae and subsequently received full ordination.

He studied the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and other major Mahāyāna sūtras as if they were subjects of prior habituation. Later, he moved to the lower monastery of Longtan, where he devoted himself single-mindedly to the cultivation of Pure Land practices for thirty years, as if it were a single day.
In the spring of the sixty-first year of the Kangxi era, he manifested [the signs of his passing].
He suffered from a slight illness and, knowing that his life’s conditions had come to an end, completed the entrustment of monastic affairs. He focused his mind solely on the Pure Land.

On the morning of the fourth day of the third month, he ordered that hot water be prepared for a bath; he gathered the assembly to recite the Buddha's name several hundred times together, and then suddenly passed away.
At the time of his cremation, the flames were like five-colored clouds and mists, spreading across the four surrounding mountains.
His worldly age was forty-eight, and his monastic seniority was thirty-one (according to the *Nanshan Zongtong*).
Changzhi (常智), whose courtesy name was Wenhui (聞慧), was a native of Muya in Huai’an. From childhood, he delighted in making offerings to the Great Being Avalokiteśvara.

Upon reaching adulthood, he donned the monastic robes and entered Wensi Temple to receive full ordination. One day, while participating in the communal recitation with the assembly, they reached the passage in the Heart Sūtra concerning “non-obstruction.”

The knots of obstruction within his breast were suddenly dissolved. He then crossed the river and traveled extensively to visit famous monasteries and consult various spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*).
After a long time, however, he found no point of realization. Upon returning home, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of the Pure Land and strictly observed the precepts.

Whenever others committed a transgression, he would invariably guide and transform them with patience and gentleness. Even toward those who were insolent, he would always respond with tactful diplomacy, never showing even a trace of resentment. Furthermore, he...

Fellow practitioners: Several months prior, while engaged in the communal practice of repentance, he knew his time had come. He informed his fellow members, and when the appointed day arrived, he gathered the assembly to pay homage to the Buddha.
He then bathed himself with warm water, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away. Upon cremation, purple lotuses as large as bushels surged forth from the midst of the flames;
upon them were layered lights, their reflections appearing like the form of a wise sage. Only after a long while did they...
[The text] was dispersed. All people saw it (*Nanshan Zongtong*).
The Western Historian said: "In clarity, no teacher surpasses Amitābha; as for virtuous friends, who can equal those in the Stage of Succession? Ancestors of the past have already spoken of this.
Yet, looking at the śramaṇas of later generations, they hold the Pure Land in low esteem, often pointing to it as 'bodhi attached to signs' (*nimitta-bodhi*). Relying on—
Unless one has been endowed with the eye of wisdom from past lives and possesses a profound and clear understanding of the Great Way, few will not be shaken or deluded by it.
Only those who have heard the wisdom and traveled extensively in study, yet find no resonance within, may come close to attaining it.
The monk Luosi (Silkworm-Weaver) was a man of unknown origin who resided at Dongyuan in Hangzhou. He had abandoned his secular life as a silk-weaver to enter the monastic order, hence his name.
He lived alone in a dilapidated hut, reciting the Buddha’s name day and night without ceasing. Seeing that he lacked [the means for offerings],...
He supported himself by living as a hired hand. He said to his former master, "If you will simply provide me with food, may I continue to spin silk for you?
The master agreed. Once he had obtained his food, his hands would click-clack and his mouth would chatter; he had no other business. This continued for several years.
One day, carrying a basket full of scraps of paper, he approached the Western Ching (Xixing) gentleman, Wu Shuxu, wishing to exchange them for a hundred cash. Wu questioned him...
For this reason, the monk replied with a smile, "Old layman, I did not dare hide anything before you. Today I am returning to the West;

I was merely intending to buy a load of firewood. Shuxu said, "If that is truly so, I shall provide the firewood for you, Master. The monk joined his palms in thanks and departed with the firewood, while also appointing a specific time for Shuxu to come and serve as a witness.
When Shuxu arrived at the appointed time, he found that the monk had already piled up the firewood and formed a pyre.
He sat down and assumed the full lotus posture upon it. As flames blazed on all four sides, the monk raised his hand in a gesture of farewell from within the fire.

Suddenly, with a single stroke of his hand across his face, his entire body was instantly revealed in a golden hue. In an instant, he vanished entirely. From atop a tree, Xu Kuian sighed deeply, saying:
"The marvelous and transcendent power of the ancient virtuous one is seen once again today. (*Ranxiang ji*)
Master Xi Shi said: "The stacked firewood burning itself out is similar yet not identical to Xingxiu’s fire emerging from the tip of his nose.
Nevertheless, who knows that what is being consumed there might not be the fire of samādhi?"

Guangzhi, whose courtesy name was Erli, was a native of Kuaiji. After entering the monastic order, he built a thatched hut at Huangjin Cave on Mount Tiantai and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism.
When Yin Tiancheng of Suzhou went to Mount Tiantai to provide meals for the monks, he was moved by Guangzhi’s spiritual conduct and invited him to reside at Wushan.
At Jieyin Hermitage, for over thirty years, he guided beings according to their capacities, directing them toward the Pure Land. Those who received precepts from him numbered in the hundreds.
He once established a period of intensive practice for reciting the Buddha’s name, continuing day and night without the sound ever ceasing.

His disciple Zao visited him and saw that on the place where Zhì used to walk, the name "Amitābha Buddha" was written in large characters, emitting a golden light. Amazed, Zao questioned Zhì about it. Zhì—

He said, "This is merely the manifestation of your own original radiance. On the full moon of the fourth month in the twenty-sixth year of the Qianlong era, he invited four of his disciples to visit the hermitage to make offerings to the Buddha.
As they were about to depart, he told them, "You should come to see me off tomorrow before noon. When the appointed time arrived...

When the assembly arrived, they burned incense and recited the Buddha’s name a thousand times. He passed away while sitting upright (from the *Collection of Verified Accounts of the Western Quarter*). "Daozheng, Daozheng.

He was a native of Hangzhou who resided at Dachun Chan Monastery to the east of the prefecture. By nature he was sincere and honest, and he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of the Pure Land. Every...
Three times a day, he burned incense as an offering and knelt long before the Buddha, reverently reciting the Name.
At the age of eighty, one day he said to the assembly, "On the twelfth day of the second month next year, I shall return to the West. When the appointed time arrived, he was free from ailment.
Someone teased him, saying, "Today is the twelfth day of the second month; why does the Master not return to the West? Zhen replied, "It is indeed so."

"Is it the Flowering Court? Having said this, he bathed, burned incense, gathered the assembly, and passed away. There was a monk named Meisong who had practiced the Pure Land path together with Daozheng;
he resided at Miaoyan Temple. That night, in a dream, someone told him: "Master Daozheng has sat in transformation."
"Why do you not see me off? Mei Song woke up and hurried to look; he patted his back and said, "We have been acquainted for many years, yet as you depart, there is no word from you.
Nevertheless, I too shall not remain long in this world. Three days later, he also passed away while sitting in meditation.
This event took place in the thirtieth year of the Qianlong era (*Ranxiang ji*).
Master Xi Shi said: "To forget his westward return when the time arrived, and to leave no word before departing—this was because he had no concern for life or death.
That Mei and Song followed in his footsteps was surely due to a prior vow."

Qian Yiyuan, whose secular surname was Wang, was a native of Haining. He resided at Zhaoqing Temple on West Lake, where he strictly observed the precepts and diligently practiced the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
Delighting in tranquility, he inscribed his dwelling “A Secluded Spot of Mount Lu” and lived there in secret cultivation.
In the autumn of the forty-third year of the Qianlong era, a fellow practitioner came to visit him. One said, "Your arrival is most timely; it coincides exactly with my departure for the West.
You may serve as my witness. He then spoke a verse and passed away while seated. His stupa was erected to the left of the monastery (from the *Ranxiang ji*).

Che Mi (Chè mí), surnamed Zhōng, was a native of Jiāxīng. By nature, he was honest and sincere. In middle age, he entered the Hùguó Monastery in Hǎining, where he received the tonsure and ordination under Master Dìnggāo. He devoted himself single-mindedly to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism.
Later, he moved to reside at Yán'ēn Monastery, where he would recite the Buddha’s name while holding his prayer beads in silence whenever he went out or came in.
He practiced only the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and possessed no other special attainments; consequently, many people treated him with indifference.

One day, he said to his fellow monks in the quarters, "I am about to take my leave of you all. When they asked where he was going, he replied, "To the Western Land [of Sukhāvatī]. They all laughed at him.

Several days later, he returned from outside and spoke again, saying, "Today I have resolved to depart. Shortly thereafter, he changed his robes, sat in the full lotus posture, and cried out in a loud voice, "I am going!"
He then became silent, and the assembly cried out that he had passed away. This occurred in the fifty-sixth year of the Qianlong era (as recorded in the *Ranxiang ji*).
[His name was] Song’an, Song’an; his origins are unknown. He resided at Baekui-am in Suiup. By nature he was simple and blunt, and he maintained the precepts under Master Ji.
Master Jili Shi possessed the roots of faith from his youth. A practitioner from Chichun village taught him to recite the *Lotus Sūtra*, through which he attained considerable insight.
Later, he resolved to practice the mindfulness of the Buddha (*nienfo*) with such vigor that he did not cease day or night. In his later years, he contracted a disease of abdominal distension;

knowing it was the result of fixed karma (*niyati-karman*), he remained unperturbed. He continued his recitation of the Buddha’s name as usual. When his illness reached its final stage, his disciples went to visit him, but he remained composed and at peace.
He then counted his fingers and said, "I shall come to visit on such-and-such a day.

When the appointed time arrived, he bathed and changed his clothes, instructing his disciples not to weep, but rather to recite the Buddha’s name aloud to assist him in attaining rebirth in the Pure Land. Shortly thereafter, he passed away with a serene expression (*Lianzong jiyao*).

Mai Chun (also known as Mai Chun). Surname Zhou; a native of Tong County. From his youth, he was studious and possessed great intelligence, and he took a keen interest in the Buddhist scriptures. At the age of nineteen, he visited Lingyin Temple and ascended the Dharma Hall;

upon seeing the plaque inscribed "Attaining Enlightenment with an Empty Mind" (Xinkong Jidi), he attained a profound realization. He subsequently left the household life at the Yanshou Hall of Tianzhu.
Having traveled extensively to visit famous mountains, he entered the quarters of Master Shu-lian at Fuyan. Master Shu-lian recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma.
One day, Shu-lian asked, "When afflictions arise, how do you bring them to rest? Chun replied, "The fundamental nature is profoundly still; what afflictions could there be?

Shu-lian deeply accorded with this, and subsequently transmitted the Great Dharma to him. Although Chun had attained the Dharma of the Chan school, he held the Pure Land practice in high esteem. Having settled at Yun...
At Fengsi Temple, [the Master] led the assembly in the recitation of the Buddha’s name, setting a period of twenty-one days as the limit, beginning again once it was completed.

He continued thus for several years without slackening. Subsequently, he again established a period of one hundred days, maintaining the recitation day and night without spreading out his bedding or mats.

In the winter of the twelfth year of the Jiaqing era, after bathing and sitting upright, he said to the assembly: "Recently, I saw a parrot reciting the names of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; its voice was subtle and wondrous."
How truly joyful! He passed away with palms joined (*Ranxiang ji*).
Lüyì Jìnglǜjìng (Law-Pure-Law-Pure), courtesy name Míngchè, surnamed Qián, was a native of Dèqīng in Húzhōu. At the age of forty, he left the household life under Kāṅzhīcí.
Seng’an succeeded in going to Dongyuan Dening Monastery, where he made the recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra* his daily practice for twenty years without interruption.
One day, a fellow practitioner named Jicheng said to him, "Your resolve for the Way is so steadfast;

it would be even better if you added the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name and dedicating the merit. Even Master Zhiyi, who attained the Samādhi of the *Lotus Sūtra*, still sought [this further]."
"You have been reborn in the Pure Land; why do you not do the same? He then presented him with the *Ten Doubts Treatise* (*Shiyi lun*) for his perusal. Jing was struck with sudden realization.

From then on, as soon as he finished reciting the sutras, he would immediately practice mindfulness of the Buddha and dedicate the merit. After more than a year had passed, in the seventh month of the eleventh year of the Jiaqing era:
He told his disciple Zeng Xiu, "Before the Mid-Autumn Festival, I shall go to the West.

On the second day of the eighth month, he spoke again, saying, "I shall depart at the hour of the Rabbit on the seventh day. When asked how he knew this, Jing smiled and said, "When the water arrives, the channel is formed."
When the appointed time arrived, he went to see him. [Jingzhi] was already sitting cross-legged in new robes. At that time, many neighboring monks came to recite the Buddha’s name to assist him.
Jingzhi stopped them, saying, "The application of effort lies entirely in one's daily practice. What is the use of digging a well when one is thirsty?
He then moved his seat into the coffin and spoke this verse: "My age is sixty-nine; My words are true and not false. Laying down these two hands, I go straight to the West."
[The practitioner] then runs forward, joins his palms, and enters stillness (*Ranxiang ji*).
Master Xishi remarked: "Formerly Renfa and later Song'an both commanded that one should chant the Buddha’s name aloud; this makes clear the vital importance of supportive conditions.
To say now that they were 'digging a well when already thirsty' is precisely because their practice had reached a state of pure maturity. It is an exhortation for others to strive with diligence."
Proceed with caution. Those who have not yet attained samādhi must not use this as an excuse.
Huiming was a native of Yinkuan County in Ningbo; he resided at Baoguo Temple in Hangzhou. He was upright by nature and knew nothing other than the practice of nianfo (reciting the Buddha’s name).

Whenever he held up the Great Name (the Buddha’s name), his voice was like the surging of the tide; even when the incense was exhausted, he remained unaware. Upon receiving offerings, he would immediately release captive creatures.

As he released them, he would recite the Buddha’s name, always dedicating the merit toward the Western Pure Land. When meeting people, he did not engage in greetings or pleasantries, but would simply say, "Death has arrived;
quickly recite the Buddha’s name. Among the monastics and laypeople in the region of Yue who knew his name, whenever they were in critical condition, they would immediately summon him.
This is the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, which serves as an auxiliary condition for rebirth in the Pure Land. Someone once asked about its significance, saying:

"I recall that in the past, when I was suffering from a fever that grew increasingly severe until I could hardly endure it, I was fortunate enough to have the name of the Buddha emerge from within my faculty of mind—one phrase following another at the crown of my head—continuing without interruption.
The demonic illness was thereby dispelled, and I eventually recovered thanks to this. From that time forward, whether speaking or silent, moving or still," [I maintained this practice].

Each [image] bears the name of a single Buddha, emerging from his faculty of mind—one phrase at a time, one after another. In the twelfth year of the Jiaqing era, he suffered from carbuncles on the back of his neck;
yet he did not utter a single groan. At the moment of death, his countenance was serene and joyful, and his hands were formed into the gesture of holding prayer beads.
He passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name after some time had elapsed. Previously, a certain person in Hangzhou had dreamed that an acquaintance, the late Master Huang, said to him:
"I urged you to take refuge with Master Huiming, but you were negligent and did not act upon it. Now, within this month, Master Huiming intends to pass away;
if you delay further, it will be too late. You must go quickly to seek him out. Your dharma name is Da Tong, and I have already [conferred it upon him]."
"You must certainly wake up and distinguish this. At dawn, Ming rose and went to the temple; by then, his carbuncle had erupted with extreme severity.

He urgently invited five companions to seek refuge [in the Triple Gem]. Ming granted their request and bestowed dharma names upon them. Ming then wrote five characters by hand, made them into lots, and placed them beside the incense altar, saying:
"In my illness, I am unable to entrust each matter to you individually. Regarding the last character of your dharma names—"
All [these names] belong to the character-based lineages (*zìpài*). You each take one according to your own conditions. As for the first character, I have just drawn the character "Da" (大).
It is as if it were a story from a dream. (*Ranxiang ji*) Master Xishi said:
Why is it that upon taking refuge, one can pre-assign a Dharma name? Long ago, when the World-Honored One was in the immeasurable...
In a kalpa prior to this, [the Master] heard the ancient Śākyamuni preaching the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and obtained a single verse from within that scripture.
He even sold his own body as an offering, vowing that in a future life he would attain Buddhahood under the same name. For this reason, the Tathāgata of today is also named Śākyamuni.
That the current Master and I likewise share this connection is due to the profound depth of our karmic conditions established over immeasurable kalpas.
Thus, those who wish to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss yet fear that their aspiration may not be fulfilled can find cause for hope herein.
Yichan Yichan was a native of Haining; by secular occupation he was a butcher. At the age of forty, he felt deep remorse for his past transgressions and thought only of leaving the household life.
Having resolved this matter, he subsequently shaved his head at Haiyin Temple in his native district and soon received full ordination.

He served as the administrative director (*kanyuan*), reciting sutras and chanting the Buddha’s name, while openly confessing his transgressions and dedicating his merit toward rebirth in the Pure Land. With sincere devotion and diligent effort, he persevered for more than twenty years without weariness.
In the twelfth year of the Jiaqing era, at the age of sixty-eight, he retired from the position of director and closed himself in retreat for several months, continuing until the twelfth lunar month.
On the twenty-eighth day, he instructed the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name for one full day and night. Early the next morning, after bathing and paying homage to the Buddha, he passed away.
His body was cremated, and dozens of white *śarīra* relics were obtained (*Ranxiang ji*).

Jixing Jixing (際醒際醒), whose courtesy name was Chewu (徹悟) and pen-name Nutang (訥堂), was surnamed Ma and a native of Fengrun County in Jingdong. In his youth, he was well-versed in the Confucian classics and histories.

After shaving his head and donning the robes of a monk, he traveled extensively among lecture halls, gaining a broad mastery of both the Xing (性, Nature/Prakṛti) and Xiang (相, Characteristics/Lakṣaṇa) schools of Buddhism. Regarding the three contemplations and ten suchnesses of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*...
The essence of his practice was particularly one of realized understanding. He studied under Chan Master Guangtong Cuiru, who clarified the matter of the "upward direction.
As teacher and disciple were in perfect accord, [Xing] received the seal of his mind. Later, when Master Cui moved to Wanshou Temple, Xing succeeded him at Guangtong.
He exhorted his junior disciples, and the style of his school flourished greatly. He often remarked that Chan Master Yongming Shou was a true master of the Chan gate; yet even he—

One should turn one’s heart toward the Pure Land; how much more so now in this final age, when it is especially fitting to follow and uphold these teachings. Thereupon, he devoted himself exclusively to the cultivation of pure karma and became a proponent of the Lotus School (*Lianzong*).
He limited his daily schedule to receiving guests for only as long as it took to burn a branch of incense; once that time had passed, he would simply engage in ritual prostrations and recitation.

Subsequently, he was appointed as the abbot of Juesheng Temple, but soon retired to Zifu Temple on Mount Hongli. His disciples, filled with longing and devotion, followed him in increasing numbers, until finally—
He established monastic communities; for the sake of the Dharma and for sentient beings, his heart never grew weary. He took nothing other than the Pure Land as his ultimate refuge.

Whenever he expounded upon the Tathāgata’s grace in rescuing suffering and gathering in joy, tears would often fall with his voice, and those who listened were likewise moved to such an extent that their tears drenched their robes.
His two-volume *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings) is particularly profound and essential. To speak briefly of my own...
At the critical juncture of birth and death, there are only two kinds of power. First, when the mind’s thoughts are manifold, it falls toward that which is weightiest;
this is the power of the mind (*citta-bala*). Second, as with a person burdened by debt, the stronger creditor drags one away first; this is the power of karma (*karma-bala*).
While the power of karma is great, the power of the mind is even greater, because karma lacks intrinsic nature and depends entirely upon the mind; thus, a heavy mind can cause karma [to manifest].
Strong! Now, if one cultivates the practice of purity with a focused mind, then that pure karma will be powerful.

When the retribution of this life ends and one passes away, one will certainly be reborn in the Western Land and not in any other place. It is like a great tree or a massive wall that habitually leans toward the west;
when it eventually falls, it will certainly not fall in any other direction. What constitutes a "focused mind"? It is our cultivation of the practice of purity with faith.
Value depth; aspire to earnestness. Because one’s faith and aspiration are deep and earnest, no heterodox teachings can shake or delude them, and no external circumstances can lead them astray.
Should one practice the Pure Land path with right cultivation, the Patriarch Bodhidharma—

Suddenly appearing before me, he urged me to abandon the Pure Land and pursue meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), claiming that by doing so I could attain Buddhahood in this very life. I did not dare to comply with his command.
At that moment, Śākyamuni Tathāgata suddenly manifested his form and said that there was yet another skillful means (*upāya*) superior to the Pure Land.
"Even if you were to command me to abandon this and follow that, I would not dare to comply with such an instruction. This is what is called deep faith.
Even if a red-hot iron wheel were to spin upon one's head, one would not, because of that suffering, lose the aspiration for rebirth [in the Pure Land].

Furthermore, even if the sublime five desires of a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) were to manifest before one, one would not, because of that pleasure, lose the aspiration for rebirth. Thus it is said.
Even when faced with the ultimate extremes of adversity or favor, one does not alter one's vow; this is called an "urgent vow. When faith is deep and the vow is urgent, this is called a "heavy mind.
By means of this, one cultivates purity; pure karma will necessarily be powerful. When karma is powerful, it ripens. If the pure karma for Sukhāvatī ripens, [rebirth there is certain].
The defiled conditions of this Sahā world will then come to an end. At the time of death, although one may wish for the realms of saṃsāra to reappear before one, they cannot do so;
yet, although one may wish for Amitābha’s Pure Land not to appear before one, it likewise cannot fail to do so.

However, this faith and aspiration must be maintained through constant practice beforehand; then, at that time, one will naturally not enter upon a forked path. As the ancient masters said when facing [death]:...
As one is about to die, the youths of the six heavens of the desire realm come in succession to lead one away, yet none succeed; one remains with single-minded devotion, awaiting the Buddha.
Only when the Buddha appears do they depart. This is the moment when the four elements disperse; this is the realm where the celestial youths offer guidance.
If one’s habitual faith and aspiration have not reached a state of tenfold firmness, how could one possibly maintain such resolve at this time, in the face of this realm?
"Is it not the case that [the Buddha] is the sovereign master? Furthermore, it is said: A Zen practitioner asked, "All dharmas are entirely like dreams.
The Sahā world is certainly a dream, and the Land of Ultimate Bliss is also a dream. Since they are both equally one dream, what benefit is there in practicing? He replied, "Not so."
From the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) and below, one cultivates the path within the dream; though one may have attained equal awakening, one still sleeps within the great dream of ignorance.
Only the Buddha alone is called the Great Awakened One. While the eyes of the dream have not yet opened, suffering and pleasure are vividly present.
Rather than experiencing the suffering of the Sahā world within a dream, why not experience the bliss of Sukhāvatī? Moreover, the dream of the Sahā world leads from dream into [further] dreaming.
A dream is that which one becomes increasingly immersed in and deluded by. A dream of the Land of Ultimate Bliss is that which, from dreaming, enters awakening, gradually leading to Great Awakening.
Although the dreams are the same, the reason for dreaming is truly different; how can they be discussed in general terms?

In the second month of the fifteenth year of the Jiaqing era, [the Master] foreknew that his time had come. He took leave of his lay patrons and entrusted them with this message: "Illusory conditions will not last long; all is empty..."
Life is to be cherished; each of you should strive diligently to recite the Buddha’s name. In years to come, we shall meet again in the Pure Land.

Half a month before his passing, he manifested illness and commanded the assembly to join him in chanting the Buddha’s name. He saw countless banners and streamers in the sky coming from the west and told the assembly, "The signs of the Pure Land have appeared;
I am about to return to the West. On the seventeenth day of the twelfth month, at the hour of Shen...
He carved [the image]. He then addressed the assembly, saying, "Yesterday I saw the three great bodhisattvas—Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta;
today I have further been graced by the Buddha’s personal arrival to welcome me away. The assembly recited the Buddha’s name with even greater intensity.

Upon waking, he sat upright facing west, joined his palms, and fixed his gaze, saying, "With each single invocation of the Great Name, one perceives a portion of the Buddha’s marks and signs. Having finished speaking, he formed a mudrā and passed away. The assembly...

A rare fragrance was perceived floating in the air as he remained in his open grotto for seven days; his countenance appeared as if alive, and his white hair turned black again. Upon cremation, more than a hundred śarīra relics were obtained.
His secular age was seventy, and his monastic seniority (*saṃgha-vassa*) was forty-nine. (From the *Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chewu*). The Western Historian says:
He cultivated both dhyāna and the Pure Land, yet focused his mind exclusively on An-yang (Sukhāvatī). Examining his traces of pure conduct...
How profound and earnest was his guidance of others! How is it that he is so identical in his path with the venerable masters of the Lotus School?
That he served as a teacher to men and acted as a Buddha and patriarch—I have seen this clearly herein.

Qixin (Qi Xin), whose courtesy name was Xianghai, was surnamed Shan and was a native of Fuchun. His father, Huazang, was extensively versed in the Buddhist scriptures and was enlightened to the ultimate truth.
He sent Xin to leave the household life and seek the precepts at Nanping, instructing him to contemplate the "Who" kōan. Xin investigated thoroughly and pursued his inquiry with diligent effort.
He once remained awake throughout the night, sitting upright in a single room like a piece of wood, utterly motionless.

On the fifteenth day of the seventh month in the first year of the Jiaqing era, while ascending Mount Wu at the hour of midnight, he saw the lights of the city reflecting off one another, dazzling his eyes and mind; he attained a realization.

Upon returning, he spoke of this to Huazang, who in turn instructed him to travel extensively to consult various spiritual teachers. When he reached Suzhou, he met Master Huiyi Chuan, who taught him the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation).
Regarding this Dharma gate, Xin immediately returned to Hangzhou and closed himself in retreat at Gumai Hermitage. He recited the name of Amitābha Buddha one hundred thousand times daily.

Occasionally he composed poems all pointing toward the Pure Land; among them was a "Song of Mindfulness" which says: "How good it is to practice mindfulness! How good it is to practice mindfulness! All matters are swept away with a single stroke.
How many times have I turned my back on my father and wandered through the dust of the world? In guest lodgings, my spirit and soul were often in disarray. I did not engage in [Chan] meditation..."
Zen. Do not boast of your teachings. A single incense burner, its spiraling篆-characters curling and winding; the frantic toil of shoulder-laden burdens has no cause.

Seeking friends and searching for masters—when will it end? Cease seeking outwardly; simply reflect inwardly. The priceless *maṇi* jewel within your robes manifests form and responds to sound with startling clarity.
Who among the six realms lacks this divine light? The water flows of itself; the mountains stand steep of themselves. Within stillness...

Observing all that comes, they enter the wondrous; they laugh at those who are busily preoccupied with fame and profit. Who can achieve this true cultivation of self-mastery? The moon sinks in the west, the bell tolls for dawn;
do not vainly say that one’s countenance has not yet grown old. Since antiquity, sages and worthies have been as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;

who among them has not been buried as bleached bones in the wild grasses? Only this mind knows neither longevity nor early death; having escaped the sea of suffering, there is no affliction. One hundred [verses].

A lifetime in this world is like a flower in the sky; having thoroughly realized the emptiness of these sky-flowers, one lets out a long, resonant laugh. The alms-bag hangs down, the staff is bent; casting aside worldly attachments, the path home is reached early.
The fixed destiny of human life has already been ordained; the Buddha’s original nature is true and spontaneous, not something forged through effort.

Dwelling idly in a hermitage, I am too indolent to discuss the Way. Officials find me difficult to conscript; my lord finds me difficult to summon. On my Zen seat, I sit all day long, forgetting all artifice;
even the blue-eyed barbarian monk cannot see into it. Drying myself in the sun on the eaves, I patch my tattered robes and eat my fill of coarse rice as circumstances allow.
I dare say that closing one's door to admire purity and loftiness is not merely a matter of looking down upon others from afar. In life, I have few friends; in death, there shall be no mourners.
When the breath ceases, this skin-sack is simply cast aside—whether buried in the earth or cremated by fire, let it be as it may. Leave no descendants to avoid the presence of the unworthy.
Do not grieve in suffering; do not laugh in joy. All is but the dream of a floating life yet unawakened. Let us all cast away our entanglements.
Fujii. Regarding the request to sing the *Kangen-kyō* (Song of Returning Home): there is one word that is most concise and essential. Sentient beings are like birds caught in a net;
if they wish to escape the net, where shall they seek it? There is only this: I urge you to practice the Buddha’s name with joy.

On the nineteenth day of the tenth month in the seventeenth year, he passed away at the Inshū-an hermitage in Higashizōen. At the time of his death, he bathed, changed his robes, and passed away while sitting in mindfulness of the Buddha.
After some time had passed, his crown was so warm that it could burn the hand; his entire body entered the stupa as lightly as a single hair. Huizang praised him with these linked verses:
"The warmth at his crown foretells rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss; the lightness of his body reveals the mind of Nirvana. He was thirty-seven years old.
(From the *Jue tou yin* with preface, in the *Ran xiang ji*).

Zhenchuan (True Transmission). His courtesy name was Zhihui; his secular surname was He. A native of Wu County in Suzhou, at the age of nineteen, he met the Venerable Monk Lan Gong, who instructed him in the Buddha Vehicle.
He received the five precepts. The lay practitioner Peng Er-lin invited him to enter Wensheng Pavilion, where he transmitted the formal offerings.
He was known as Dizi. Together with others, he practiced the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi). At the age of twenty-eight, he entered the monastic order at Chongfu Temple in Hangzhou.
There, he studied the profound meanings of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. When he expounded these teachings for others, his phrasing and meaning were clear and lucid.
Later, he resided at Lengyan Temple in Jiaxing, where he vowed to raise funds to carve the woodblocks for the Tripitaka. As the day for commencing the work drew near, he suddenly fell ill.
He retired to Fengchao Hermitage in Suzhou, setting his mind solely on returning to the West.

At the end of the first month in the seventeenth year of the Jiaqing era, he said to his disciples, "Do not be surprised; tomorrow I shall depart. Then, at the hour of midnight, he suddenly rose from his seat.
Facing west, he recited the Buddha’s name and passed away with a smile at the age of fifty-three (*Sancha Rojeonjip*).

The Western Historian says: Publishing scriptures is a supportive condition; reciting the Buddha’s name is the primary practice. It was indeed fitting that, when illness struck, he devoted himself exclusively to this primary practice.

Dachun, whose courtesy name was Cuixiu and style name Xitan, was surnamed Zhu and a native of Tongxiang County in Jiaxing. Having undergone tonsure from a young age, he resided at Juehai Temple in Jiaxing.
He cultivated the Pure Land practices with great diligence for sixteen years and constructed a hall for the Three Holy Ones of the Western Paradise.

In both spring and winter, he opened sessions for the recitation of the Buddha’s name, inspiring those from near and far; monastics and laypeople alike gathered like clouds. He twice practiced the *pratyutpanna-samādhi* (the walking meditation).
One night, in a dream, he saw a great lotus flower descend from the sky. From that time on, his insight and realization became transcendent.
His eloquence was unimpeded. The layman Peng Er-lin, having heard of his spiritual practice from afar, invited him to reside at Liu-shui Ju and Wen-xing Ge.

There he led the assembly in the recitation of the Buddha’s name with rigorous daily discipline and constantly lectured on the *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra* by Yunqi and the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school.
For ten years he persevered without weariness; subsequently, he assumed the abbacy of Nan-ch'an Temple, where he restored all that had fallen into ruin. Pure...

After his activities had ceased, he withdrew to the Shusheng Hermitage and redoubled his devotion to the practice of *nienfo*. In the winter of the eighteenth year of the Jiaqing era, he manifested signs of illness.
In the spring of the following year, having completed all affairs concerning the monastery, he sent a hand-written letter from his disciple Wuling, who was at Nan Chan, summoning him to come, saying:
"I am about to depart for eternity; I require you for one final farewell. On the thirteenth day of the second month, he gathered the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name and bathed himself.

He bathed and changed his robes. Sitting in the full lotus posture, he spoke a verse, saying: "For many lifetimes, I have been entangled in turbid suffering; in a single moment, I have attained carefree transcendence.
Joyfully beholding the manifestation of Amitābha’s form, I see clearly that another heaven has opened. With palms joined, he passed away at the age of sixty-three.
At fifty-seven years of monastic seniority (*saṃgha-lakṣa*), [he passed away]. (From the *Xīntán yín gǎo*, *Rǎnxiāng jí*).
Língchè, Língchè:

a native of Hángzhōu. He left the household life at Bǎoshòu Monastery in the prefecture. For over ten years, he applied himself with diligence to the practice of Buddha-recollection (*buddhānusmṛti*).
When he was over fifty years old, he fell ill. He gathered the assembly to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, setting a period of seven days. He himself followed along despite his failing strength.
On the third day, he addressed the assembly, saying, "I shall attain birth in the Pure Land. May you all exert yourselves. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
This occurred in the twentieth year of the Jiaqing era (Record of the Incense Collection).
Daoshou, a native of Fengyang, left the household life on Mount Jiuhua. For thirty years he traveled extensively through monasteries, his alms bowl and staff solitary and simple;

he lived in tranquil detachment, finding self-sufficiency therein. Later, he resided at an ancient temple in Zhongdai Town, Jiaxing, where he closed his door and recited the Buddha’s name for four years.

In the spring of the twenty-third year of the Jiaqing era, [Master] Cai suddenly entered the city by small boat and exhorted donors everywhere to focus their minds on the recitation of the Buddha’s name with extreme earnestness.

The following day, several people who shared his affinity went to visit him; finding the door of his quarters unopened, they pushed it open to look inside and saw that he had already passed away while sitting in the lotus posture (from the *Ranxiang ji*).
Liequan, whose courtesy name was Tiansheng, was a native of Haining. He became a disciple of Master Dinggao and resided with Chemi at Yanyen Temple.
He was diligent and devoted in his recitation of the Buddha’s name. In the winter of the twenty-third year of the Jiaqing era, he said to others, "I am about to pass away."
He departed from his four neighbors, leaving them all in a state of wonder and astonishment. They wished to escort him back home, but he declined, saying, "Do not do so;
the time has not yet come. The following evening, he performed his evening recitations as usual, but it was not until the second watch that he returned to his quarters.
When the monastic community rose at dawn, he was found sitting cross-legged, having passed away. (From the *Ranxiang ji*)
Fodu Fodu was a native of Xi County, Anhui Province. He resided at Nanchan Temple in Suzhou. He observed the practice of not eating after noon and never let his side touch the mat.
He specialized in the cultivation of Pure Land practices. In the spring of the twenty-third year of the Jiaqing era, he fell ill; he took leave of his fellow practitioners and sat upright.
There was a monk named Juesiang from Jiahe who also resided at Nanchan Temple. He shared a deep friendship with Fudu Dao.

His appearance was extremely unattractive, and many people looked down upon him; he remained silent all day long. He observed the precept of not eating after noon and performed the Forty-Eight Vows and the Great Compassion Repentance every morning.
At other times, the sound of the Buddha’s name never ceased from his mouth. At night, he sat upright facing west.
Thus it was for twenty years. When [his teacher] passed away into liberation, he said, "He has gone; I shall follow him.
He bathed, burned incense, and facing west with palms joined, he passed away (*Ranxiang ji*).

Jueyuan Jueyuan, whose courtesy name was Xinghai, was the son of the Zhang family of Dingyuan, Anhui. From childhood he was exceptionally gifted; at the age of nine, he had mastered all five of the Classics by heart.

Upon reaching his early twenties, he entered the local prefectural school, and his reputation for literary talent grew daily. Nevertheless, he had no intention of pursuing an official career, and whenever he composed a work...

He contemplated the nature of the world and read the *Avataṃsaka* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras, finding many passages that resonated with him. Before long, his parents passed away one after the other, whereupon he resolved to leave the household life.

He went to Mount Jiashan in Jinling under the guidance of Vinaya Master Qishi to have his head shaved, and then paid homage to Vinaya Master Fengchong Haoqing to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
At that time, he was already forty years old; considering his late entry into the monastic order, he practiced asceticism and maintained his precepts with firm resolve.

He observed the precepts: refraining from false speech, abstaining from eating at improper times, not touching gold, silver, or precious objects with his hands, and not wearing garments made of animal fur or silk.
Having completed his study of the Tripitaka at Touzi, he practiced the two periods of *dhūta* austerity and traveled extensively to consult various spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Upon hearing that Chan Master Jie’an of Jiaoshan was a renowned and virtuous master of the Dongshan lineage, he went specifically to visit him. Their karmic conditions and spiritual resonance were in perfect accord; thus...

He received the seal of transmission and again resided in the mountains to study the Tripitaka, whereby he entered even more deeply into the ocean of the teachings. Regarding the profound principles of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he alone attained personal realization;
reciting them aloud and opening the texts with his hands, he did so no fewer than several hundred times, until he could recite them from memory without omitting a single character.
He constantly expounded the Great Meaning for both the monastic and lay communities, piercing the obscure and clarifying the subtle until his listeners were suddenly enlightened.

Consequently, he designated his own title as "One True Dharma Realm. Subsequently, he settled his mind in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*An-yang*), daily reciting the name of the Buddha of the West one hundred thousand times;
for several decades, his side never touched his mat. In his later years, Master Cheng of Shigu invited him to reside at Gaomin Temple.
He had long suffered from an ailment in his feet; although it grew increasingly severe, he did not cease even for a moment from performing prostrations during the six periods of the day.
Furthermore, he added the practice of the Puming Chan (Universal Radiance Repentance) and the Forty-eight Vows of Amitābha.

Having performed these prostrations, he would immediately recite the names of the Buddhas without ceasing, never speaking of other matters when meeting people, but only earnestly exhorting them toward the pure karma of the Western Paradise. This continued for over ten years.

Zai. Many who were versed in both the black-robed and white-robed traditions held his character in high esteem. In the sixth month of the twenty-fourth year of the Jiaqing era, he suddenly desired to return to Mount Jiao;
although Master Cheng insisted on keeping him, he could not be persuaded. Less than a month after his return, he manifested slight illness.

On the morning of the twenty-sixth day of the eighth month, having requested a bath, he sat upright reciting the Buddha’s name as if entering meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). At the time of his cremation, auspicious clouds swirled across the sky. There was...

Light of five colors radiated upward from the base of the flames. He obtained three large grains of *śarīra*, as pure and lustrous as jade, which are currently enshrined at his native mountain. His worldly age was sixty-nine.
He composed one hundred poems on the Pure Land, which circulate in the world under the title *Ranxiang ji* (Anthology of Perfuming with Incense).

Master Xishi said: "The ancients held that one who is urgent in both the Mahāyāna vehicle (*yāna*) and the precepts (*śīla*) possesses the highest grade of rebirth. However, if one possesses the vehicle but lacks the precepts..."
They will flow into the realms of ghosts and spirits. Such is the source of upholding the precepts and such is the manner of combined cultivation;
is this not what is meant by "neither the vehicle nor the precepts being neglected"? Those who hold the wooden fish in contempt while engaging in lofty talk of Prajñā—alas, how perilous!

Zhengzheng Zhenzhen (字 Dazong), a native of Xiangtan County in Huguang, formerly studied under Master Zhao Yuezheng of Gaomin Temple. The gentry invited him to preside over the ancient monastery of Juefeng.
Upon his initial arrival, the walls were in ruin and the buildings were dilapidated; people could not endure the hardship. However, [he remained].

In truth, he was at ease. Before long, offerings for charity gathered in abundance, and all that had fallen into ruin was restored to newness. He successively constructed various halls and pavilions and further established several hundred *qǐng* of arable land.

Leading the assembly in the recitation of the Buddha’s name, he would not reject even those who came seeking the Dharma, however lowly or destitute they might be, instructing them instead in the Dharma-gate of holding the Name.
At that time, officials in high positions and gentry, as well as monastics and laypeople from near and far, all...
He served their ranks. The Grand Historian Yao Jifu and the Inspector Zhang Huishu were particularly supportive and protective of him.
One day, Huishu invited Zhen to sit together upon a couch and brought forth his two concubines, ordering them to receive the scriptures. Zhen said, "As for the method of receiving the scriptures..."
"One must set up a proper altar in the middle of the courtyard; only after burning incense and paying respectful homage may one proceed.

Otherwise, it is a violation of the Dharma. Huishu followed these instructions. Once he left his couch, the beam fell down and the couch was shattered. Huishu marveled at this and led his two concubines together to uphold the precepts.
Later, he dismissed the two concubines to become nuns. They cultivated the Pure Land with great diligence. Not long after, Zhen became resolute and retired into seclusion.

Zhi secluded himself from all external conditions and composed several stanzas on the Pure Land. On the ninth day of the first month of the first year of the Daoguang era, he instructed his dharma-heir, Tuo Fan, to visit his quarters.
They engaged in an extensive discussion regarding the joys of the Land of Peaceful Nurturing; Zhi’s countenance was harmonious and his spirit serene.

He then struck the fish-shaped gong to signal the time for reciting the Buddha’s name. He ordered Fan to go to the hall to eat congee. When Fan returned, Zhen had already passed away, dressed in new robes.
(Dyeing with Incense Collection). Regarding Donggua Wuheshang (Pumpkin Master):
his name was omitted [in records]; his surname was Sun. He was a native of Hangzhou. He was given this name because he was fond of eating pumpkins. He left the household life [to become a monk].
Huayan An was a man of profound silence. He would wander through the streets and markets all day long, regardless of cold or heat, for more than ten years, such that no one could fathom his purpose.
He was friends with the monk Huizhao of a neighboring hermitage. One month before he was to pass away, he told Huizhao:
On the sixth day of the New Year, I shall depart; you ought to come and see me off. When the appointed time arrived, the Master returned from a meal at Fahui Hermitage and saw Zhao already there.
"How have you come? he asked. Zhao smiled and said, "You made an appointment with me, so I came specifically to see you off.
The Master said, "Had it not been for your words, I would have almost forgotten. Thereupon, he bathed, changed into fresh clothes, and completed his prostrations before the Buddha.
He said to Zhao: "Now that you have set out on your journey, you must not be without a verse. Write one for me. The verse says:

"Throughout the day I wander the streets and alleys, My heart is busy with mindfulness of the Buddha. The people of this world do not recognize it; There is another heaven beyond. He passed away with a serene expression (*Ranxiang ji*).
Master Xi Shi said: "When the time arrived, he forgot his scheduled date of return; previously there was the testimony of his realization, and now we see it again.
How is it that his life and death are so self-possessed? Upon investigating the reason why he has reached this state, there is no other cause: it is because the mind is itself the Buddha."

Nowadays, people devote but a brief moment each day to the merit of reciting the Buddha’s name; moreover, they are unable to unify their minds upon the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), yet still hope for auspicious signs at the time of death—how difficult this is!

Dingji (定基), whose secular name was Linxiu (琳琇), was a native of Linhai. He entered the monastic order at Mount Tiantai. After receiving full ordination, he traveled extensively to visit various masters.
In his later years, he resided in a quiet chamber in Suzhou, where he remained in seclusion for nine years. He vowed never to consume salty flavors and drew blood from his own tongue to write.
He recited the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in eighty-one fascicles and made it his daily practice to chant the name of Amitābha Buddha.
In the first year of the Daoguang era, he traveled to Mount Mao to pay homage at the Aśoka Stūpa, offering incense from his arm as an offering.

Within the stūpa, two śarīra relics appeared—one yellow and one white—each as large as a lotus seed and so brilliant that they dazzled the eyes. Upon returning home, he contracted a malignant illness (gùjí) for which neither medicine nor treatment was effective. His fellow practitioners...
Zhengchao and Jie went to visit him. They exhorted him to practice single-mindedly by reciting the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth in the Pure Land.
Jie said, “So be it,” and immediately placed an image of the Buddha who Leads the Way before his bed. He then had the monks within the hermitage take turns reciting the Buddha’s name for seven days.
Suddenly, he rose from his seat, sought a bath, changed his clothes, and said, "Go quickly and invite Master Cheng to come. His disciples followed his instructions.
When Cheng arrived, Tanji expressed his gratitude, saying, "I was graced by your instruction to practice *nianfo*. This morning, I saw the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta leading me forward;

I have attained rebirth in the middle grade of the intermediate lotus. Thereupon, he closed his eyes, joined his palms, and passed away. The assembly smelled a wondrous fragrance that lingered for a long time.

Xi (Sheli Ruiying Lu). At the age of fifty-eight, Wuling—whose courtesy name was Yequn and whose style name was Huanru—was the son of the Jin family of Haichang in Zhejiang. From his youth, he possessed a spirit that transcended the mundane world.

Zhi would prostrate himself every time he saw the Buddha. By the age of nine, he became ill; he repeatedly petitioned his parents to allow him to leave the household life, and they granted his request.
He then shaved his head at the Western Wing of An-guo Temple in his home city and took the Venerable Xiang-long as his preceptor.
Subsequently, he received full ordination at Zhaoqing Temple in Hangzhou. At that time, Master Shitan Chun was opening a Nianfo Hall in Suzhou.

He resided by the flowing waters of Zhoushou, where Lingguo followed him with full devotion. Six times a day, he maintained his recitations without slackening. Furthermore, he performed prostrations word by word before the *Avataṃsaka*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Vajracchedikā*, and *Awakening of Faith* sutras.
Seeing that Lingguo’s spiritual foundation was firm and secure, Master Chun immediately conferred upon him the monastic robe and whisk.
Regarding the Dharma-gate of Pure Land, Lingguo believed with single-minded certainty. His father had passed away early; he exhorted his mother, Lady Zhou, to set out on the journey [to the West].
He made a vow that his mother would subsequently remain free from illness and pass away while reciting the Buddha’s name; her elder brother, Lianyin, was moved by this and left the household life.

After Master Chun passed away, Ling succeeded him at Nanchan Temple. After three years, he retired and resided at the Weituo Hermitage in Songjiang, a small retreat of only a few pillars where the clamor of the world could not reach.
He lived there together with Lianyin, making the recitation of the Buddha’s name their daily practice. Once, while in the midst of it...

During a night of meditative contemplation, he saw the myriad stars in the heavens gathering from the four directions to form the four characters "yi fo nian fo" (recalling and mindful of the Buddha).
These characters were several fathoms in size and shone with a brilliant, dazzling light. From that time on, his eyes became bright and luminous.

All who heard of this—monastics and laypeople alike, as well as farmers, merchants, and even cowherd boys—saw it and were moved to reverence; those who were inspired to practice mindfulness of the Buddha numbered no fewer than several [thousands].
One thousand people. Since Ling had dedicated his will to the practice of pure karma, he reflected upon those who had attained rebirth in the Pure Land from antiquity onward.

He noted that since the *Records of the Sages and Worthies of the Pure Land*, there had been no subsequent collections; yet, eminent individuals continued to appear, and it would be improper for them to remain submerged in obscurity without their legacy being transmitted.

Thereupon, he extensively gathered materials and conducted wide-ranging inquiries, compiling this *Jianxiang Ji* (Collection of Those Perfumed by Incense) in one volume. From the Jiaqing era onward, all those who were perfumed by the incense of the Dharma...
This Dharma gate has been recorded without omission. Five years later, the book was completed and carved for circulation in the world.
In the spring of the eighth year of the Daoguang era, he suffered from dysphagia. He gathered his monastic and lay friends and informed them that the time for his departure would not be long.

"I pray that you all will cherish yourselves and focus your minds on the recitation of the Buddha's name, so that we may meet again in the future. He composed a couplet for his portrait hall, which begins with the word "mud" (ni).
The ox’s bellowing causes the moon in the river’s heart to fall; the wooden horse neighs as it returns to the clouds over the sea.

Beyond medicine and treatment, he resolved his mind solely on returning to the West. In the fifth month, his illness grew severe. When people came to inquire after his health, he would say only, "The matter of birth and death is great;

each of you must exert yourselves," and then murmur the Buddha’s name. On the seventeenth day, facing west, he sat in the lotus posture and recited the name. Someone asked about what he would do at the moment of departure.
"What is the phrase? he asked. [The Master] replied, "Amitābha Buddha. After a long silence, his voice gradually grew faint;

he passed away peacefully at the age of sixty-one. He had sat in meditation for thirty-five summers. Three days after his death, the coffin was closed, and his countenance remained as if alive. (From the *Ranxiang xují*) Master Xishi said:
To lead his mother to rebirth in the Pure Land and to inspire his elder brother to leave the household life—this may be called the ultimate expression of filial piety and fraternal duty.
As for the appearance of characters formed by stars, this was simply the manifestation of the radiance of the mind resulting from the ultimate height of sincerity and devotion.
Those who cultivate the practice of purity should not harbor any doubt or hesitation regarding this.
Yuanrong Yuanrong (圓融圓融), whose secular name was Zhufeng (竺峰) and family name Yao (姚), was a native of Deqing County in Huzhou.

At the age of twenty, he left the household life and received the tonsure at Yanxia Temple on Shiwuling Hill in Hangzhou. He subsequently received full ordination at Zhaqing Vinaya Temple and maintained his precepts with steadfastness.
He was without flaw and was deeply devoted to the practice of mindfulness for the purpose of rebirth in the Pure Land as his definitive vow for this life.

He did not reside in a hermitage, but constantly relied upon others for his cultivation, believing that this would allow him to avoid the distraction of a cluttered mind. Furthermore, he did not dwell permanently in one place;
he remained where conditions were harmonious and departed when they were not. His spirit was free and easy, and he was not bound by dogmatic attachment. As for the places where he stayed:
He took no pleasure in following the crowd in worldly affairs, but constantly remained in quiet seclusion with his gates closed. He practiced both ritual prostrations and mindfulness in tandem:
when not prostrating, he was mindful; when not mindful, he was prostrating. There was not a single moment of interruption, nor did he ever introduce other methods as secondary practices.

He spent the remainder of his life devoted solely to these two matters. Once, during the midday of a certain day, while reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha, the sound of the fish bells rang out clearly and resonantly.
He should have spent the entire night, continuing until the late afternoon of the following day. People saw that he never ceased his practice and called out to him in loud voices;

only then did he stop. Yet he said to himself, "It has only been about half a day. When asked if he was hungry, he replied, "Sweet water like honey is constantly filling my mouth and I am always swallowing it;
my enjoyment is immeasurable, so I do not think of food at all. His side never touched the mat.
For several decades, he had few dreams. When he did dream, it was never apart from reverent mindfulness, nor were there any other distracting conditions.
Within his dreams, he constantly saw Buddhas and Bodhisattvas appearing as if alive and active, occasionally uttering words of encouragement.
At times, the Honored Deity Vaiśravaṇa would lead him in the practice of Buddha-recollection. Such was the nature of his dreams. In the third month of the tenth year of the Daoguang era.
On the nineteenth day, he passed away at Tianhua Monastery in the East Garden of Hangzhou. Several days prior, he had manifested a slight illness;
knowing that his time had come, he addressed a few words to the abbot and then remained silent, reciting mantras within himself without uttering any further words.
After his passing, the crown of his head was shown to remain warm. He was cremated at the Universal Stupa of Longqing Temple; as there was not much fragrant wood, it was completed in an instant.
The cremation was completed. His worldly lifespan was sixty-four years. He did not maintain a retinue.
(From the *Ranxiang Xují*) Master Xishi said: "To dwell in impermanence is true liberation; not to maintain a retinue is true purity.
That the cremation was swift and complete is surely a clear sign that he had no lingering attachment to worldly conditions.
Wukai (悟開), whose courtesy name was Huoxian (豁然) and style name was Shuiyun Daoren (水雲道人), was surnamed Zhang and a native of Mudu in Suzhou. Orphaned at a young age, he was intelligent and studious;
he took delight in the foundational learning of the Classics and Histories while remaining indifferent to fame and official rank. As his family was poor, he abandoned the Confucian path.

One day, Jia saw a monk carrying on his back the *Jingshe Shengsi Wenju* (The Text on Awakening from Birth and Death) while walking through the marketplace selling fish, urging people to recite the Buddha’s name.

He was suddenly and profoundly awakened, whereupon he received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts. Subsequently, he took leave of his family and went to receive the tonsure under Master Wen of Xiangfeng.
He then received full ordination from Master Rujian of Gaomin, remaining there to observe the summer and winter retreats, where he engaged in intensive inquiry and diligent practice.
He investigated suffering but could not enter it. One day, by chance, he stepped upon it and broke through; the iron shoe was gone, leaving no trace.

He attained the saying, "To come forth fully costs no effort," which is the fundamental phrase of inquiry. Suddenly, everything became vast and clear. He then further studied the enigmatic *kōans* of the ancient worthies.
He reported everything truthfully and completely. He subsequently established the Dharma at Xianqin Temple in Jingnan, but retired from his post before long.
He traveled through various places such as Yunjian, Lianchuan, and Zhixing, all of which were by watersides or beneath forested slopes.

Whenever he undertook construction or repairs and offerings were insufficient, he would empty his own alms-bag; if he could not remain in a place, he would pack up and depart without any sense of attachment. Later—
He returned to reside at Baozang-an on Mount Lingyan. Wherever he went, laypeople who were converted to his teachings were especially numerous.

He took the Pure Land as his ultimate goal and authored the *Hundred Questions on Buddha-Recitation* to instruct future students. He inscribed a verse for himself, saying: "With a heart of great compassion, I propagate the Dharma of Buddha-recitation;
I look up to the Honored Ones of the Triple Gem, entreating their compassionate protection. By means of this firefly’s light..."
