Light transforms into the lamp of wisdom, illuminating the world; it leads one deep into the Buddha. Recalling the Buddha, may I vow to go and sit [in meditation];
returning, I shall deliver all sentient beings. In the West, never to regress, until the attainment of Bodhi.

In the tenth year of the Daoguang era, during the summer, he fell ill. He sent a letter to his friends far away, earnestly exhorting them that the matter of birth and death is of great importance. Furthermore—
There was a statement that he would return to the West at the end of autumn. Having completed all matters pertaining to his permanent residence in due order, he ceased taking medicine and food.

At dawn on the twentieth day of the ninth month, he sat in the lotus position facing west; with palms joined, he recited the Śūraṅgama-mantra until its conclusion, followed by the invocation of the Buddha’s name and the name of Avalokiteśvara.
After a long while, his voice grew faint, and he passed away suddenly. This occurred exactly two days before the commencement of the season of "Beginning of Winter. On the following day...
He was placed in the shrine; the crown of his head remained warm. Several hundred people who escorted him all offered words of praise (*Ranxiang xuji: Nianfo baiwen*).
Fang Hai, whose courtesy name was Puteng and style name Xitai, was surnamed Cui and a native of Wucheng in Huzhou. At the age of twenty-one, he entered [the monastic order].

He underwent tonsure at Huading Temple on Mount Tiantai and subsequently received full ordination from Chan Master Ji Yun of Qingliang Temple, where he devoted himself to reading the Tripitaka and became thoroughly versed in all the treatises.
Later, he took up residence at Beidu Hermitage in Suzhou, where he single-mindedly promoted the Pure Land teachings and widely exhorted both monastics and laypeople;

those who followed him with faith and devotion were very numerous. Subsequently, he encountered the deaths of both his parents, during which time he performed daily prostrations to the Avatamsaka Sutra.

Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and various Mahāyāna sūtras, he dedicated his merits on behalf of his relatives. Throughout his life, he composed countless poems on the Pure Land and transcribed numerous sūtras and śāstras.
In the seventh month of the twenty-first year of the Daoguang era, he suddenly said to others, "Within this month, I shall depart.
Entrust all my unfulfilled vows to you. The following day he fell ill; on the twenty-seventh day, he beheld a banner.
A banner fluttered and beckoned, and he said, "The Buddha has come to welcome me. He asked for a brush and composed a verse, leaning over his desk and writing rapidly:
"For seventy years, dreams and illusions have been many; A single phrase from Amitābha has exhausted them all. Now I enter directly into the stage of the Tathāgata;

With both emptiness and existence forgotten, I pay homage to Potalaka. Thereupon, he cast aside his brush and passed away. His secular age was seventy, and his monastic seniority was forty-nine. (From the *Xiyu*)
*Taiseng Gao*). Changmao, whose style name was Zaijing, was a native of Shaoxing. At the age of twenty-five, he entered the monastic order at Jixiantang in Nanhai.
He went before the Śarīra stūpa at Mount Mao and burned his finger as an offering to the Buddha. He traveled extensively to visit masters and sages at famous mountains.
In his later years, he resided at Songyun Hermitage in Suzhou, where he devoted his entire life to making offerings to Amitābha Buddha and Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.

Whenever he encountered people, he spoke of cause and effect and exhorted them to practice the Pure Land path; those who took refuge in him numbered in the thousands. Throughout his life, he never failed to perform the *yankou* (flaming-mouth) ritual for hungry ghosts, saying:
Because he lacked virtuous conduct, he accepted silver coins from others, giving them away as soon as he received them.

He had carved several editions of Buddhist scriptures, as well as works such as the *Wanshan tonggui* (The Convergence of Myriad Good Deeds), and he also cast three large bells. He made a vow to deliver sentient beings from the hells.
On the twenty-third night of the first month in the twenty-eighth year of the Daoguang era, he suddenly fell ill with a stomach ailment; knowing that his end was near, he paid homage to the Buddha.
He recited the sutras with even greater diligence and strictness. He sent word to invite his disciple [Name] to come.
When it was nearly midnight, the attendant urged him to wait until dawn. He replied, "The White Bodhisattva has arrived; I shall certainly depart at the fourth watch.

Without ceasing, he recited the Buddha’s name from his mouth. He ordered that he be bathed and changed his robes. Indeed, at the fourth watch, he sat upright and passed away at the age of eighty-three.
Upon cremation, over ten grains of ash-colored śarīra were obtained. (Recorded by Wang Yinxuan. The Western Historian says:
People suspected that the White Bodhisattva was an impermanent evil spirit; thus, when the Master passed away in the West, those who doubted him and those who believed in him were each half.
I have previously heard the Master say: "The spirits of the rivers, the canals, the altars of land and grain, do not dare to arrogantly receive the [offerings of] the Bodhisattva..."
Regarding the title of "Sakyamuni": if even a deity is not [to be taken as] such, how much less so a ghost? As for the one called Bai (White), he was likely an emanation of Avalokiteśvara;
observing his peaceful composure when relinquishing his life and comparing it with his lifelong conduct, there is no doubt that he attained rebirth in the Pure Land.

The General Discourse states: Since the teachings and practices of the Lotus School (Lianzong) have spread, those among the determined who have heard its influence and turned toward its transformation have been numerous.

Yet, while those who recite the Buddha’s name are as thick as cow hair, those who achieve rebirth in the Pure Land are as rare as the horn of a unicorn. To investigate the root of this ailment, it is simply because their faith, practice, and vows lack earnestness.
As for the aforementioned masters, some clarify the "upward" direction with the perfect integration of principle and phenomena, while others specialize in the Pure Land...
If one acts with firmness in precepts and patience, one will ultimately transcend saṃsāra and ascend to the realm of the sages. How profound is his skill in guiding future generations!
As for those whose bodies are śramaṇas but whose minds are not, how could they not feel shame and exert themselves upon seeing this?
The Second Nun of Lake Upper who Attained Rebirth: Regarding the nun of Lake Upper, her personal history is unknown.
She was extremely devout and meticulous in her recitation of the Buddha’s name and the sutras, and she maintained the precepts with rigorous discipline. There was...
The practitioner came once every year; when he arrived, they would engage in long discussions for days before he departed.
One day, the nun made an appointment with the practitioner in advance, but he did not arrive as expected. She declared that she was about to pass away and could not bear to part from this friend.
She waited for several more days, but he still did not come. She then ordered a palanquin to be placed upon a broken bridge and took a single stick of incense in her hand.
He entered the shrine with composure. Shortly thereafter, fire broke out and he spontaneously burned himself to death. Spectators gathered like a wall around him;
even when his body had already turned charred black, the sound of his reciting the Buddha’s name did not cease. (From *The Commentary on the Text of Yin and Deeds* by He Shiyan)
Benyin (also known as Zisongqi) was a native of Wu County. Having suffered from many illnesses since childhood, he made a vow to renounce the household life.
At the age of twenty-five, his parents escorted him to the city, where he received the tonsure at Yuan Tong’an and subsequently received full ordination. He then purchased several rooms of his own.
He resided there in a place named Guanhuan (Contemplating Illusions). His observance of the precepts was pure and clear, and he diligently cultivated meritorious deeds.

He visited various famous monasteries, making offerings to the Buddhas and providing meals for the Sangha, dedicating the merit toward rebirth in the Pure Land. In the eighth month of the forty-fifth year of the Qianlong era, he returned from Jiuhua Mountain and established a retreat to perform the Great Compassion Repentance.
When barely two weeks had passed, he suddenly felt a slight ailment and said, "Is my life’s karmic connection coming to an end? Thereupon...

He ceased his repentance rituals and focused exclusively on reciting the Buddha’s name. By the beginning of the tenth month, he lay upon his bed for seven days, reclining on his right side facing west, recollecting the Buddha without interruption.
Thereafter, having settled his final affairs, he commanded his disciples to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
When they had completed three recitations, he passed away in silence. (From the *Xifang gongju jiyàn*)

Suqin, whose courtesy name was Yuecheng, was a native of Wuxi. He entered the monastic order at the age of nine. Upon reaching maturity, he encountered a nun who inspired him to focus exclusively on the recitation of the Buddha’s name, practicing it without interruption whether walking or standing.
He subsequently resided at the Baiyi Hermitage in Nanyuan, Suzhou, where he restored the temple hall.
In the Hall. He was diligent in the practice of *nienfo* (Buddha-recitation). At the age of fifty, he first received full ordination (*upasampadā*).

By the age of fifty-five, in the third month of that year, at the first crowing of the cock, he summoned his disciples and said, "I am about to depart. His disciples replied, "The Master has no ailment; why do you speak such words? Thereupon, they wept. Zhiqin said, "Fools!
What benefit is there in weeping for me? It is enough to take Buddha-recitation as your true task. He then sat in the lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).

He sat facing west. They all recited the name of the Buddha together until the incense wick was exhausted, at which point he passed away. This event occurred in the fifty-third year of the Qianlong era (as recorded in the *Xifang gongju jiyàn*).

Lüzong Lüzong (Lüzong Lüzong). His courtesy name was Shengke. He was a native of Jiading. Having lost his mother at the age of three, his grandmother took him to the Yuantong Hermitage in Suzhou, where he subsequently shaved his head, received full ordination, and became a monk.
In his youth, he delighted in prostrating before the Buddha; as he grew older, he recited the Lotus Sūtra, though he found it difficult to master.

Having mastered the meaning of the teachings, he traveled to Mount Jin and Chongfu Temple in Hangzhou, where he engaged in intensive study and investigation for several winters. Upon returning home, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism.
He visited various famous mountains on numerous occasions to make offerings to the Buddhas and provide meals for the monastics. At the age of fifty-three, he contracted a coughing illness;

consequently, he closed his retreat quarters and did not emerge, making the Western Paradise his ultimate goal. When he reached the age of sixty-four, on the full moon of the first lunar month, he gathered the assembly of monastics and laypeople together.
He called upon the name of the Buddha until mid-afternoon. Looking around at those beside him, he exhorted them to persevere in their practice with words that were most earnest and poignant.
Then, raising his hand, he called out three times: "In the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful Amitābha Buddha!"

He passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. The fragrance of lotuses filled the room. This event occurred in the fifty-fifth year of the Qianlong era (as recorded in the *Xifang gongju jiyàn*).
By Fochi.
Fochi, whose courtesy name was Jilian, was a native of Changzhou County. From his youth, he had no desire for the household life.

Upon reaching adulthood, his mother sent him outside the Chang Gate to Yuhua Hermitage, where he shaved his head and received the full precepts. Subsequently, he resided at Chongfo Hermitage within the city.

She entrusted [the temple] to Nido Jian, who succeeded her as the abbess. She raised over a thousand taels of gold to commission sandalwood statues of the Three Holy Ones of the Western Paradise, eight feet in height.
Every year, she established a seven-day retreat, gathering monks of pure conduct to hold a Buddha-recitation assembly.

She traveled to various famous mountains to make offerings to the Buddhas and provide meals for the monastics. Furthermore, she established thirty mu of land for Tiantong Temple in Changzhou. In her later years...
He was single-mindedly cultivating pure karma. Three days before his passing, he saw the Bodhisattva manifest before him, attended by two youths.

At times, he remarked on the fragrance of chrysanthemums; Qí said, "This is the fragrance of the blue lotus. On the final day of the eighth month in the fifty-sixth year of the Qianlong era, a laywoman came to inquire after his illness.
Qí had her helped up, gathered the assembly to burn incense, and led them in reciting the Buddha’s name for about two [hours].

Discussing matters within the inner quarters to dispel the silence; people say this evening is the Lantern Festival. Having finished reciting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, there is nothing more to do;

with a resonant strike upon the zither, we speak of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Beneath the lotus feet, [the mark] is as large as a wheel; the spring breeze by the Yi River—

Do not lament that news from Huayuan has been cut off; by the stream, spring remains as full as ever.

He also commissioned an artist to paint a diagram of the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), based entirely upon the three Pure Land sutras. Regarding the adornments of both the environment and the inhabitants, he revised the draft four times over the course of half a year.
It was thus completed. He inscribed a verse himself, saying: "If one wishes to thoroughly understand All Buddhas of the three periods of time, One should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm:
All things are created solely by the mind. I read this verse from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and entered the gate of the Pure Land through faith.
By virtue of the pure vows of all Buddhas, wondrous adornments are accomplished. These pure vows are like space, not rejecting any variety of forms; they possess boundless merit.
Water wells up, manifesting precious lotus flowers; upon each flower dwells a sentient being, each endowed with the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Precious ponds and jeweled trees surround precious railings, while tiered and exquisite pavilions fill the entire realm of empty space.

Some bathe in flowing streams of fragrant water, some enjoy supreme and wondrous flavors, some sit cross-legged or walk in meditation, some recite sutras or listen to the Dharma, and some carry [offerings] in their robes and baskets.
Flowers are offered to the Buddhas of the ten directions or to assemblies of superior sages; having completed these acts, one enters the Bodhimanda.
There, flocks of birds join with celestial music to emit harmonious and elegant sounds. From hearing, one proceeds to reflection and cultivation, transcending all in a single thought-moment.

How much more so for those of Immeasurable Life, who sit peacefully upon jeweled lotus pedestals; their clouds of compassion cover humans and devas, raining down the universal moisture upon all faculties, so that upon hearing the Dharma, they attain liberation.
Liberated, they proceed directly to the stage of the next successor to Buddhahood. Such acts of benefit—how can their limits ever be fathomed by thought?
It is like that painter who, through the transformation of a single mind, manifests this abode of the Jewel King without departing from the tip of a single hair;
yet it is neither I nor anyone else. One is omnipresent within all. Both the painting and the person who painted it ultimately do not exist at all. May those who see or hear of this [realize this].
As for this: "Just as I have resolved my mind, by relying on the merit of this single thought-moment, I shall personally attain the stage of non-retrogression;

what need is there to speak of ten thousand billion stages? They are all fully present right where one is. Furthermore, I take pity on sentient beings of the Final Dharma age who lack the correct eye and thus collide with one another.
He composed the *Treatise on Resolving Doubts Concerning the One Vehicle* to bridge the barriers between Confucianism and Buddhism;

The world has widely transmitted and recited these accounts. Furthermore, he once pooled ten thousand taels of gold, managing its lending and borrowing to establish Buddhist temples, carve out the scriptures of the teachings, and provide meals for the monastic community.

He opened the Qinqu Hall (Hall for Assisting the Needy) to aid those in poverty, established "kinship-sustaining fields" to support impoverished clans, organized relief assemblies to assist widows, and instituted "releasing life" assemblies to preserve the lives of all creatures; each of these undertakings had its own [purpose].

On the morning of the twentieth day of the first month of the first year of the Jiaqing era, he composed a verse on his departure from this world, saying: "Appearing and disappearing within the dust-motes of Jambudvīpa..."

He then turned westward, sat in the lotus posture, and passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name. This occurred precisely on the day the imperial seal was opened at the government office. He was fifty-seven years old.

The Master Xi Shi said: "I have heard that two forests are not as good as one forest; it is better to leave Mount Lu for Mount Xi.
I privately found this statement profoundly true. Upon reading the writings of Yi Xing, I marveled at how his choices regarding what to abandon and what to pursue were so appropriate.
Reading the *Jueyi lun* and the *Nianfo lun*, I realized there is neither one nor two, neither self nor other, and I was suddenly left feeling a sense of profound disillusionment."
Lü Weiruo was a native of Qiantang.

He delighted in goodness and was fond of charity, and he was devoted to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism. For over twenty years, he maintained a vegetarian diet (*ka-su*) and recited his liturgical prayers morning and night without interruption.
On the first day of the second month in the third year of the Jiaqing era, he fell ill. At that time, Zhang Quan of the Xiao River...
On business, he arrived in Hangzhou and stayed at his family home. One night, he dreamed of a monk sitting in meditation in the courtyard chanting the Buddha’s name.
He asked the monk, “What is the purpose of reciting the Buddha’s name? The monk replied, “Lu [name] possesses roots of goodness; before long, he shall return to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Do you not know this? Upon waking, he found the dream extraordinary. At dawn, he told his son Wenyan, who said with a somber expression, “My father, in the first month...”
In the latter part of the month, he entrusted his final affairs, stating that he would attain rebirth in the Pure Land on the seventh day of the second month.
That his dream was thus true is now evident. On the sixth day, his bedroom was filled with the fragrance of lotuses, which did not dissipate throughout the night.
At dawn the following day, the fragrance became even more intense. She declared, "Amitābha Buddha and all the Bodhisattvas have arrived.
Thereupon, she sat cross-legged with palms joined, chanted the name of the Buddha, and passed away. Zhang Quan composed a biography for her (in the *Ranxiang ji*).
Zeng Geng was a native of Baoshan, Jiangsu. He was the son of the Inspector Yin Xian. Having passed the Xianliang examination in his prime, he did not seek official office.
He delighted in goodness and took pleasure in charity, especially in the practice of releasing living beings (*fangsheng*). His household strictly abstained from slaughter; a monk bestowed upon him—

His recitation of the Buddha’s name became even more earnest. On the second day of the tenth month, he told his family members, "The time of my departure is today.
You should all recite the Buddha’s name for me; do not let me know of any other matters. He then rose of his own accord and wrote a letter.

Having entrusted his final affairs to his preceptor, Master Zhizhao, he passed away after an hour had elapsed, while his family burned incense and he maintained a state of right mindfulness with palms joined (from the *Ranxiang ji*).
Lü Xiqiao, whose name was passed down by his characters, was a native of Suzhou. In his youth he possessed great talent, yet he was repeatedly rejected in the provincial examinations.

Consequently, he resolutely conceived the aspiration for transcendence and, together with his wife, Lady Zhou, cultivated the Pure Land practice. He had only one daughter, who remained unmarried at his side.
One day, while ill at Xiqiao Bridge, she said to Zhou Shi, "In seven days I shall depart. Do not let my daughter know;
I fear her weeping would disturb her correct mindfulness. Zhou Shi replied, "I agree. When the appointed time arrived, she bathed, changed her clothes, and sat upright facing west.
As she recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* to the passage concerning the white cranes and peacocks, she raised her head and gazed upward.
When he saw something [unusual], he would depart in silence. This occurred during the sixth and seventh years of the Jiaping era (1726–1727) (*Records of Recent Verifications of Rebirth*).

Ling Shu, whose courtesy name was Jiren, was a student of the local school in Lou County, Songjiang Prefecture. He delighted in expounding upon the Learning of Nature and Principle (*Xingli*), and his words and deeds were sincere and steadfast.
Liṅ Shushi was indeed respected by his fellow villagers. In his later years, upon reading the *Yunqi Fahui* (The Collected Teachings of Yunqi), he developed faith in the Buddha.

He frequently sat in meditation reciting the Buddha’s name, maintaining a fixed daily practice morning and evening. At that time, most people in Songjiang were unaware of the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation;
Liṅ Shushi championed it, and those who followed his lead soon became numerous. In the autumn of the twelfth year of the Jiaqing era, he fell ill and said to his relatives, "I am departing."
"I must take advantage of the fine moonlight on the Mid-Autumn Festival. On the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival, he indeed passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name;
at that time, the moon was as bright as day (*Ranxiang ji*).

Shenchang, courtesy name Zilin, was a martial arts student from Wuxing during the Yuanhe era. By nature, he was grave and serene, supporting himself by teaching children. Subsequently, he turned his heart toward the Pure Land;

whenever there was a seven-day period for reciting the Buddha’s name, he would invariably participate. During the intervals between his teaching duties and at the end of each year, he would invariably...
While residing at Nanchan Temple practicing *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation), he suddenly said to his son one day, "I wish to return home.
His son was surprised by this, and the following day he manifested a slight illness. He summoned several śramaṇas to assist him in recitation, and with palms joined, he passed away.
There was also a layman named Gu who likewise resided at Nanchan Temple practicing *nianfo*. He departed first; at the time of his western return, all the family members heard the sound of lotuses.
Flowers and incense were prepared as he wished to invite monks to assist with his final recitations. The layman said, "There is no need; I have already sat within a lotus flower.
I see the Buddha emitting light that illuminates me. Since I am now within that light, there is no need for lamps or candles.

Thus, after three days, he passed away in auspiciousness. The fragrance did not dissipate until three days later. This account is recorded in the *Jiaqing 15th Year [Record]* (contained in the *Xigui Jianwen Lu*).

Jiang Guimeng was a native of Kuaiji. In his prime, he traveled through various regions serving in official retinues. He delighted in performing acts of goodness and paid particular attention to the Pure Land school.
The recitation hall at Lengyan Temple in Jiaxing and the society for releasing living beings were both established by him and his companions during his later years.

He returned home and constructed three pure rooms as a place for his dwelling. Within them, he enshrined an image of Amitābha Buddha and daily recited the Great Name (Nianfo) one hundred thousand times, doing so without interruption for several years.
In the [blank] month of the sixteenth year of the Jiaqing era, he knew in advance that the time had arrived.
Three days before his passing, he took leave of all his relatives and friends; on the appointed day, he invited ten monks to the quiet room to perform recitations.

The Buddha sat cross-legged in the courtyard. The assembly circumambulated him while reciting his name. As the sun was about to reach its zenith, just as they were offering incense, he passed away with palms joined (from the *Ranxiang ji*).

Cao Shengyou of Jiaxian suffered from a wind-related illness that left his hands and feet paralyzed. He traveled to Tianzhu in Hangzhou to offer incense and made a vow before the Buddha to seek rebirth through the recitation of the Buddha’s name, pledging never to turn back from this resolve.
From then on, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he focused on the Buddha.
The chanting did not cease. Whenever his thoughts reached a point of intense urgency, he would inevitably weep bitterly with tears streaming down. This continued for ten years.

On the eleventh day of the seventh month in the sixteenth year of the Jiaqing era, he instructed his son to go to Diquan Monastery in Beigang and invite six monks to come to the house to recite the Buddha’s name.
On the fourteenth day, the monks arrived. Shengyou said, "I shall depart for the West on the sixteenth day; please [recite the Buddha's name for me]."

The Master and others assisted him for three days; his gratitude was profound. Beginning from that very day, he recited ten sticks of incense daily, alternating between walking and sitting meditation.
His spiritual friend followed him every day. On the evening of the sixteenth, while sitting in meditation, the incense had barely reached two inches when he passed away (*Ranxiang ji*).
Master Xishi said: "In the past, people who recited the Buddha's name would weep and shed tears of bitter grief; nowadays, however, they do so merely to curry favor and purchase fame.
Even if they are courageous for a time, they soon lapse back into negligence and laxity. That effort is great yet achievement is meager is due to this very cause. Be cautious!"
Feng Tinggui, Feng Tinggui. A native of Yuanhe in Suzhou, he received and upheld the five precepts.

He once practiced at Pufu Chan Monastery, prostrating himself before the *Avataṃsaka* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras one thousand times daily, without ceasing through cold or heat. Later, while residing at Nanchan, he continued his practice in the same manner.

In his leisure time from studying the sutras, he never ceased reciting the Buddha’s name. In this manner, for over twenty years, in the spring of the eighteenth year of the Jiaqing era, he preternaturally knew that his time had come.
He took leave of all his relatives and friends and passed away peacefully while reciting the Buddha’s name. A wondrous fragrance lingered for three days (*Ranxiang ji*).
Pu Wenrong was a native of Wujiang. In his middle age, he took refuge with the monk Xiangqian of Jiedai Temple and received the five precepts.
He resolved to recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land. For several decades, he never ceased his daily recitation of the Buddha’s name. He had two sons.
Once he had left home, Xu Jiang Chan Monastery was also frequently visited by his father’s residence. Father, son, and brothers were of one mind in reciting the Buddha’s name.
In the eighteenth year of the Jiaqing era, Wenrong reached the age of seventy; feeling a slight illness, he knew that the time had come.

He instructed his two sons to join him in chanting the Buddha’s name, and with palms joined, he passed away. An extraordinary fragrance filled the room, which did not dissipate for the entire day (from the *Ranxiang ji*).
Zheng Zhaorong, courtesy name Tingxun, was a native of Shengze in Wujiang. From his youth, he was devoted to the practice of benevolence at Qiaizhai.

The man urgently sought deliverance, and the spirit said, "If you wish to extinguish your transgressions, you must consult with the virtuous man Xu Da-jun; only then may it be done. Upon waking, the man acted according to these words and was thus granted release.

As for Xu Da-jun, he had long cultivated pure karma. Zhao Rong was his close relative. Upon hearing of these matters, Zhao Rong came to believe in and turn toward the practice of Buddha-recitation (*nienfo*).
He gradually increased his efforts and, with a sense of deep resolve, donated ten thousand pieces of gold to establish a Hall of Goodness (*shantang*) to relieve the poor and distressed.
He dedicated his merits toward rebirth in the Pure Land. When guests arrived, he had no other business and would not exchange a single word with them.

In his later years, he personally prepared a long-finished cypress coffin for sale. Carrying a rosary and some coins, he would frequent the quarters of the poor, encouraging them to recite the Buddha’s name.

Even when encountering the bitter cold of midwinter, he did not hesitate to take off his own garments to clothe others, regardless of the cost. This was in the twelfth month of the eighteenth year of the Jiaqing era.

He was afflicted with a slight illness. On the day of the full moon, his son wished to take leave of him to travel elsewhere. Zhao Rong said, "If you go, you must return quickly; I shall depart on this very day.

In his early thirties, his family was poor, so he made his living as a tutor. Even when he ranked first in examinations, he showed no sign of joy. He once said to those who knew him:

This occurred on the twenty-third day of the second month in the nineteenth year of the Jiaqing era (*Ranxiang ji*).
Shen Tingyu, Shen Tingyu.

A native of Beiban in Jiaxing. By nature upright and prudent, he would always personally attend to whatever task he encountered. Yet, he would chant Buddhist verses aloud with a steady and unceasing flow.
Although people might laugh at him, he paid no heed to them whatsoever. He continued in this manner for several decades.
He himself said, "The more I practice mindfulness of the Buddha, the more proficient I become; the more I engage in worldly affairs, the more detailed and clear my understanding becomes.
At the age of seventy-three, manifesting a slight illness, he suddenly said to his family members, "The Buddha is coming. Light a candle for me. He personally burned incense and passed away.
This was the nineteenth day of the third month in the nineteenth year of the Jiaqing era (1814). (*Ranxiang ji*)
Master Xi Shi said: "The more one becomes proficient in the practice of nianfo (buddha-recitation), the more detailed and clear one’s handling of affairs will become.

This is truly the state where movement and stillness are as one, having entered deeply into samādhi. Those who devote their minds to fame and profit say that when dealing with worldly matters their minds are distracted and they have no leisure for nianfo;
yet when the moment of birth and death arrives, they must let go empty-handed. Who is to blame for this?"
Shi Jingyan of Huating was a man of upright character and meticulous conduct. Whenever he planned for others, he would always exert his utmost sincerity, and many among his relatives relied upon him.
In the spring of the twenty-third year of the Jiaqing era, he fell ill; medicinal treatments proved ineffective, and by the summer, his condition had worsened.
The illness worsened. His cousin, Zheng Huizhan, came to visit him. Feeling pity for him, he said, "Your younger brother’s illness is critical. Why do you not recite the name of Amitābha Buddha?
The sutras state that even ten recitations at the moment of death can lead to rebirth in the Pure Land. Jingyan replied, "I regret that throughout my life I did not know how to practice nianfo;
now I am unable to recite it. What is to be done? He then wept bitterly. Huizhan said, "It does not matter, younger brother."
"Listen to my thought; you may visualize it within your mind. He then chanted the Buddha’s name clearly and loudly, and Jingyan also recited along with him in a high voice.
After only a few dozen invocations, he suddenly said, "Amitābha Buddha and the various Bodhisattvas are mostly before my eyes.
Having finished speaking, he passed away (*Ranxiang ji*).

Zhang Xiaolin, whose style name was Lùquán, was a native of Huátíng. He served the Buddha with great devotion and delighted in giving alms; there was no one who came to him in distress whom he did not assist.
Daily, he recited the *Vajracchedikā*, the *Amitābha*, and other sutras, while also maintaining ten thousand recitations of the Buddha’s name. In the twentieth year of the Jiāqìng era...
In the third year, he rose at dawn and told his family members, "I have dreamed that a lotus flower has blossomed.
On a certain night in the first month of the following year, he lit incense and faced west, chanting the *Amitābha Sūtra* and the *Heart Sūtra* each once aloud. He then performed three prostrations.
He sat cross-legged with palms joined, silently reciting the Buddha’s name. At midnight, he passed away with a smile on his face. A rare fragrance filled the room.
Previously, the fourth son of Xiaolin, named Jizhong, had followed his father in practicing the Pure Land path. He distributed alms to relieve the needy just as Xiaolin had done;

he maintained an extremely frugal lifestyle for himself, never wearying of vegetarian food throughout the year. He was filial toward his parents, and when his mother died, his grief was so profound that it emaciated him to the bone.

He stood up and vomited several sheng of blood, saying, "My father has three elder brothers; I am going. He then sat in the full lotus posture before his mother’s coffin and silently recited the Buddha’s name.
After three days, he passed away while holding his prayer beads. This was recorded in the local gazetteer (*Ranxiang ji*).
Fanggang, whose courtesy name was Tiehua, was a student at the school in Huating. He maintained a close spiritual friendship with the abbot of Liansheng Monastery and Xuan’an.

Understanding the Dharma gate of Buddha-recitation, he subsequently observed a lifelong vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha’s name with diligence for several years. In the twenty-third year of the Jiaqing era...
In the autumn of that year, he fell ill. Knowing that he would not recover, he ceased eating and took only water. He instructed his younger brother to invite Xuan’an for a night conversation, saying:
"I have received the Master’s instruction on the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation and have practiced according to it. Now, on the fifteenth day, I shall depart.

Because my mind is filled with gratitude and cannot leave, I have invited you for this parting talk. I hope you will come on that day to assist me. When the appointed time arrived, [the brother] came as requested.
He then dictated a couplet: "The ten recitations are worthy of reliance; do not let slip the single thought at the moment of death.
Sentient beings are pitiable; first settle one's own three lives. When the appointed time arrived, Xuan’an came. Gang said, "A short while ago, I saw the Great Monk (the Buddha) coming to welcome me.
You should quickly burn incense and recite the Buddha’s name a thousand times, and then I shall depart. The assembly chanted the Buddha’s name, and he indeed arrived.
A thousand voices. With palms joined, he closed his eyes (*Ranxiang ji*).
Pan Wanzong, Pan Wanzong, a native of Liqing Port in Wujiang, lost his son in middle age; he gave rise to the aspiration for transcendence and traveled to the South Sea.
At Mount Foding, Wan Zong requested ordination from Master Cangwu. Master Wu said, "You have a mother living; it is not yet appropriate.
Furthermore, cultivation does not depend on leaving the household life. It is sufficient to find a good friend and practice constant熏習 (xūnxí—spiritual permeation).

You may stop now. Later in life, Wan Zong maintained a lifelong vegetarian fast and served the Buddha. His lower body had long suffered from a scabies-like ailment, which suddenly spread to his head and face at this time. It was extremely severe.
He was deeply distressed and intended to drown himself. His friend from beyond the secular world, Dingchuan, stopped him, saying: "Illness arises from karma, and karma originates from the mind.
If you harbor resentment and sink into the waves, then the roots of delusion will be firmly planted, leading to even greater suffering in future lives; can you not fear this?
If you can instead repent, take self-reproach, and endure according to conditions, it will further your spiritual cultivation. Thus, calamity becomes the foundation for blessings."
Therefore, the sutras praise the practice of right mindfulness, noting that it is especially vital at the moment of death; this is solely because the power of the mind is inconceivable.

At the mere mention of the myriad teachings, he attained sudden enlightenment. From then on, his recitation of the Buddha’s name became even more diligent. One year later, his illness was completely cured.
In the middle summer of the twenty-fourth year of the Jiaqing era, he saw oil-colored clouds swirling above the door of his pure chamber, partially revealing a gourd.
The reeds emitted a radiant light, which he observed with private wonder. On the first day of the tenth month of that year, he manifested a slight illness.

Three days later, having bathed and changed his robes, he sat upright upon a rope bed and instructed his wife to assist him in reciting the Buddha’s name. After some time, he passed away peacefully. His wife cremated his clothes;
after the fire was extinguished, three images of the Holy Ones appeared within the ashes, their features distinct and the folds of their robes perfectly formed. Furthermore—
On the day of his soul-summoning ritual, he produced a single undershirt; upon the ashes appeared dozens of large characters, all of a crimson hue.
Alas, they were swept away by an ignorant person. People from far and near marveled at this wonder. He was sixty-six years old (*Jianxiang ji*).
Shen Shuhua, style name Zhucha, was a *xiaolian* (honorary graduate) from Qiantang. From her youth, she had revered and placed her faith in the Triple Gem and practiced virtuous deeds with diligence.

She frequently carved Buddhist scriptures and various virtuous texts for printing and distribution, and she was especially earnest in her practice of abstaining from killing and releasing captive animals. She devoted herself wholeheartedly to these matters.
He traveled about. In his middle years, he received the five precepts and observed the long fast while serving the Buddha, dedicating his mind solely to the Pure Land.
He recited the name of Amitābha fifty thousand times every day without interruption for several decades. Later, he was selected for a teaching post in Ning County, but he declined and did not go.

He painted a figure of himself sitting cross-legged upon a lotus pedestal to manifest his resolve. One night at the fifth watch, he suddenly beheld a brilliant light within his room and thought it was dawn.

He rose immediately to prostrate himself. After a short while, it grew dark again. This continued for half a month. One morning, as he was just finishing his recitation, he felt his body become exhausted;
nevertheless, he continued to silently hold the Buddha’s name without ceasing. On the following evening, with palms joined, he passed away.
This occurred on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month in the twenty-fourth year of the Jiaqing era (from the *Ranxiang ji*).
The Master Xi Shi remarked: "In antiquity, there were those for whom the radiance of a mirror appeared at the top of a wall, and those for whom the light of the moon appeared atop a stupa.
The *Wangsheng ji* (Anthology of Rebirth) describes these as clear evidence of the body and mind becoming translucent and pure. Might the luminosity within the room not be of this same nature?"
Shen Yuzun, a native of Mazhuang on the shores of Lake Zhenzhai, maintained his daily recitation of the Buddha’s name from childhood until old age without interruption.
On the day before his death, he summoned all his relatives and friends to bid them farewell. When the appointed time arrived, he bathed, changed his robes, and went outside to sit.
In the hall, she passed away while joining her palms in prayer and reciting the Buddha’s name. At the time of her death, a wondrous fragrance filled the room and reached the neighboring houses.
She was sixty-seven years old (*Ranxiang ji*).

Ma Jingxiu, Ma Jingxiu, was a native of Jinshan County in Songjiang. In his middle years, he took a sincere interest in the Way. Together with several like-minded companions from his village, he cultivated the Pure Land practice.
His vows were earnest and practical, and he delighted in doing good without weariness. He was particularly courageous and diligent in abstaining from killing and releasing captive creatures.
He associated with the monk Hui-can and the monk Song-tao, who together sustained his practice; his aspiration to seek birth [in the Pure Land] became even more earnest.

He immediately received the Upāsaka precepts and applied himself with diligent resolve for several years. Later, he suffered from a swelling of the jaw that made it difficult for him to turn over in bed;
yet his will did not slacken in the slightest. Just then, the monk Song-tao came to inquire after his illness and stayed to assist him in reciting the Buddha’s name. Three days later...
He saw before his bed a small golden stupa descending through the air, accompanied by lotus flowers of four colors, exceptionally fresh and vibrant.
He then joined his palms in reverence and thanked the assembly, saying, "The Teacher has arrived," and as he repeatedly invoked the name of the Buddha, he passed away (*Yanxiang ji*).
Xu Renshu, surnamed Xu, was a native of Nanhxiang in Dantu. He was pure and sincere by nature. His father, Wu Cheng, had diligently cultivated the Pure Land practice;

Renshu, too, placed firm faith in the Triple Gem and constantly recited the Cundī Dhāraṇī. After reaching adulthood, he pursued his studies in the city, and whenever he obtained funds for his livelihood, he would [dedicate them].

He would immediately release living beings to relieve their suffering. Wucheng wished to betroth him a wife, but he declined. At the age of twenty-two, he went to take the provincial examination and contracted a disease of coughing up blood.
Several years later, his condition gradually worsened into a chronic ailment, and he lay groaning upon his bed. Wucheng enlightened him, saying:
Illness is summoned by past karma. Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land is the unsurpassed King of Physicians.
If you can be reborn in that land, the chronic ailment of ten thousand kalpas will be cast off in a single morning. Ren Shu was suddenly enlightened;
he then invited Master Xuegu of Zhulin Temple, set up a seat in the courtyard, received the Three Refuges and Five Precepts, and with sincere repentance, resolved his will [upon liberation].
In the western quarter, on the eighth day of the fourth month, he invited monks to recite the Buddha’s name for a period of seven days.

When the period was complete, he immediately shaved his head and donned the black robes. His relatives were overcome with grief, but Ren Shu said, "Depart quickly; do not disturb my right mindfulness."
From then on, his power of recitation increased even further. On the first day of the fifth month, he again had monks invited to perform seven days of Buddha-recitation.
He then ceased eating grains and drank only water; he lay flat on his back, unable to lift or turn himself over. On the evening of the sixth day, he said to Wucheng:
"Tonight’s full moon is sufficient. He then lit lamps and burned incense. At midnight, a red light suddenly illuminated the sky from outside the window, flashing twice in succession.
Ren Shu, exerting his own strength, turned onto his right side, joined his palms, and passed away with a smile at the age of twenty-five.
Wucheng, whose courtesy name was Xinsen, had verses and gāthās on the Way that circulate in the world; now four of them are recorded here.

First: One says, "The mind is like floating clouds, idle wherever it goes; fundamentally it does not abide in the extremes of existence or non-existence. Yellow flowers and green bamboos are all the ultimate truth;
once one attempts to investigate them, one falls into conceptualization. Another says, "Diligently cultivate pure karma and detach from worldly conditions."
Without the need for thought, it is naturally clear. If doubt gives rise to conceptual views, dense clouds and thick mist will shroud the blue sky.
One says: "Discussions of the school and lectures on the teachings abound in this world; people compete to speak of their cleverness and claim their insights are lofty.

How can these compare to firmly cultivating true practice? A single phrase of Amitābha is the sword that slays demons. Another says: "For ten thousand kalpas one has been submerged in delusion; regret and awakening come too late."
This morning I have finally realized that the road has many diverging paths; when illusory conditions and karmic retributions are exhausted, one attains the state of no-outflows.
May I claim a single branch of the lotus in the pond of the seven treasures. (A Verse and Preface on the Way)
Continued Compilation of the Records of Sages and Worthies of the Pure Land, Volume II;
Continued Compilation of the Records of Sages and Worthies of the Pure Land, Volume III;
Lay Practitioners Who Attained Rebirth, Part Four, Section Two.

Pei Yongdu. Pei Yongdu was a native of Taizhou in Jiangnan. His family had resided for generations in Qu塘 Town (Qutang Town), where they made their living through farming. By nature he was serene and indifferent to worldly desires, yet he would invariably act upon whatever was good.
From his youth, he had been a devoted believer in the Buddha-dharma; as an adult, he maintained a vegetarian fast and recited the Buddha’s name without ceasing.
After some time, he took refuge with Master Guguang of Gaomin Temple and received the full precepts of an upāsaka.
His practice was strict and pure, never lacking in any respect. His wife also turned her faith toward the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation and received the precepts of an upāsikā.
Although husband and wife lived together in the same room for several decades, they maintained such pure conduct that no one could find cause for criticism.

In their early years, they had no son, only a daughter who also observed the vegetarian fast and honored the Buddha. Before long, she earnestly requested to leave the household life, and her parents granted her wish.

They shaved her head, provided her with monastic robes, and she received the full precepts of a bhikṣuṇī. They then permanently relinquished their residence to establish a nunnery, entrusting it to his wife.
The nun practiced the Pure Land path; she had built a separate quiet chamber for herself and lived alone there reciting the Buddha’s name for several decades.
Later, when she was nearly seventy years old, one day she told her relatives: "Five days from now, I shall depart from you.
Please cremate my remains. This body is like an illusion; do not mistakenly cherish it. When the appointed time arrived, she sat upright.
He passed away while reciting the name of the Buddha. His family followed his final instructions and performed the cremation.

They obtained more than a hundred *śarīra* relics, each like a bean in size and translucent with five colors. They subsequently stored them in a lapis lazuli bottle and enshrined them within a hermitage.
This was an event from the early years of the Daoguang era (as recorded in the *Ranxiang xují*).
Zhong Jiushi, Zhong Jiushi.
A native of Hangzhou, his family resided by West Creek. He was a man of great integrity and generosity, possessing deep faith in the Triple Gem.

There were dozens of monasteries and thatched huts in the vicinity, all of which Jiushi protected and maintained; he provided for them with unwearied devotion. However, due to certain circumstances, his resources were occasionally depleted.

He possessed much gold, yet never showed a trace of resentment. When engaging in trade with others, he never practiced even the slightest deception. His wife, Lady Shen, practiced the Pure Land path together with him.
Liu Jiushi performed various meritorious deeds, and she always delighted in assisting him. Their son and daughter were both simple, frugal, diligent, and conscientious.
In the early summer of the sixth year of the Daoguang era, Jiushi manifested a slight illness. On the morning of the twenty-fourth day, [he passed away].
He said to his wife, "Because I have been loyal and honest in my daily life and have maintained pure and earnest vows, I have been received by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This afternoon, I shall depart for the West. You should perform good deeds according to your capacity and always remain steadfast in guarding my resolve.
At noon, he said, "Light incense and candles for me," and further addressed Shen-shi, saying, "The days remaining for you are few; keep this in mind."
The Buddha’s essential teaching has been stated; having finished speaking, she passed away at the age of fifty-two. In the seventh month of the following year, Lady Shen also manifested illness.
She invited her husband’s elder brother, and after completing the entrustment of all household affairs, she sat in stillness reciting the Buddha’s name. On the twenty-first day, she passed away.
He said to his children and grandchildren, "Be good people," and then he passed away at the age of fifty-four (*Ranxiang xuji*).
Zhou Guang, whose courtesy name was Xilian, was a student from Jiangning. By nature he was pure and generous, and he was indifferent to honor and profit, despite his family background.
He attained high status and distinction, yet was entirely devoid of the frivolous habits typical of the sons of wealthy families.

In his middle years, he observed a lifelong fast and devoted himself to the Buddha, reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* daily and chanting the Buddha’s name tens of thousands of times, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land.

Whenever he met with friends, beyond a few words of greeting, he would immediately expound upon the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, earnestly exhorting them. He gathered funds to reprint the *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra* (*Wangsheng lun zhu*) and personally [supervised the project].
He personally collated [the text] and circulated it throughout the Jianghuai region. Even in his old age, his spirit remained alert and vigorous; his practice of nianfo grew increasingly keen.

In the autumn of the twenty-second year of the Jiaqing era, he suffered from a severe case of hernia that was extremely critical, yet he maintained the recitation of the Buddha’s name without ceasing. His illness soon subsided.

Some people may refer to this in such a way: "At that time, I initially found the suffering unbearable; however, I subsequently reflected that since the body is merely provisional, the suffering is likewise not real.
Moreover, the distinction between the body and the mind is clearly defined as subtle and coarse. That body experiences suffering of its own accord, and I can do nothing about it;
my mind recollects the Buddha of its own accord, and that [body] likewise cannot do anything about me. Thus it begins.
It was as if his body and mind stood in opposition; gradually, he became aware only of the mind and ceased to perceive the body, whereupon his suffering finally came to an end.
He soon passed away. He once composed over a hundred poems on the Pure Land, which were published for the world. One of them says: "Early I cast myself into pure tranquility for rest;
Cease from debating existence and non-existence amidst turbid dust. When afflictions blaze, test your power of concentration; As for the arising of thoughts..."
Exerting effort at the place of arising, burn incense and diligently recite the names of the Three Thousand Buddhas; follow your intent as you turn the hundred-and-eight beads of the rosary.

The compassionate mother leans against the gate pillar, her eyes gazing in vain; how pitiable that her departed child still wanders lost on the path. One says: "The obstacles to the Way in this Sahā world run rampant;
yet when the Land of Lotus Blossoms is mentioned, even dreams become pure. A single breath not sustained leads to the regret of a thousand kalpas—how could one spare even a moment of time?"
The names of the six periods [of practice] are as follows: like a hen brooding her eggs with continuous warmth; like fire melting gold, refining it until it becomes ever more pure.
When the faculties of the emotions are completely eliminated in this very moment, the true nature will naturally manifest in its perfect clarity.

(From the *Ranxiang ji jingtu yong*). Master Xishi said: The Buddha taught that suffering has nothing greater than having a body; therefore, having a body is itself the presence of karmic transgression.
Where there is karmic transgression, there is suffering. To truly know that the body is merely a provisional construct and suffering is not ultimate is to return to the root and exhaust the source;
therein, transgressions vanish and the mind is extinguished. How wise indeed is the Lotus of the West!
Lu Kun, a native of Jiangning, was by nature compassionate and charitable, and he placed his faith in the Triple Gem. His younger brother served as an official in another region;
Kun once visited his office and saw that the kitchen was occupied daily with the slaughter of animals. Stricken with pity, he frequently exhorted him regarding the law of cause and effect.

His younger brother continued this practice without ceasing. Consequently, Lady Kun made a vow to observe the vegetarian diet; she drew blood from her tongue within the official residence and transcribed the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land.
She then took her leave to return home, where she devoted herself to reading and instructing her children, finding joy in the Way.

Not long after, her son entered the local school; she then had him teach her to read so that he might support himself. From then on, she no longer inquired about household affairs, but devoted herself single-mindedly to the recitation of the Buddha’s name.

Whether in cold or heat, or during illness, she never wavered for even a moment. She maintained a close friendship with Zhou Guang, and they constantly exhorted one another in their Pure Land practice.
Because she had been constitutionally stout, her diligent adherence to a vegetarian diet caused her to gradually become thinner and thinner until, in her later years, her physical form—

His bones became emaciated and his frame stood upright. He redoubled the frequency of his recitations and prayers; there was no time or occasion when he did not dedicate his merits toward the Western Paradise.

He had always delighted in reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Whenever he knelt before the Buddha to recite it, even if he grew exhausted and prostrated himself, he would not rise until the scroll was finished.
Once, when she was stricken by a grave illness and on the verge of death, her family prepared for her funeral arrangements.
In a state of daze, Lady Kun saw eight Buddhist monks, each over ten feet tall, enter her chamber and set up an altar to perform Buddhist rites on her behalf.
As Kun was reciting the *Amitābha Sūtra*, she suddenly awoke; the sound of the sutra still lingered murmuring in her mouth, and her illness had vanished as if lost. After more than... [time elapsed].
At that age, he passed away without illness (*Ranxiang ji*).
Wu Yunseng, whose courtesy name was Changdao, was a native of Xi County in Huizhou. In his youth, he traveled between Suzhou and Hangzhou for trade; one day, by chance...

At Tiger Hill, he encountered a monk. The monk gazed at him intently and said, "You possess considerable roots of goodness; however, it is a pity that you will face a calamity involving water at the age of twenty-nine.

What should you do? Yunsheng was deeply terrified and sought a strategy to avoid this fate. After a long silence, the monk said, "From this day forward, abstain from killing and practice the release of living beings.
Every day, recite the Buddha’s name with sincere devotion and maintain the *Dabei Zhou* (Great Compassion Mantra). In this way, you may perhaps escape it."
Ear-yun ascended and received it with faith, practicing it accordingly, and constantly used it to exhort others. When he reached the age of twenty-nine, he was returning to his hometown via Hangzhou;
he boarded a boat at the riverbank, and there were seventeen people on board. After they had traveled some dozens of li, the boat set sail.

Just as the tide arrived, a massive wave surged forth with such force that his life was in imminent danger. Suddenly, he recalled the words of the previous monk and hurriedly joined his palms to recite the Buddha’s name.
Before long, the boat capsized and Yunsheng fell into the water. Amidst his confusion, he heard a voice say, "Wu Yunsheng has merit for encouraging others to recite the Buddha’s name;
you may escape this calamity. When he opened his eyes and looked around, he found himself already upon the shore. Thus it was.

He was rescued by fishermen who pulled him out of the water. His hat and shoes were all swept away by the current, yet he alone still firmly held in his hand his rosary of eighteen beads, which he had used daily for reciting the Buddha’s name. The sixteen people on the same boat had already been drowned and left no trace.
From that time on, his faith in the inconceivable merit of reciting the Buddha’s name grew even stronger; he never returned to his hometown again.

He established a hall for the exposition of the Dharma on Mount Wu, saying that by means of this he could discuss cause and effect with others, which would lead them to become even more diligent in their own practice.
He once burned incense from his own arm to form the four characters for "Seeking Rebirth in the Western Land," thereby manifesting his vows and conduct.

Following the legacy of Yunqi, the people of Hangzhou were largely knowledgeable about and inclined toward the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation; however, those who actually engaged in the practice were mostly elderly, and only on a monthly basis...
One day, while reciting the Buddha’s name within the temple, he remarked that this was called the "Assembly of the Aged," whereas young people did not participate;

furthermore, he dared not gather many people in the assembly for fear of the suspicion of heresy. Yun-sung sighed with resolve and said, "The Dharma of reciting the Buddha’s name makes no distinction between old and young.
Buddhism is the orthodox teaching, and our dynasty holds it in high esteem. Thereupon, he guided each person individually. This is...

At that time, Master Yan Jin was serving as the Salt Commissioner in Hangzhou. Since Yunsheng had an old friendship with him, he solicited contributions of two hundred taels of gold to serve as the initial offering.

He then inaugurated a Buddha-recitation assembly at Baicheng Temple on Mount Ziyang. During each session, he expounded upon the benefits for the participants and extensively explained the law of cause and effect;
he exhorted those who had not yet resolved to practice to resolve their minds, and [encouraged] those who had already resolved...
As for his mind, he exhorted them toward diligent progress. Furthermore, within the city, at locations such as Xianlin Monastery, he convened assemblies for exhortation and conversion;
those who followed his faith increased daily, with no fewer than a thousand people attending each session.
They were all uniformly respectful and prudent, entirely devoid of the habit of clamor. The western hall of the monastery, along with its sixteen-foot statue, were also renovated at this time.
One clear morning, people all saw a white light, like a rope, emanating from the nose of Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva;

it wound its way through the palace courtyard and only faded after several moments had passed. From that time forward, the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name flourished greatly throughout the city of Hangzhou.
In the area between the city and the countryside, it has become a common sight for men and women, old and young, to hold prayer beads in their hands and murmur mantras;
they no longer find this strange. The name of Yunsheng is known to all, from women to children. Whenever a festival date arrives, everyone waits expectantly for his arrival.
At West Lake there is Lingfeng Temple, the site of the legacy of Chan Master Fuhu, which has fallen into ruin.
A long time had passed since [the temple] fell into ruin. Yunsheng made a vow to restore it in the first year of the Daoguang era.
After several years of labor, the work was finally completed. He passed away at the age of sixty-six. At the moment of his death, his right mindfulness was clear and distinct;

he said that he saw countless bodhisattvas walking before him. He then sat cross-legged and passed away peacefully. This occurred on the first day of the fifth month in the ninth year of the Daoguang era.
(Xianxiang Xují) Master Xishi said:
Lu Kun recited the Buddha’s name primarily seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, while simultaneously seeking to escape the sufferings of illness in his present life.

They constantly guided others to practice *nienfo* (recollection of the Buddha), originally intending to escape calamity, yet they further obtained auspicious responses at the very moment of their passing.
Who would say that the merit of *nienfo* benefits only the afterlife? Consider those two gentlemen: both practiced with sincere effort and maintained unwavering, steadfast faith.
Nowadays, people exert their strength for but a short time, indulging their whims in greedy pursuit; unable to achieve even a one-in-ten-thousand chance of success, they consequently—
This means that [the people] claimed the Buddha lacked spiritual efficacy and utterly abandoned their former merits; it is truly lamentable.

Fan Yuanli—his courtesy name was Yonghe—was a native of Qiantang. In his youth, he studied Confucianism and practiced its principles with sincerity and integrity. He was filial toward his parents. His father...

When his father was ill, he cut flesh from his thigh to compound medicine and presented it to him; consequently, the father recovered suddenly. When his mother, née Yu, fell ill, he again cut flesh from his thigh, and she was likewise cured.

Upon the deaths of his parents, his wife followed them in death. At that time, he was still in the prime of his youth, yet he sighed with resolve to cast off worldly ties and frequented the circles of those who cultivate the truth (*yangzhen*).
After more than ten years, he had achieved considerable efficacy. Later, upon reading the writings of Yunqi, he attained a profound realization and subsequently went to Yunqi.
He received the five precepts and maintained them with single-minded resolve. He would not wear even a hair from an animal or silk produced by a silkworm upon his body.

He completely abandoned his former habits and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of the Pure Land. Regarding the method of visualization (*guanxiang*), he was particularly meticulous and precise.
Previously, when his mother was approaching death and was delirious and agitated, Yuanli had exhorted her to focus her mind on the visualization of Avalokiteśvara. His mother followed his advice.
One day, he suddenly said, "I see Bodhisattvas coming to welcome me; I am about to reach a supreme and wondrous place.
Having spoken these words, he passed away peacefully. Thus, Yuanli deeply believed in the efficacy of meditative visualization.

By nature compassionate and kind, he delighted in giving, performing such deeds as releasing captive animals and relieving the poor with meticulous care and diligence, never sparing himself of toil or exhaustion. Whenever he encountered monks in poverty or distress, he provided them with offerings.
There was no lack of anyone among the monastics and laypeople who had not heard his name.

In the summer of the eighth year of the Daoguang era, he closed the gates at the Great Cave Pavilion south of the city to observe a hundred-day period of Buddha-recitation. One day, while in a state of quiet repose, the profound power of his prime years suddenly manifested;
he perceived the vital energy of heaven and earth within the void, flowing like fine threads and surging like rushing currents through his mouth and nose.
It penetrates straight through to the *dantian* (elixir field), merging with one’s own primordial vital energy (*prāṇa*).
At this time, the state of lightness and ease is beyond description. Suddenly, an infant several inches tall emerges from the aperture at the crown of the head and hovers playfully before one.
After a short while, it re-enters through the crown. From then on, whenever one reaches a state of profound stillness where thought is forgotten, there invariably occurs—
The infant’s coming and going was as before. At first, he was greatly pleased; however, he soon reflected:

"Could this not be what is referred to as one of the fifty kinds of demonic hindrances (*bhūta-graha*) in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*? If I treat this as something extraordinary, I shall fall under the sway of various evils.

Furthermore, the practitioner of Buddha-remembrance should set his will upon the Western Pure Land. Since the sacred realm does not manifest there, why take this to be so? Thereupon, he frequently applied mindfulness and illumination, and right mindfulness became manifest.
After this, the infant no longer emerged. From that point on, he attained a profound realization of the principle of "Mind-Only" (*cittamātra*).
His faith in the power of practice and vows became increasingly pure and sincere. He often said to others: "This was the first and most perilous pass of my life;

had I not been alert and aware for even a moment, I would have fallen into heterodox paths. Thus, one must be cautious in the practice of cultivation. In the summer of the eleventh year, he raised [his child].

He stayed at Jizhao Temple outside the Qingtai Gate. There lived a blind old woman named Shen who was devoted to the practice of nianfo (reciting the Buddha’s name), but she was obstructed by her daughter-in-law.
Yuanli heard of this and said, "This can be remedied. Her only concern is poverty;

if I provide her with the necessary provisions, she will surely have no excuse [to stop]. He then entered the city and raised several bushels of rice per month, which the old woman took for her sustenance.

Outside, there was another who had even reached her daughter-in-law; they were all joyful and offered no resistance. Yuanli further expounded upon the benefits of reciting the Buddha’s name and instructed them in repentance and the making of vows.
After several months, a neighbor came to inform him, "The old woman who previously recited the Buddha’s name has passed away to the Western Paradise.
When he asked for the details, [the neighbor] explained fully how things had been since she began receiving his offerings.
He was diligent in the practice of Buddha-recitation. As for his repentance and making of vows, when a certain month arrived, he foreknew the time of his departure and informed his daughter-in-law.

When the appointed time came, he bathed, changed his clothes, and passed away while sitting with palms joined. He had previously left a message of thanks to Master Fan, stating that he still lacked funds for a coffin and burial;
his daughter-in-law intended to sell their daughter to provide them. Yuanli immediately consulted with virtuous friends and obtained the necessary funds for the funeral.
After some time, he entrusted it to a neighbor to take away. Ten days later, Yuanli went to that house to inquire about it.

Upon arrival, he found his daughter-in-law there, holding a rosary in her hand and chanting the names of the Buddha with her lips moving. As soon as she saw Yuanli, she greeted him with joy and offered thanks.
Just as they were about to sit down, the neighbors from the surrounding houses flocked together, all vying to catch sight of Master Fan’s face, and immediately began speaking to one another.

To relate the recent events concerning the old woman, it was exactly as the neighbor had previously said. He then pointed to a young girl and said, "This is the one who was spared from being sold by grace.
When asked where the coffin was, she replied, "Since the body was encoffined and laid to rest, the neighbors deliberated together:
'If the people of that city are still willing to travel such a distance to perform acts of merit, how can we, as our neighbors, simply sit idly by?'"
He went to see [the site] and subsequently gathered funds to purchase the land; on the same day, he interred his son’s long-stalled coffin alongside it.
Yuanli returned home with a joyful heart. That winter, the meritorious deeds he had overseen were brought to completion.
In the first month of the following year, his dharma companions visited him in succession, conversing earnestly as if they were about to part for a long time. His son was from Songjiang.
He gave him instructions, saying: "When you go outside, attend well to your own affairs. I am old;

should any unforeseen misfortune occur, be careful not to fall into a state of panic, hastily abandoning your primary duties and failing those who entrusted you with this task. His son took these words to heart, regarding them as the excessive worries of an elderly man.
On the twenty-fourth day, he rose early and said to his family members: "Today, I feel my vital energy..."
It was urgent. Yet, as if he were his usual self, he ate congee; after the meal, he visited a neighbor’s house and lingered there for about an hour before returning home.
Once back, he sat upright in the hall and recited the Buddha’s name. When his nephews questioned him, he shook his hand to stop them. By noon, his breath had gradually become faint.
He then passed away. On the following day at the hour of You (5–7 p.m.), he was encoffined; the crown of his head remained warm. He was sixty-three years old.
This occurred during the twelfth year of the Daoguang era (*Ranxiang Xují*).
Master Xishi remarked: "Observing the farewell letter from Yonghe to his son, one cannot say that he did not settle all his affairs in advance."
It was not that I foresaw the time had arrived. If so, why did I not speak of it clearly? I replied: "What is prized in foresight is the value of self-knowledge, intended only to steady the mind;
it is not for the sake of seeking praise from others. Moreover, when the time arrives, virtuous friends gather together, which may provide the benefit of aiding the Path.
Even if one’s kinsmen were to surround one, weeping and wailing, how could this [be compared to such aid]?"
"Is this not a case of seeking success but instead meeting with failure? There is indeed a profound reason why Mr. He remained silent.

Sun Fu’s great-grandson, Sun Fuyuan, styled Minsi, was a schoolboy from Renhe. By nature he was kind and compassionate; from his youth, he delighted in reading the *Yinggan pian* (Treatise on Retribution) and the *Yinshu* (Book of the Hidden).

Zhiwen established a vow to practice accordingly. His residence was directly opposite a butcher’s shop. One morning upon rising, he saw a pig being slaughtered and immediately made a vow to abstain from killing.
He purchased the pig and released it at Yunqi; although he could not entirely renounce meat, he regularly maintained a vegetarian diet.

Even mosquitoes, gnats, fleas, and lice did not incidentally harm him. After his maturity, he daily recited the name of the Buddha, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and the *Great Compassion Repentance*, while also maintaining a ledger of merits and faults.
Within barely two years, when walking at night without a lamp, there was suddenly light before his eyes.

He redoubled his efforts and performed various meritorious deeds, regarding the relief of the poor and the release of captive creatures as his most urgent duties, regardless of whether the matters were great or small.

He exerted all his strength in these endeavors. Later, while he was managing salt-tax affairs, he was beset by a whirlwind of dust and turmoil; the luminosity that had appeared during his nightly practice gradually faded. He then exclaimed in alarm, "I have greatly erred!

He subsequently resigned and returned home, striving with renewed diligence as before, whereupon the luminosity manifested once more. Thus, he gained further conviction that the principle of karmic response is not in vain.
He devoted himself single-mindedly to the recitation of the Buddha’s name and meditative visualization, directing his intent toward the West without interruption for several decades.
Beyond the seventy-day mark, he redoubled his diligent practice and repeatedly experienced auspicious responses. At times, he dreamed of a great star as large as a bowl illuminating his own body;

at other times, he dreamed of kneeling before a white lotus flower, reciting scriptures in the presence of the Buddha. One night, as soon as he had laid his head upon the pillow, he heard a voice say:
Virtue is accumulated by oneself; blessings come from Heaven. With eyes open, there was nothing to be seen, yet the sound of a voice was clearly audible in her ears.

On the twenty-first day of the second month in the twelfth year of the Daoguang era, while she was prostrating herself in worship, she had a fleeting vision of a person wearing a *kāṣāya* robe standing before her meditation mat.
When she bowed her head in prostration, it touched the hem of that garment; when she raised her head, it was gone once more.
He saw him occupying the high seat. After three days had passed, he felt his physical strength was exhausted and weary;

as he lay down reciting the Buddha’s name, the wondrous marks of the Muni appeared again between the windows. On the morning of the second day of the third month, he rose early with a serene and joyful spirit;
he moved and sat about at will, showing almost no signs of illness. By evening, he instructed his family members, saying, "Tomorrow, buy two snails for me."

He carried several hundred catties of eels and loaches and released them into rivers and ponds, saying, "When I die, you must all diligently recite the Buddha's name and practice the release of living beings;
perform good deeds and do not forget these words. At that time, he was sitting upon a rope bed, immediately taking up his pen by the lamp.
He personally wrote a preface for a text on the release of captive creatures (*fangsheng wen*). His calligraphy was upright and formal, without the slightest error.
Upon finishing the writing, he lay down peacefully and passed away while softly reciting the Buddha’s name at the age of seventy-five (*Ranxiang xují*).
Master Xishi remarked: "It is only natural that such profound merit in visualization practice should repeatedly evoke auspicious responses; yet, as for his hearing the voices of others..."
To behold the sacred countenance within the void while prostrating—though it is said to be moved by single-minded sincerity, does this not border upon the work of Māra?
I have recorded it for now, awaiting those of discerning wisdom to correct it.
Zhang Qingxin, courtesy name Liu Hua, was a recommended scholar from Jinshan. Orphaned at a young age, he served his mother with filial piety.

Upon reaching adulthood, he traveled extensively to famous scenic sites and delighted in associating with fellow seekers outside the conventional world (fangwai jiao). He remained indifferent to fame and fortune. At over thirty years of age, he took refuge under Yequn.

Ling Gong, whose Dharma name was Zhendan, experienced a sudden and vast awakening upon performing circumambulatory prostrations. He observed the precepts against consuming meat and alcohol, maintained a perpetual fast while reciting the Buddha’s name, and practiced the abstention from killing and the release of living beings.

All the members of his household joyfully followed these practices. From morning until night, the sound of the Buddha’s name resounded continuously, remaining as constant for thirty years as it was on a single day.

The inhabitants of the town of Zujing where he resided were all transformed by his virtue and became kind and upright. In his leisure time, he would count [the beads of] his rosary with his own hands.
Those who invoked the name of the Buddha were as numerous as stars. Qingxin once observed the *śīla* retreat for fourteen days at Chongfu Temple.

After the retreat concluded, he traveled to sacred mountains and visited the sea to pay homage, visiting various masters to study extensively. His realization of the nature of mind became increasingly profound, and he resolved to return to the West [the Pure Land].
In his leisure time, he composed several volumes of the *Zhanpu Ju Shiji* (Poetry Collection of the Campaka Dwelling), which accorded with the intent of the Buddhas. His Way...

In the winter of the eleventh year of the Guanghua era, he manifested a slight illness. He instructed his son to visit Chongfu Temple to establish a water-land *dharmadhātu* ritual assembly (*shuilu daochang*).
In the fifth month of the following year, his illness became critical, and he said, "Within three days, I shall return to the West. My kinsmen and relatives must not grieve or be distressed.
He then ordered that Master Hongji be invited to come, and had his family members recite the Buddha’s name in unison. On the fourth day, he bathed and sat in the full lotus posture.
He passed away while seated. His crown remained warm for one day and night. He was sixty-two years of age (*Ranji Xuji*).
Ding Fan Gui, courtesy name Xiao Shan, was a student at Jinshan School. From childhood he devoted himself to the studies for the civil service examinations and did not discuss the Buddha-dharma.
