Nor did he slander others. Only when his parents sought to betroth him a wife did he resolutely refuse, saying, "I am pursuing my own aspirations.
Those close to him occasionally observed him and came to realize that he had long been practicing pure deeds in secret, and that he had merely not manifested them outwardly until now.
In the summer of the twelfth year of the Daoguang era, he suddenly developed a hemorraghic condition, which persisted until the night of the sixteenth day of the eighth month.
Suddenly, he smiled and said to his parents, "The conditions for my karmic retribution have been exhausted; I am now departing for the Western Land.
He chanted the Buddha’s name a thousand times with clear resonance and then passed away at the age of twenty-two (*Ranxiang xují*).
Li Qin, whose courtesy name was Xiangtai, was a native of Renhe. From birth he was of a pure and generous nature, never at odds with others. He was exceptionally intelligent and fond of learning;

there were no works among the Classics, Histories, Philosophers, or Collections that he had not perused thoroughly. Yet, he remained indifferent to fame and profit, having no intention of seeking advancement, and instead aspired to transcend the mundane world.
Lǒng studied under masters of the Yuanxue (Original Learning) school; his aspirations were pure and his character was bright and untainted.
In his middle years, he placed his faith in the Buddha Vehicle and received the five lay precepts, taking the Dharma name Miaojing. From then on, he cultivated his practice with constant diligence.

Regarding the matters of the Chan school, he achieved considerable realization and awakening, yet he specifically took the Pure Land as his final destination. He once said: "A mere half-knowledge and partial understanding will ultimately..."
My return will not be of benefit; I would rather adhere to the secure and reliable Dharma than dare to speak grandly and deceive myself.

Because my family is diligent, our wealth is not abundant, yet I bestow alms without regret. Furthermore, I am free from self-conceit and boastfulness. Regarding matters concerning the Triple Gem, I have applied my utmost devotion to honor them.
I once carved a sandalwood Buddha image and a pagoda for the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and erected two inscribed steles, both of which stand by the sea.

At Chao Temple, when the funds for construction were insufficient, he pledged his property as collateral to complete the sum. Subsequently, he carved a stone stele depicting the entire world of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) to record his faith and vow.
One day, while he was staying at the temple to provide a meal for the monks, a thief took advantage of the opportunity to scale the wall and enter his room.
It was not until dawn that he realized it; the doors and windows stood wide open, yet no items had been lost. This was surely due to the intervention of spirits.
May the deities protect this work. The Venerable Jiantang of Guoqing Temple was a preeminent figure among the monastic communities of recent times;
he passed away early in Hangzhou, leaving behind a single volume of his draft writings. I have diligently collected and published them for circulation. Originally, I had never even met Master Jian.
In the summer of the twelfth year of the Daoguang era, her niece Xinggu was on the verge of death. Qín attended to her day and night, guiding her toward right mindfulness.

In the end, she was able to pass away while reciting the Buddha’s name. Not long after, Qín herself fell ill. A physician said, "This is caused by accumulated exhaustion and injury to the vital energy (*qi*).
You should rest and maintain tranquility; otherwise, I fear the condition will deepen. After the physician had left, Qín said, "This is precisely the opportunity for the final command."
"I have gained little but lost much; alas, what can be done? He redoubled his diligent recitation of the Buddha’s name and personally oversaw the completion of all meritorious affairs.
In the tenth month, his illness became critical. At midnight on the eleventh day, while sitting cross-legged and holding the Buddha’s name, he passed away peacefully.
Three days prior, he had asked his family for a monk’s cap; they hurriedly fashioned one for him, and he immediately donned it.
On his head, he said with joy: "I have always possessed this plain robe; what I lacked was only this.
Now that I may wear it upon my crown to behold Amitābha, my wish is fulfilled. I am fortunate to be enshrouded in this very garment to realize my aspiration.

The following day, when the coffin was being prepared, those close to him tried lifting the cap to look inside; warm vapor billowed forth like the lifting of a lid from atop a cauldron. He was forty years of age.
Seventeen (Continuation of the Collection on the Perfume of Defilement).
Zhang Dunwu.
Zhang Dunwu, also named Yao Tai, styled Xutang, was a supplementary student at the Changzhou Academy. In his later years, he was deeply devoted to the Pure Land.

[She] practiced the *karma* [of Pure Land devotion] with Master De of Shanqing Hermitage. After a long time, her pure practices became increasingly refined. She maintained a lifelong vegetarian fast (*cháng-zāi*).
Later, because she was advanced in years, she reduced her food intake. Her eldest daughter urged her to break the fast, but the younger daughter said, "Minor filial piety is of no benefit;

it is sufficient to use this as a ticket for rebirth in the Pure Land. Not long after, the younger daughter fell ill. During her illness, she completely ceased reciting the Buddha’s name. Dunwu remarked in astonishment, "The illness..."
"My gravity is deficient; truly, this is to be feared. Should I not reflect upon myself? Thereupon, he daily recited the Buddha’s name one hundred thousand times.
One day, he suddenly said to Master De, "In times of sudden crisis, do not summon me at an improper time; I pray you will surely assist me."
After several days had passed, at night, he knocked on Master De’s door, wishing to invite several fellow practitioners of the Pure Land.
Master De thought that since both Dunwu and his wife were not yet ill, it must be their daughter who had passed away; he first sent several monks ahead and followed after them.

Upon arriving, he found that Dunwu had already passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. Ten days later, his daughter also passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name. Only then did he realize that her illness had been severe all along.
He meditated solely to encourage his father’s efforts. At that time, in the fourteenth year of the Daoguang era (Record of Hearing and Seeing the Western Return), the Western Historian said:

"To cause his father to observe the fasts and precepts, to rouse his father to courageous diligence, and to bring his father to rebirth in the Pure Land—this is the ultimate expression of filial piety."
The young woman was truly adept at providing inspiration, and Xutang was likewise delighted to follow her guidance.
That Xutang passed away and the young woman followed him in death—was this not a convergence of causes and conditions, one who had come forth by virtue of past vows?
Cáo Xiéhé, Cáo Xiéhé—his dharma name was Guǎngzhì and his courtesy name was Shēngwǔ. He was a native of Shàngyuán in Jiangnán. His family had long been engaged in the dyeing of crimson in Sū.
In the autumn of the seventh year of the Dàoguāng era, Xiá Wénróng was invited to attend to the illness of his wife. Wénróng instructed her in the Pure [Land practice].
The Earth-Dharma Gate. He followed it, but later he became suspicious of it. He said to Wenrong, "People say that you deceive others by means of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation).

Why is this? Wenrong replied, "To lead people through deluded karma to suffer the fruits of retribution and transmigrate through the three miserable realms is what is called 'falling into a foreign land.
That may be called deception. But to exhort people toward precepts, concentration, and wisdom so that they are reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss—this is the ultimate [truth]."
"Bodhi" (Awakening) is simply an exhortation for people to return home; how could it be a deception? Hedyang attained realization upon hearing these words. He asked, "How can one return home?

He replied, "Taking the observance of precepts as the foundation and the cultivation of merit as the support, while upholding the Name until one reaches the state of 'single-mindedness without distraction'—this is the news of returning home.
Hedyang then departed with great joy. Having returned, he took refuge under Master Beidu Hai.
In the spring of the following year, he received the five precepts from Master Yi at Vulture Peak (Riujū). One night, he suddenly dreamed that a black mountain stood before him;

he wished to ascend it, but a mountain stream blocked his way, and there was the appearance of a red sun sinking in the west. Upon waking, he realized that his worldly attachments were nearing their end, and his spiritual practice progressed even further.
Of his family assets worth three thousand *kan* of gold, they were completely exhausted through acts of giving within a few years. In the fourth month of the fourteenth year—
Having exhausted his resources, he ceased his work and returned home. Previously, Xiehe had exhorted his mother to cultivate the Pure Land practice.
Because she had no son, the mother ordered him to take a concubine. He said to her, "It is sufficient that you and I be reborn together in the Pure Land.

In the five turbidities, there are many matters for creating karma; one need not concern oneself with the continuation of the lineage. Subsequently, he escorted his mother back to their hometown. Not long after, his mother recited the Buddha's name and—
He passed away. In the sixth month of that year, Xihe manifested illness. Six days later, he likewise died while sitting peacefully, reciting the Buddha’s name.
His daughter witnessed this and gave rise to deep faith; she recited the Buddha’s name for forty-nine days before passing away in a state of auspicious seated liberation (*Xigu Jianwen Lu*).
The Western Historian says: "Within a hundred days, three people had perished. In secular society, would there not have been public censure?"
That members of one family were together entrusted to the womb of a lotus is truly a cause for celebration; this is indeed something that can be spoken of only by those who understand.
Pan Zunmao, whose courtesy name was Yilan, was a native of Wu County. Though he worked as a minor merchant, from his youth he turned his heart toward the Buddha-vehicle.
He practiced the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land with diligence, following a daily schedule of recitation and meditation.

Compassionate and fond of giving, he took pity on the orphaned and the destitute, protected all living beings, and rejoiced in every merit, such as providing meals for the Sangha and repairing temples. In his daily life, he maintained a simple and unassuming standard of living.
At the age of thirty, he contracted a disease that caused him to cough up blood. He then resolved his mind to prick his tongue for its blood and transcribe the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Upon completing the scripture, his illness subsided. From then on, he secluded himself from worldly entanglements and devoted himself single-mindedly to meditation and recitation. Within his single room, there was an incense burner and a water jar.
Clad in a solitary, cold hempen robe, he daily expounded the Dharma of non-arising to his family members.

Whenever the weather was fine and pleasant, he would go out to visit famous monasteries such as Xiao Temple, where he formed a bond of forest-dwelling practice with one or two fellow monks of meditative wisdom.

He was especially inseparable from the venerable Master Deqing. Once, following Master Deqing to Mount Mao, he made offerings for the Nirvāṇa at the front of the Aśoka Stūpa and beheld [the sacred image].
Regarding the auspicious signs of the śarīra relics, [he] offered incense with his arms raised in reverent devotion and sought rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).

In the spring of the fifteenth year of the Daoguang era, his chronic illness flared up again; knowing that he would not recover, he spoke to Master De, saying, "My illness is critical. I have resolved to make plans for my return to the West (the Pure Land).
I pray that all my pure companions will come to my home daily to assist me in reciting the Buddha’s name. Because I am so earnest in holding the name, I can [recite it] two or three..."

At that time, he did not give rise to distracting thoughts; he simply could not see the Buddha coming. "Alas! How can this be? he lamented, reproaching himself for his deep karmic obstructions and shallow roots of merit.
He wept bitterly with tears streaming down. Master De offered him various instructions and exhortations.

On the following day, he said to Master De, "A great white light has come from the West, illuminating my body and mind. The joy is beyond words. His recitation became even more earnest. One night, he dreamed—

He wandered through the realm of the Lotus Pond, which was adorned with supreme wonders as described in the sutras. The next day, he suddenly arose and said, "I have seen countless Buddhas filling the void.
Through the power of my courageous mindfulness, I have attained birth in the middle grade of the Pure Land.

He sent word to his fellow students, saying, "Exert yourselves in practice and come early to the Pure Land; do not obstruct yourselves. With palms joined in recitation of the Buddha's name, he passed away at home.
The person obtained a record of their daily tasks; they held the sutras and recited the Buddha’s name, registering [their practice] day by day.
For twenty years, it was as if it were but a single day (from the *Biography of Pan Yilan* composed by Monk Jue’a).
Song Lailei, style name Wangshan, was a native of Suzhou. At over sixty years of age, he heard the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land and daily recited the Buddha’s name tens of thousands of times.
He said, "I rely upon these six characters to bring this life to its conclusion. Later, he resided at Qianwanli Bridge.
The Jiang family served as the host for the temple. Because [Master] Lai observed the fasts and recited the Buddha’s name, the host attempted to prohibit him from doing so, but could not succeed;

he subsequently took his leave. Later, he moved his seat to another location. The teacher and the students were in harmony, and he said to his disciples, "This schoolhouse is very good. Would it be acceptable if I were to pass away here?
One day, when the students entered the schoolroom, they saw Lai with his palms joined in prayer, reciting the Buddha’s name. After a short while, he entered again as before.
Therefore, as he was departing, a sheet of paper was found beneath his inkstone; it appeared to be a note written three days prior regarding the scheduled time [of his passing].
A strange fragrance filled the room and did not dissipate for an entire night. This account is recorded in the *Daoguang 15th Year* (by Song Meipu).
Zhou Qingsun, whose courtesy name was Yuntian, was a student at the National Academy in Suzhou. He was filial toward his mother and had married into the Kong clan of Qufu.

Subsequently, the Kong family invited him, intending to assist him in obtaining an official post through a special precedent. He set out with his wife and children, but their boat capsized in the river.
The river surged; his wife and children all perished, while Qingsun alone escaped with his life. Thereupon, he renounced all pursuit of advancement and retired home to serve his mother.

He devoted himself to the cultivation of pure karma, styling himself the Layman Yibai. By nature he was cautious and timid: fearing that his precepts might be broken, he did not dare accept offerings;
fearing that his fasts might be interrupted, he did not dare maintain them; fearing the profundity of the sutras and treatises, he did not dare read them. At that time, Master Ding of Tiejun...

He praised Qing-sun’s goodness, saying, "In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, one must never know contentment. If you continue to starve yourself in this manner, how can you hope to resolve the cycle of birth and death in many lifetimes?
Qing-sun remained silent. One day, he suddenly went to Ding-gong’s place, prostrated himself on the ground, and said, "Only today have I come to understand your goodness.
Recently, I have been reading the Tripiṭaka and have gained immeasurable, wondrous benefit. I have now made a firm resolve."
He had observed the long fast for a long time, and his practice of reciting the Buddha’s name was also highly effective. Had it not been for you, he would not have reached this state.

After several years of diligent cultivation, on the fifteenth day of the eighth month in the fifteenth year of the Daoguang era, he consumed a single bowl of congee at dawn; his chopsticks suddenly fell to the ground, and he passed away without illness.
Sengjue’a was at Zhujing, which was his very hermitage. During the latter part of this month, he suddenly dreamed of Zhang Dunwu and Qingsun.
Qingsun did not speak; Dunwu said to Jue’a, "I have exerted my utmost effort and can only reach the Western Land;
I do not equal his high rank and station. Upon waking, he marveled at this. In the ninth month, his younger brother arrived at the hermitage. Jue’a—
He related his dream, through which he first learned that Qingsun had already passed away (*Xigu Jianwen Lu*).
As for Layman Chen:
his name has been omitted. He was a native of Changshu and the paternal uncle of Shi Yingmoucai. Every morning during his lifetime...
He would rise, burn incense, and silently recite sutras and prayers for the Buddhas, such that no one in the family was aware of it; this was his secret practice (*guhyacaryā*).

He continued this without interruption through wind, rain, cold, and heat for many years. In the seventh month of the fifteenth year of the Daoguang era, he himself declared that he would return to the West on the twenty-third day of the ninth month.
His family did not believe him, as he had been free from illness. Then, three days before his passing...
He manifested a slight illness, yet his daily activities remained as usual. When the appointed time arrived, he sat upright and passed away. His family members gathered around and called out to him;
he then opened his eyes and spoke a few brief words, after which he said, "I am going," and finally closed them. A wondrous fragrance emanated from the pores of his body.
After he was encoffined, the room remained fragrant for three days. (Record of Recent Accounts of Rebirth)

The Master of Western History (Xishi) said: "When one cultivates the practices of Esoteric Buddhism, the internal refinement must necessarily be profound; that the body emits a wondrous fragrance is the means by which it is manifested.
— By the worthy man of our land.

Yu Bangxian was a man from Shaoxing. In his youth, he pursued the life of a merchant. At over sixty years of age, he ceased his business and began practicing the Pure Land path together with his wife.
In addition to reciting the Buddha’s name, each of them would regularly prostrate before the eight sections of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
In the eighteenth year of the Daoguang era, at the age of eighty-six, his wife first fell ill; Bangxian also became ill. One day, his wife said to her daughter-in-law: "For my sake..."
She took leave of her father-in-law, saying, "I wish to depart. Her daughter-in-law was surprised and informed Bang-hyeon. Bang-hyeon said, "Please wait three days; you may go together with me.
When his wife heard this, she replied, "Yes. Indeed, when the third day arrived, they both passed away at the same time.
This occurred on the twenty-third day of the sixth month (as related by Zhu Yintang).
Wu Zongwei, courtesy name Qiuting, was a native of Yuanhe. His father, Wu Lian, cultivated the practice of Pure Land and attained rebirth there; these matters are recorded in his own biography.

His mother, Lady Zhou, suffered from chronic liver disease. Zongwei served her with the utmost filial piety; when her illness became critical, he cut flesh from his own thigh to offer her as medicine. Her illness...
After he had returned, his mother passed away. During the forty-nine days of mourning, Zongwei pricked his own blood to transcribe the *Kṣitigarbha-pūrvapraṇidhāna-sūtra*.
He subsequently turned his heart toward the Buddha Vehicle, becoming proficient in both its doctrine and its practice; elders and the infirm from all quarters spoke highly of him.
Later, he devoted himself exclusively to the Pure Land path, styling himself the Layman Yirú. He maintained a lifelong fast and received the five precepts, establishing a lotus society at Jiyé Ān.
In our community, regarding all virtuous deeds such as releasing captive animals, distributing robes, and providing coffins for the deceased, he always assisted with his full strength.
One day, manifesting illness, he knew in himself that he would not recover. He wrote a letter to his fellow practitioners, exhorting them in every way toward the Pure Land.

He remarked that of his lifelong practice, during this illness only half remained; there was retreat and no progress—how difficult, how difficult it is! May you, honorable gentlemen, take this to heart.
He lamented, "I have always thought that I would attend to worldly affairs during my healthy days and only apply myself to spiritual practice when I am ill.

It is too late for regrets; my self-deception has been no small matter. His grief was as profound as this. On the day before his death, his friend Qian Wencan visited him and asked whether he was reciting the Buddha’s name.
At that time, Zongwei’s speech had already become labored; he asked for a brush and wrote: "The suffering of death is such as this. Rebirth [in the Pure Land]..."
His vow-power became even firmer. On the following day, he passed away. His final instructions were: do not cremate his robes; do not perform the ritual of "receiving the death" (jiesha);
and do not paint his portrait. This was on the twenty-sixth day of the seventh month in the eighteenth year of Daoguang (as recorded by Wu Jinfan).

Zhang Chiyen, a student at the National Academy in Changshu, was naturally fond of wine and considered himself superior to others. Whenever he heard people discuss Buddhist scriptures, his voice and countenance would immediately turn fierce and aggressive.
One day, while casually reading accounts of cause and effect and the cycle of rebirth, he suddenly attained clarity regarding birth and death.

This was a momentous matter. He consequently abstained from killing and eschewed alcohol, daily reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī*, and the names of the Buddhas, dedicating these merits toward rebirth in the Western Pure Land and repenting for the karma of his illness.
Thereafter, he severed all consumption of pungent roots and meat. At that time, he was suffering from a wind-disorder (*vātavyādhi*), and the right side of his body was withered and paralyzed.

When some advised him to eat meat as a means of recuperation, he merely declined with a smile. In the spring of the nineteenth year of the Daoguang era, he personally transcribed the *Samantamukha-parivarta*.
He printed several fascicles of the *Pumen pin* (Universal Gate Chapter) and distributed them, saying to others: "This is a compassionate vessel for the ocean of suffering;
do not let it pass you by when you face it. That autumn, he dreamed of swallowing a lotus flower. From then on, he redoubled his diligence. He told his younger brother, Erdan:
"I must recite the *Pumen pin* ten thousand two thousand times before my vow is fulfilled. When Erdan questioned him as to why, he sighed and said: [The rest of the passage follows].
"There are four sufferings in the world: birth, old age, sickness, and death. I have experienced three of these;
only death remains to be reckoned with. Yet, it too approaches ever more swiftly. Should one not prepare the provisions for the journey early?

On the night of the eleventh day of the first month in the twentieth year, as I lay down at dawn and could not sleep, I heard Yiian reciting the "Universal Gate" chapter of the Lotus Sutra with a clear and resonant voice. I questioned him about it.
At that time, Chiyen was in a deep sleep and had not uttered a sound; it was evidently recited within his dreams.

When he rose the following morning and finished his daily recitation, he went to visit a relative on some business. Suddenly, phlegm surged up and choked his throat; he was hurriedly sent home, where he lay upon his bed unconscious.
On the evening of the thirteenth, his friend Xie Fengwu came to inquire after his illness and ordered incense to be burned and candles to be lit.
Before his couch, he handed over his usual rosary to him. Suddenly, [the deceased] raised his hand and began counting the beads, reaching them to his chest;
his gaze shone upward and his entire body moved, after which his breath ceased. The assembly concluded, "This is a Sugata; he will surely be reborn in the Western Paradise.
Only his wife did not believe this, and she prayed toward the coffin, saying, "If it is truly so, you must inform me within a dream. After five days had passed...
One day, she dreamed at night that someone spoke to her, saying, "Do not weep, do not weep! This person of your household has already departed for beyond ten million billion Buddha-lands.

Upon waking, she found this strange; however, throughout her life she had never recited the *Amitābha Sūtra*, and thus she did not know the meaning of the five characters "ten million billion Buddha-lands.
The following day, she questioned the assembly, and only then did she learn that it was her husband who had gone.
There are clear proofs of rebirth. Er Dan, whose courtesy name was Meishu, also cultivated the practice of Pure Land;
he compiled the *Record of Recent Verifications of Rebirth* (Wǎngshēng Jìnyàn Lù) for circulation in the world.
Jinting Dong (金庭棟), courtesy name Youlan (友蘭), was a native of Suzhou. He was a devoted practitioner of the Pure Land school. In the winter of the twentieth year of the Daoguang era, he fell ill;
knowing his end was near, he invited his preceptor, Venerable Liangkuan (亮寬), along with several virtuous friends, to come to him.
He addressed them, saying, "My life and death are about to be decided. I pray that you all assist in creating these auspicious conditions.
The assembly raised their voices in unison, chanting the Buddha’s name. After a long while, he said, "At this moment, the ground appearing before my eyes is composed entirely of the seven treasures;
yet when one treads upon it, it is soft and supple. The sounds heard by the ears are subtle and difficult to describe. Furthermore, to the far west, I see gold..."
The eight characters for "Sukhāvatī" were extremely clear. A friend corrected him, saying, "You are mistaken; what you are reciting now consists of only six characters.
Dōtei pointed with his finger to the rafters and said, "Is it not 'Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss'—are these not eight characters?
After a long while, he joined his palms and told his teacher, "Disciple, I am going," and then passed away (*Wǎngshēng Jìnyàn Lù*).

Xu Xi, courtesy name Mengbai, was a student at the expanded curriculum school (zēngguǎngshēng) in the Wuxi Academy. In his youth, he traveled through Qianzhou and Dianchuan, where he took in the splendors of the mountains and rivers; his mind and spirit were vast and open.

Whenever he encountered instances of integrity, filiality, or chastity, he would invariably commemorate and promote them. In his middle years, he served in various administrative posts outside his home province until the age of forty.

Later, he encountered Zhu Linshu, who brought him a copy of the *Longshu Jingtuzhuan* (Pure Land Text of Longshu) as a gift. He subsequently took refuge in the Buddha Vehicle and changed his name to Menglian.

He observed the ten-day fast and established a daily regimen of Pure Land recitation, vowing to travel westward. He went to Zongsheng Hermitage and took refuge with Master Liangkuan, receiving the Dharma name Ruchao.
For over sixty years, his practice became increasingly dedicated; he followed Master Yigong of Lingjiu to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.

Regarding the Precepts: At that time, the Lushi Hermitage within the city was soliciting contributions for the construction of the Great Universal Hall (Dàtōnggé). Xī provided financial assistance with great effort.

In the summer of the twenty-first year of the Daoguang era, he suddenly purified his household affairs and said to his family members: "When a person reaches seventy, they are already celebrated as having attained 'rare age' (gǔxī).
I am now seventy-two; this autumn, I shall surely return [to the source]. He then composed several verses titled *Fǎnběn Suǒyán* (Words on Returning to the Source).

Admonitions on Matters Concerning the Time of Death. First, it is said: Human life is like a temporary lodging; birth is inevitably followed by death, and death is indeed the natural course of human existence.

Yet, because the affection for one’s spouse, children, and grandchildren is deep, they consider this to be a final and eternal parting, unable to restrain themselves from wailing and lamenting in grief.

Little do they realize that one receives fully and returns fully, and that a peaceful end is itself a blessing. Furthermore, since we have already cultivated the practice of Pure Land, this is precisely...

Desiring to escape the sea of suffering and proceed directly to the Land of Bliss, one hopes that at the moment of death the mind will remain single-minded and undistracted, so that one may be reborn there according to one's wish.
If one hears the sound of lamentation and weeping, one will inevitably be pulled by attachments and emotions, causing the heart to become scattered and distracted.
In that case, all my daily practice would have been useless. The affection of my family members for me, who weep for me, is precisely what will bring me harm and injury.
Be mindful that when my breath is about to cease, each person should assist me by reciting the Buddha's name.

One must not wail or weep in confusion. One must wait for one or two hours after the eyes have closed before moving; changing the clothes and turning the body should rather be done slowly than hastily.
Formerly, when Master Shao Kangjie’s father, the Elder of Yichuan, was at the point of death, he said to his family members:
"Wait until I have been placed in my coffin before you weep; do not cry out urgently so as to cause me to lose my way. This account appears in the *Kangjie*.

This is an external transmission that may be taken as a model. Furthermore, he composed the "Four Essentials of Chan and Pure Land," saying: "If you recite the Buddha's name without practicing Chan, you are being honest and acting like a dull-witted person;

when the Buddha is realized as the very mind, this surpasses contemplating the *huatou*. If you practice Chan without reciting the Buddha's name, you must truly achieve the 'dropping of the bucket bottom.
If there is even a single point of doubt, you will find it difficult to apply effort at the ultimate limit. To both recite the Buddha's name and practice Chan—this is the second [essential]."
This is precisely "One. In the essential practice of *cánniàn* (investigative mindfulness), one must be like glue and lacquer; otherwise, it is easy to become lax and negligent.

If one neither practices mindfulness nor engages in investigation, yet attains the Dharma, one may then abandon the method. If one has not yet reached the shore, wishing to cross over suffering but having no raft, [one must persevere].

That autumn, he indeed fell ill. Every day he invited the monk Shanyou to his home to recite the Buddha’s name. Before his bed, he made offerings to an image and offered incense. From the twentieth day of the seventh month...
He fell ill on the first day of the month. By the twenty-first day of the eighth month, when the month was complete, he had not consumed a single grain of rice, drinking only water and thin gruel.

When physicians were summoned and medicine offered, he resolutely refused to take it by mouth. As his illness reached its final stage, he passed away while holding his palms together in prayer and reciting aloud with clarity.

His wife was surnamed Yan. In her daily life, she also maintained her recitation of dharanis and the Buddha’s name. At the age of seventy-three, she suffered from diarrhea and remained bedridden, unable to rise.
She had long been afflicted with deafness, but one day her hearing suddenly became clear; all physical pain within her body vanished. Her son was named Li Fang.
He presented the teachings of the Western Paradise, saying: "I have indeed been mindful of the Buddha from time to time, never allowing it to be forgotten.
When the second watch of the night arrived, I said to my family members, 'I shall depart at dawn.

I then rose and sat up, chanting clearly while counting a string of prayer beads until my strength was exhausted and I could no longer sustain myself; I returned to bed. When dawn broke, I said, 'The time has come,' and once again I rose and sat up."

He joined his palms in reverence. Li Fang urged him to proceed directly to the Western Pure Land, to which he responded with firm resolve, saying, "Yes. Thus he passed away (as recorded in the *Fanben Suoyan* by Xu Jiafu).

Qian Wanyi, courtesy name Yishan, was a native of Changshu who resided in Meili Town. His family had been engaged in the wine trade for generations, but he subsequently took up the precept against killing and cultivated the practice of Pure Land Buddhism, striving to reform his former ways.
He had only one son, who died of tuberculosis; as the boy chanted the Buddha’s name before passing away, those nearby...
They mocked him. Nevertheless, Wan Yi continued to support the Buddha as before. One night, the shop caught fire. Looking toward the sky, he prayed, "My karmic lot is that this building should burn;
I pray only that the neighboring houses remain unharmed. After the fire was extinguished, the neighbors were indeed uninjured.

Initially, Wan Yi had exhorted his mother, Lady Wu, to observe the perpetual fast and recite the Buddha’s name, and she followed his advice. Soon thereafter, she herself also abstained from meat and blood; however, her residual habits had not yet [fully vanished].
He abandoned [the habit]. Although he was fond of drinking wine, his close relative Xie Fengwu exhorted and warned him, and he made a determined effort to eliminate it.
In the spring of the twenty-second year of the Daoguang era, his wife passed away; he remained composed and serene. When someone urged him to take another wife, Wan Yi refused him, saying:

"I have a son who died in infancy; what would be the point of taking another? Moreover, my ambition lies in transcending the world; how could I concern myself with such trivial matters as lineage and succession? This...

In the summer of that year, he suffered from a coughing-up-of-blood ailment. He redoubled his efforts in reciting the Buddha’s name, and his resolve regarding birth and death became even more urgent. By the beginning of the seventh month, his illness had become critical;
whenever he attempted to eat, he would vomit. Fengwu went to visit him and informed him of the accounts of ancient worthies who, by abstaining from food, beheld the Buddha.
He said with joy, "There is such a great opportunity; I shall courageously undertake it.

That very next day, he bathed and washed himself, went before the Buddha to offer incense and make a vow, observed the fast for seven days, provided funds for the release of living beings, and sought rebirth in the Pure Land.
He recited the Buddha's name day and night without ceasing, eating only melons when thirsty. When others asked him why he did not sleep throughout the night, he replied that he felt no fatigue.
He said, "It is beneficial that I do not sleep, for it allows me to practice the Buddha-recitation extensively. When I was not ill, I could find no peace;

now that I am ill, I have leisure and this is precisely the time to apply myself with effort. How could there be any weariness? When the seven-day period came to an end, his consciousness became confused and disordered.

He was given thin gruel to eat, which immediately caused him bitter bloating and distress. After a long while, his delirium grew even more severe. Terrified, he joined his palms above his pillow and ordered his finger to be burned.
Fengwu said, "At this moment, making such a vow and burning your finger are not as effective as focusing your mind solely on the Western Paradise.
Thereupon, he closed his eyes and recited the Buddha’s name; at first he struggled, exerting himself with fierce diligence. His spirit—
His resolve was firm and settled. Furthermore, he obtained the assistance of some dozen people, who maintained the sound of the Buddha’s name day and night without interruption.

On the evening of the tenth day, he said that he saw a person come before his bed and command him not to eat any melons or fruits. When asked who he was, the person replied, "I am a messenger from the higher realms.
Having spoken, he vanished. The following day, he suddenly beheld the three holy ones of the West, radiant with light and endowed with the marks of excellence.
Standing before him, he intended to leap into the golden platform. Hearing a voice from the air say, "Your body is not yet pure," he was immediately commanded to bathe in fragrant water.
Upon finishing his bath, the three sages appeared before him as they had been before.

He further said to his family members, "I have already traveled to the Pure Land and seen countless lotus flowers; I sat within them, and the bliss was beyond description. He then pointed to his own body.
He said, "This is not my body. At dawn on the twelfth day, he told his mother, "The Buddha has filled the room.
Facing west, he sat cross-legged with palms joined and passed away at the age of thirty-eight (from the biography of Qian Yishan compiled by Xie Fengwu).

The Western Historian says: Though he encountered adverse circumstances, his original resolve did not waver; though entangled in the suffering of illness, he maintained his right mindfulness with steadfastness.
In the end, he was moved by auspicious signs to ascend the Golden Terrace and his spirit roamed the Lotus Realm; that he attained such a high rank is beyond doubt.
Alas! How courageous indeed was this traveler between China and India!

Hua Han-cha, whose courtesy name was Chuan, was a native of Suzhou. Over seventy years of age, he encountered the virtuous man Jiang Wenxun, who instructed him in the Dharma gate of *nianfo* (recitation of the Buddha’s name) and invited him to receive his support.
His faith became profound and sincere, and he took refuge under the Venerable Jingmao.
One day, while prostrating before the Buddha, he suddenly saw lotus flowers filling the void. From then on, his power of mindfulness became increasingly pure.
On the evening of the nineteenth day of the first month in the twenty-fourth year of the Daoguang era, he recited the names of the Buddhas until midnight, his voice never ceasing.
When people questioned him, he said, "I am about to depart for the Western Paradise. The following morning, he dressed himself in ceremonial robes and intended to go to Jiang Wenxun.
He took his leave at home, but because it was raining, he stayed behind. His family, believing him to be free from illness, paid no heed. After a short while, they went in to see him;
he had passed away, sitting cross-legged with palms joined. (Recorded by Yang Oucha and Zhou Shangwen).
Fang Buying, courtesy name Xiaoxiang, was a native of Kunshan. He was skilled in calligraphy and painting and possessed many artistic talents.

Having studied the art of spirit mediumship (*fúluán*), he followed the divine teachings and recited the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī*. Every morning upon rising, he would perform his fixed devotions several dozen times. Subsequently, he encountered Zhang...

At dawn, she exhorted [her followers] to cultivate the Pure Land, whereupon she began to focus her mind exclusively on proceeding toward the West. One day, she manifested a slight illness; her daily activities remained as usual.
In the evening, she said to her servant, "The time for my departure is tomorrow. You must be careful not to inform the mistress. The servant replied:
"I did not tell you because I feared that after the event, there might be resentment. [The friend] said, "Even if there were resentment, you spoke of the matters of birth and death;
these are not things that others can know in advance. Bu-ying nodded his head. The next day, a friend came to visit him.
Bu-ying invited him to sit by the steps and said, "Recite the Amitābha Sūtra for me. The friend said, "I have not practiced or studied it; how shall I do so? Bu-ying then took out the sūtra.
He gave it to him, saying, "I shall instruct you. Thereupon, he recited the sutra from beginning to end with composure. As soon as he raised the Buddha's name, his gaze shone upward;
with a smile and a twitching of his beard, he looked intently at [the master] and had already passed away (as recorded by Wang Shixin).
Zhu Linsu, whose courtesy name was Wenquan, was a student at the school of Xinyang. Approaching fifty years of age, he contracted a life-threatening illness and was struck with great fear.

Consequently, he turned his mind toward the Inner Canon (Buddhist scriptures), never letting go of the volumes from his hands. He frequently presented books encouraging virtue to others, his resolve remaining steadfast.
Regarding his benefit to others: at that time, Venerable Ryōkan retired from Seirin-ji and resided at Sonshō-an. He maintained pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).

Rinsho took refuge in him and received the five precepts, receiving the Dharma name In’yu. He established a religious society at Sonshō-an that met once a month to perform the Sūtra Repentance of Siming.
Together with the members of the society, they encouraged one another and gave lectures on the Pure Land teachings. Later, his two eyes became dim.

His vision failed, so he could no longer read books; nevertheless, his diligence in reciting the scriptures increased. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he silently recited the name of the Buddha of the Western Paradise without ceasing.
At the age of seventy, he manifested illness for several months. A few days before his passing, he saw white light within his dreams and composed three verses. The first says:
"Once drawn into the dust and toil of worldly life by fame and profit, one busily pursues them..."

Aware of my transgressions, family members reproach me from all sides until resentment fills my ears. With no means for livelihood, I pass my old age in despondency. Finding joy in the Way and contentment in poverty, I know that destiny exists.
Keeping my mind pure and nurturing my nature, I await the higher realms. Responding to the world as conditions arise, I bring closure to past karma;

like illusory scenes or empty flowers, I let them shift and change as they will. One says: "A traveler in a foreign land for seventy autumns—how could these fluctuations between rise and fall have occurred without cause?"

Turning back, he realized the shore and returned directly; unchanging yet following conditions, he wandered with ease. One version says: "Karmic retribution is now exhausted; fortunately, my self-nature has not been deluded.
Treading the path of non-arising, I have led my mind to the West. Then, as he rose from his seat to recite the Buddha’s name, he passed away.
More than an hour after his breath ceased, his palms remained tightly clasped and would not open. This occurred in the twentieth year of the Daoguang era.
Winter month of the fifth year (as recorded by Guo Yangshan and Xu Jafu).
Chen Huang, whose Dharma name was Guangsheng and courtesy name Xitang, was a native of Shimen in Jiaxing. He engaged in trade in Suzhou and observed the lifelong fast.
He served the Buddha and was upright and outspoken by nature. He took refuge with Master Beidu Hai and subsequently received the five precepts from Master Lingjiu Yi.
Every day, he joined Zhu Linshu in establishing a *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) society at Dinghui Temple; though his schedule was busy, he never ceased this practice.
In the tenth month of the twenty-fifth year of the Daoguang era, he suffered from diarrhea. On the sixth day, his friend Tan Yunping went to visit him.
Huang said, "Your arrival is most timely. I wish to depart early tomorrow morning; please go to Little Potalaka to bid farewell to Zhu Yintang.
At that time, because the distance was great and it was already late, Yintang did not arrive. Huang then looked at his younger brother and said, "You study medicine;
try taking my pulse for me. From now on, whenever a pulse pattern resembles this, you must never [prescribe] it again."
This was to show the way. After a short while, he calmly recited the Buddha’s name. At midnight, his voice gradually grew more intense. Someone asked him, "Do you see the Buddha?
He replied, "I see the Great Monk; it is simply far away. When dawn broke, he passed away peacefully. He was fifty-five years old.
Four years later, there was a man named Xue Shaoji in Suzhou who, during Huan’s lifetime, had frequently hosted him at his home and encouraged him to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name.

Later, he also resolved his mind toward faith and practice. At the age of sixty, when his illness became critical and his consciousness grew clouded and confused, he suddenly uttered a sound like the ringing of a bell, saying:
"This moment is most urgent; why do you not recite the Buddha's name? You must lie facing west. Shaoji then turned himself over on his own.
When the family members went to look, it was unmistakably the sound of the bell at his lips. Shortly thereafter, Shaoji passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name. This is [the account].
This occurred in the third month of the twenty-eighth year of the Daoguang era (as recounted by Qian Anxuan and Zhu Yintang).
The Western Historian says: It has been heard many times that those who rely on auxiliary conditions can attain rebirth;
yet, for one who passes away several years ago to still cherish the deep affection of old friends, manifesting spiritual traces to provide guidance and deliverance—this truly transcends all ages.
What a remarkable and extraordinary matter this is!
Guo Guangguang, whose courtesy name was Shangbin and also known as Yangshan, was a native of Yuanhe in Suzhou. He was a man of pure integrity and conscientious character. His profession...

As a physician, he did not calculate his fees; whenever a patient summoned him, he would go at once. In his middle years, he followed the Western Teachings and received the precepts of refuge from Master Beidu Hai.
His dharma name was Guangren. Every morning upon rising, he would quietly sweep his small room and silently recite the Buddha’s name, doing so without ceasing through cold or heat.
His ancestors had left him a fish pond located at Wutang north of Lumu, which he leased out to others.

He caught fish to provide for the expenses of ritual sweeping and offerings. Having repeatedly discussed this with his kinsmen, he emptied his purse to replace their funds and requested that an inscription be carved on stone.
He donated the site as a "River for Releasing Life," saving countless living beings. He often told his family that there would be misfortune in the eighth month of the Jihyou year.
In the spring of the twenty-ninth year of the Daoguang era, the cyclical year being Jihyou, he fell gravely ill at home.
The people around him were filled with fear. Guāngwǎn shook his hand and said, "Do not worry; the fragrance of the chrysanthemum has not yet been smelled, so my life is not yet ended.
When the eighth month arrived, he fell ill again and summoned monks to chant the Buddha's name. On the fifth day of the month, his family asked when his passing would occur.
Guangguang raised two fingers. On the evening of the seventh day, he passed away with his palms joined; warmth surged from the crown of his head and only dissipated after a long while.
He was fifty-six years old. (Recorded by Guo Chensheng). Master Xishi said:
"I have known Yangshan at the Discourse on the Way Assembly. His gentle and harmonious air overflowed from his very countenance."
Furthermore, when I inquired about his cultivation of pure karma, I was already certain that he would surely be reborn [in the Pure Land].
In the end, he did not fail to meet my expectations. Is it not all the more praiseworthy that he sacrificed his clan and gave up the river?

The general discussion states: From antiquity to the present day, there have been many talented individuals and eminent scholars who have discoursed upon the Way and debated virtue; such figures are not rare to encounter.

Yet, if one seeks those who, at the moment of death, remained serene and composed while manifesting various auspicious signs, one might find not even a single person among hundreds, thousands, or tens of thousands.

As for those who attain rebirth through this practice of mindfulness of the Buddha alone, some perceive extraordinary fragrances filling their rooms, while others behold transformation-buddhas welcoming them into the air;
such various auspicious omens are too numerous to enumerate fully. Yet, the deluded ordinary people of the world fail to take heed of these signs.
On the contrary, they have aligned themselves with the ranks of the Confucianists, disparaging and rejecting [the Buddha].
Consequently, they have ultimately sunk into the ocean of suffering, where no one can rescue them. How tragic!
Wangsheng Wusheng, the fifth in the miscellaneous lineage of those who attained rebirth, was a native of Hangzhou.
Both his grandfather and father were students of the Imperial Academy. At the beginning of the Shunzhi era of the Qing dynasty, the imperial army surrounded [the city].
In the city, his parents were separated; he was captured as a child and sent to serve under the command of General Zhang. At that time, he was only thirteen years old.
He lamented to himself, "I am originally the son of a Confucian scholar, yet now I am so base and lowly. This must surely be the result of my past karma.

He then made a vow before the Buddha to observe the fasts, recite the Buddha’s name, and daily chant the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, dedicating the merit toward rebirth in the Western Paradise. At the age of sixteen, his original...

The government issued grain to fulfill the labor service quota; he immediately used the proceeds from the grain tax to purchase incense for offerings to the Buddha and knelt while reciting the sacred name of Amitābha.
On the twenty-second day of the tenth month in the fourteenth year, he suddenly informed the local official that he wished to depart for the Western Pure Land.

The official did not believe him and rebuked him as a madman. The following day, he again requested leave before the Provincial Commander-in-Chief. The Commander-in-Chief was enraged and issued a formal reprimand.

The official bound him and beat him fifteen times, yet he harbored no complaints. He then took his leave of the various military camps and set a limit for himself to pass away on the first day of the eleventh month.
On that day at the fifth watch, he bathed, burned incense, and completed his prostrations before the Buddha. He then went once more to the official’s boat to bid farewell.
The official was greatly enraged and dispatched soldiers to track him down. They saw him facing west, performing three prostrations, sitting upright, and speaking.
The verse says: "While his body was in the midst of the camp, he left the household life; his donning of armor was his wearing of the *kāṣāya*.

With every stroke of the sword, he beheld Amitābha Buddha face-to-face; with every arrow shot, he pierced a white lotus. The verse ended, he spontaneously spat forth fire and incinerated his own body.
The officials and leaders of the entire camp all gazed from afar and prostrated themselves; the official’s entire family observed the fast and maintained the precepts (*liánzàng*).
Shen Chengxian, Shen Chengxian.

A native of Kunshan, he resided in Xuanhua Ward and was by trade a carpenter. Over seventy years of age, he observed the fasts and recited the Buddha’s name, single-mindedly cultivating the Pure Land.
Though his hands never ceased from wielding the axe and chisel, the sound of the Buddha’s name never left his mouth. The tenth year of the Kangxi era...

In the third month of that year, he knew in advance that his time had come. Three days prior, he took leave of all his relatives and friends, saying that he was about to depart for the Western Land and would not see them again thereafter.
He told his family members, "Tomorrow is the fifteenth; I shall depart. At dawn the following day, he bathed, changed his clothes, and sat cross-legged facing west.
He brought a clean desk before him, burned incense, and recited the Buddha’s name until he passed away (*Xigu Zhizhi*).
Zhou Xuantang.

Zhou Xuantang was a native of Qianyang. Having initially entered public service, he soon came to see through the nature of worldly affairs. He immediately cast off all corrupt and evil ways and sat in meditation within a single room.
There, he recited the *Baiyi-zhou* (Mantra of the White-Robed One), observed the fasts, released living beings, and extensively practiced skillful means (*upāya*). Upon seeing those who were poor...
He provided protection and relief to those who were destitute according to his ability. Later, he encountered the practitioner Dàozhān, who exhorted him to cultivate the Pure Land.

Consequently, he resolved to recite the Buddha’s name with keen diligence, never flagging during the six periods of the day, and he further taught this practice to his friends and associates; many among them came to have faith and incline toward it.

He once carved a copy of the *Jile jinliang* (The Ferry of Ultimate Bliss) and distributed it widely. In the spring of the fifty-first year of the Qianlong era, during a time of famine, he raised funds for relief within the district.
As for the congee and gruel, Xuantang exerted himself with all his might, attending to his duties day and night.

One morning at the fifth watch, he suddenly rose, sought a bath, changed his clothes, and said to his wife and children: "The time has come for me to be born in the West. Do not follow the ways of the world;

simply recite the Buddha's name with a single mind. Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away, without uttering a single word regarding household affairs. That very morning, there was still...
People saw Xuantang at the soup kitchen, coming and going to inspect it (from the *Lianzong jiyao*). Master Xishi said:
"Since Xuantang had already attained rebirth in the Pure Land, why was he still at the soup kitchen?
It is likely that he displayed such miraculous traces to prevent people from harboring doubts or slander. Does this not further reveal the vastness of his vow-power?"

Yao Sheng, Yao Sheng, served as a laborer for Changzhou County. His family was poor; after his wife passed away, he did not remarry. He yielded his labor duties to others and devoted all his heart and mind to the affairs of the monastery.
He was upright by nature and could directly rebuke others for their faults. At night, he would settle [his mind].
He sat firmly and recited the Buddha’s name ten thousand times without interruption. When he was over twenty years old, he passed away due to illness;
he died sitting upright, with fragrance filling the room and his crown appearing as if scorched. Lord Ding of Tie composed a poem in praise of him, saying: "Sweet springs and *zhicao* fungi..."

Originally there is neither root nor source. This lay practitioner comes from the West; he extensively delivers all those with whom he has a karmic affinity. When his affinities are exhausted, he simply returns home.
His heels are free from all entanglements; such a person is most difficult to encounter. With lofty aspirations, he gazes far and long. (From the *Xigu Jianwen Lu*)

Song Baoguan was a man from Huating. His family was poor, and he made his living by selling soy sauce. He served his mother with filial piety, providing her with delicious food and never delegating these duties to his brothers.
Upon hearing others speak of the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, he came to believe in it deeply and began to practice accordingly. One day, he addressed his mother:
He said, "My mother has an elder brother; I shall return west. He then immediately recited the Buddha's name and passed away while seated.
This occurred in the sixteenth year of the Jiaqing era (*Ranxiang ji*).
Chen Dexin, whose courtesy name was Dakun, was a farmer from Suzhou. While seeking coolness on a summer day, he happened upon a village inn where he saw the *Jingxin lu* (Record of Reverent Faith).

He requested that the village tutor explain it to him, and upon doing so, he attained a profound realization. Subsequently, he went along the streets to collect discarded paper. [He resided at] Peng Er-lin’s house.

When the Master heard of this, he summoned him into Wensheng Pavilion and exhorted him to practice the *nien-fo* samādhi. Although De-xin was originally illiterate, he followed these instructions with profound sincerity.
Later, he gradually became able to write. Before long, he served at Miaojitang in Suzhou, overseeing matters such as releasing captive animals and burying the dead.
Whenever he saw skulls, he frequently sighed in lamentation, realizing that the world is impermanent; thus, his recitation of the Buddha’s name grew even more earnest.

He was diligent in his practice and remained unmarried throughout his life. At the age of sixty-nine, his physical health remained as robust as ever. Suddenly, realizing that the time had come, he went to bid farewell to his relatives and friends.
When the appointed hour arrived, he sat silently inside his hall with the door closed for a long while. His colleagues pushed open the door to look inside;
they saw a single Buddha image upon the table, two candles shining brightly, and the air filled with the scent of incense. With a mind of virtue, he passed away sitting facing west.
This was an event that occurred on the full moon of the eighth month in the eighteenth year of the Jiaqing era (*Ranxiang ji*).

"The Beggar of the East Gate, the Beggar of the East Gate" resided in a single dilapidated house by the Mingxing Bridge in Songjiang; every day he would go toward the city gate to recite the *Heart Sutra*.
He possessed one scroll of a sutra. When someone asked for a single coin, he would thank them with repeated voices if given it; yet even when scolded, he paid no heed.

He would simply provide enough parched grain and husks for one day, then close his door and recite the Buddha’s name. Cai Xizhai, the Provincial Governor, marveled at this and personally offered him money and rice, wishing to repair his hut.
The mendicant declined them, whereupon Xizhai said, "What I offer is all from my modest salary; how could it..."

"Is this not the Water of Thievery (Dàiquán)? The beggar said, "I have long known that you, sir, maintain such strict integrity and purity. I feared that for the sake of food, clothing, or shelter, I might shift from my original resolve.
Since there is no other way, please allow me to drink as a monk for your sake. He then took the gifts with him to Dongchan Temple to perform offerings.

Once he had finished, he returned to his dilapidated hut and continued to recite the Buddha's name as before. During the Jiaqing era, he passed away while sitting upright, free from illness, to the amazement of the villagers.
He was buried behind Taohua Hermitage (*Ranxiang ji*).

The "Dull-headed Daoist," the "Dull-headed Daoist," surnamed Wang, was a native of Zhili. He was extremely simple-minded. When his parents passed away and he lacked food, he lay exhausted in a dilapidated hut. There was no...
Whatever he planned, [the master] would sometimes give him money, yet never distinguish between the large or small amount.

The Daoist Chen of the capital took him as a disciple, ordering him to sweep the ground and gather firewood daily. In the evening, he was tasked with reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha several hundred times and performing prostrations, using the burning of incense as his measure of progress.
Chitou could not chant the Buddha’s name in rhythm; he was frequently drowsy and wished to sleep. The Daoist used a long pole...
He struck him, saying, "You are so ignorant and dull-witted; do you still not know what diligence is? This continued for three years.
One night, he let out a great laugh, "Ha ha! The practitioner struck him again, whereupon Chitou said, "Today, you cannot strike me."
