It has not yet vanished. How could one raise it up to manifest it everywhere within the inner chambers?
Regarding the seventh category of living beings, the chicken:
During the Chongzhen era of the Ming dynasty, there was a man named Wu Xueya who served as the Judicial Intendant of Fuzhou. Throughout his life, he had reverently upheld the Buddha-dharma.
At the Kaiyuan Temple in that region, many monks consumed meat and did not observe the precepts. Xueya requested an inscription to be carved on a stone to prohibit such practices.

One day, while sitting in the meditation hall, a rooster let out a cry that sounded like the chanting of the Buddha’s name. He had it caught and said to the monks: "If [you truly practice the Dharma, why do you act otherwise?]"
His colleagues said, "It has been a long time since this temple has kept living creatures; how could there be a chicken here? Now we see that even such an animal possesses Buddha-nature.

You have shaved your head and donned the robes of a monk, yet you break the precepts far more than this creature. Thereupon, the temple monks established a vow of fasting and purification, and they took the chicken back to their quarters.
It constantly recited the name of the Buddha without ceasing. Later, when the official was passing through Danyang on his way to a new post, they escorted him as far as Haihui Hermitage.

This was because it served as a place to receive the public, inspiring faith in those from both near and far. When a rooster arrived at the hermitage, [the monk] immediately chanted the Buddha’s name and passed away standing.

A stupa was subsequently built for him and offerings were made there. Furthermore, there was a monk named Jueyuan from Zhongzhou who vowed to provide meals for the monastics at Donglin Temple on Mount Lu.
He established a checkpoint to solicit donations. At that time, a monk guarding the checkpoint returned from begging for alms in the city of Huaihua, accompanied by a large rooster.

While on his way back, the monks escorted him to Pāṭaliputra and closed the gate behind them. The rooster flew out from atop the roof and pursued them to the checkpoint, circling there and refusing to leave.
It remained at the gate for three years. Later, it was taken to the East Grove (Pūrvaśaila), where it received the precepts.

When the assembly ascended the hall to recite the Buddha’s name, the rooster suddenly followed along. After the occasion for providing meals to the monks concluded that year, the rooster sat in meditation and passed away; it was then buried.

Beside the temple, there are further accounts recorded of a snake that listened to the Dharma in Jiangxi, a cat that attained parinirvāṇa while sitting in Lúzhōu, a monkey that attained parinirvāṇa while sitting in the Gorges, a sparrow that attained parinirvāṇa standing upright at Zhàgāo Town in Cháo County, and a pig that attained parinirvāṇa while sitting after being released by the Grand Councilor Huáng Tíngcuì.
Such various spiritual wonders cannot be fully recounted. (Táng Yízhī, *Jīnyùchéng* and *Jìngtǔchénzhōng*)
The general discussion states: In this world of the five turbidities, defiled minds easily flare up while pure virtues are difficult to accomplish.

Thus, a sutra says that a single day of courageous practice in the Sahā world is superior to a hundred years in a Pure Land. Now, when comparing the ease of non-human beings to that of human beings, it is even more difficult for us.
Yet, with a single thought of sincere devotion, one is liberated from the three miserable realms; if this is true even for non-human beings, how much more so for humans?
O person! *The Continued Compilation of the Record of Sages and Worthies of the Pure Land*, Volume Four (End):
The Collection on Planting Lotuses.
The Layman Lian Gui compiled the *Continued Collection of Records of Sages and Worthies of the Pure Land*, gathering verified accounts of rebirth totaling over one hundred entries.
However, those obtained after the work was completed were likewise numerous.
I have therefore set them aside as a separate volume, without categorizing them by type or arranging them chronologically, recording them as they came to my knowledge through hearing and sight.

It is titled *Zhonglian ji* (Collection on Planting Lotus). Taking the words of Master Siqi as a model, I share with you the intent of one who plants lotus seeds, awaiting those who will compile the three volumes in the future to extract them.
Autumn, the ninth month, the thirtieth year of the Daoguang era. Recorded by the student of Pure Land practice, Chen Benren.
Shànlóng, a native of Línghǎi County, Tāizhōu, was sixteen years old when he left the household life at Báilóng Monastery in Sūzhōu. He visited...

He contemplated the saying, "Who is it that recites the Buddha’s name? and attained awakening. He sat through the night without lying down and did not eat after noon. For three years, he maintained a vegetarian diet of plain food.
He pierced his tongue to draw blood with which he transcribed the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

Daily, he maintained a fixed regimen of reciting the Buddha’s name sixty thousand times, one copy of the *Lotus Sūtra*, and performing one thousand six hundred prostrations before the Buddha. Wearing a single robe throughout both winter and summer, he refrained from idle talk and exerted himself in his practice.
His illness worsened, yet he redoubled his diligent practice. One night, while in meditative contemplation, he heard a voice from the air announcing:
"You shall attain rebirth in the Middle Grade; be careful not to slacken. Thereupon, he set aside all medicinal treatments and focused his mind solely on proceeding toward the West.
On the sixth day of the fourth month, he passed away while sitting upright. This was in the second year of the Daoguang era, at the age of twenty-six.
Dachandachan (達禪達禪), surnamed Di (狄), was a native of Jia County. He left the household life at Jingde Temple in his home district. He had twice practiced the Pratyutpanna Samādhi.

Later, he resided at Dichun Hermitage in Beigang; the sound of his reciting the Buddha’s name constantly reached outside his door, and whenever he saw someone, he would immediately exhort and admonish them.
Regarding birth and death, one day he said to his disciple Jingyu, "I shall certainly depart next year; you all must not forget the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.
The following year, he presided over a period of nianfo (Buddha-recitation) at Qingjing Hermitage.
On the third day, he manifested illness, yet he continued to enter the hall to recite the Buddha’s name. After some time had passed, he sat upright and passed away.
Wang Junrong, Wang Junrong.
A native of Taicang, he maintained the precepts and pursued his studies from childhood; his realization of the Dharma was exceptionally profound.

Later, he cultivated the Pure Land, reciting the Buddha’s name ten thousand times daily. On the second day of the eighth month in the fifty-sixth year of the Kangxi era, he knew in advance that the time had come.
He requested the Pure Name Hermitage (Jingming’an). When Elder Qianxing arrived, he was asked to serve as a witness. It was noon.

Master Qian said, "It would be appropriate for the date of your departure to be a day later. He replied, "I am determined to leave today. He then took up his brush and composed a verse; with palms joined, he passed away.
His final instruction was that he be enshrined in a coffin. His daughter embraced him to place him inside, but her strength could not prevail. She therefore prayed silently.
...him. Suddenly, he ascended lightly into the air. He was eighty-one years old.
Tang Jingyuan, whose courtesy name was Jungu, was a state student at the National Academy during the Yuanhe era. He diligently cultivated the Pure Land practice; whenever he recited the Name, he—

He pointed with his finger at a pearl. At the age of seventy-four, he passed away without illness. More than an hour after his breath had ceased, his fingers still moved, making gestures such as counting on his fingers.
(Liu Shen Zaiyuan)

Shen Zaiyuan, whose courtesy name was Gui'e and self-styled name Ke-seng, was a native of Wujiang. In his middle years, he engaged in the business of trade; however, after reaching over sixty, he ceased such pursuits and devoted himself wholeheartedly to the Pure Land.

He maintained a lifelong vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha’s name more than ten thousand times every day. By nature, he was compassionate and forgiving, and whatever surplus he possessed [he gave away].
He would frequently provide relief to the poor and release captive animals. In the autumn of the sixteenth year of the Jiaqing era, a monk arrived unexpectedly and went straight to his quarters;

after speaking but a few words, they attained a profound and penetrating realization of the ultimate mystery. Furthermore, [the monk] entrusted him with the instruction that on the day of his eventual passing, he must forbid his relatives from weeping.
Having finished speaking, he departed. Daozai was moved by this feeling; he lit incense outside the gate and offered his respects from afar. That winter, he manifested illness.
The sound of reciting the Buddha’s name never ceased from his mouth. He abstained from grain for seven days, subsisting only on water.

On the morning of the sixth day of the twelfth month, he ordered forty-eight pairs of candles to be lit, set up an incense altar in the hall, washed his body, changed his clothes, and sat upright with palms joined.
He chanted the names of the Buddhas aloud; his attendants called out in unison to assist him. After a short while, his breath became like smoke, and his voice gradually faded until it ceased.
He was seventy-two years old. At his enshrouding, his countenance appeared as if he were still alive.
Wang Jiliang, a native of Jinshan County, was fifty years of age. He took refuge in the Triple Gem, recited the Buddha’s name, and practiced the release of living beings with unwavering devotion.
In the second month of that year, he fell ill; he rejected all medical treatment and medicine, maintaining the recitation of the Buddha’s name day and night, abstaining from speech.

Regarding his family affairs, he said only: "I look forward to the day; I shall depart. When the appointed time arrived, it was indeed so. Two days after his death, someone went to retrieve his prayer beads;
even after he had passed away, they were still tightly gripped and could not be removed.
Xia Yaowen.
A native of Huating, he observed the fast and recited the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion to the Pure Land for over forty years. His entire family abstained from meat and alcohol.
In the tenth month of the fourth year of the Daoguang era, he fell slightly ill; on the fourteenth day, he commanded his attendants to help him rise and joined [his palms].

He passed away while recollecting the Buddha with his palms joined. His final instructions were that he be encoffined; at the time of being placed in the coffin, his body remained supple, his neck was warm, and his complexion did not change.
He was seventy-five years old.
Layman Cao, Layman Cao.

His background is not well known. He maintained the fasts and recited the Buddha’s name with diligence for many years, yet he remained humble and earnest, as if fearing that he might fail to achieve his goal at the moment of death.
In the winter of the twentieth year of the Daoguang era, he fell slightly ill. One day, his...
At dawn, his son went to pay his respects and noticed that his father’s facial expression was unusual. Pointing into the air, he said, "Do you see the Buddha and the assembly of bodhisattvas?
I did not expect that the merit of holding the Name would reach such a state. You shall serve as my witness;
I am now following the Buddha back to the West. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
"Old Lady Shao, Old Lady Shao! This is Shao Ziyin of Changshu, the mother of a Maocai (a scholar of talent). She had long been a devoted follower of the Buddha.
In the twelfth month of the eighteenth year of the Daoguang era, she fell slightly ill. Suddenly, she said to Ziyin: 'Tomorrow, you must welcome your sister home. Ziyin followed her instructions."
No one could fathom what she meant. The next day, when the daughter returned home, the old woman said, "I wish to depart today, to bring an end to the karmic ties between mother and daughter.
Upon hearing this, the daughter wept. The old woman laughed and said, "Life and death are but a single illusory manifestation.
She then spoke of other matters. At noon, she said, "The time has come. When her daughter asked where she was going, the old woman pointed toward the sky with her finger and said:
The Buddha came and then departed.
As for Lady Zhang:
she was a native of Jinshan County who married Mr. Wang. Her elder paternal aunt, Lady Wang, cultivated the Pure Land practices and attained rebirth there. This is her story.
I have seen the *Jingtu shengxian lu xubian* (Continued Records of Holy and Sages of the Pure Land). Lady Zhang had believed in the Pure Land since childhood.

She was simple and unadorned by nature and had long suffered from illness, yet she never ceased her recitation of the Buddha’s name. Having received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, she expressed no desire for domestic ties.

Although she had been betrothed at a young age, she married in the twentieth year of the Jiaqing era. After more than a year, she returned to her mother’s home for a visit; it happened that her illness became critical.
He invited both monastics and laypeople to recite the Buddha’s name in unison. Before long, he became short of breath; they helped him up and seated him facing west.
He recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* and the names of the Buddhas, his eyes shining as they gazed upward, his face bearing a smile. After a short while, he passed away.
Lady Ding, Lady Ding, was a native of Jinnshan; she was the wife of Zhang. Her elder paternal aunt, Lady Wang, exhorted her to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
On the same day, they both received the lay precepts. Lady Wang passed away first; seeing her aunt’s correct mindfulness at the moment of death, Lady Ding was further moved and inspired.

He chanted his daily recitations at fixed times and dedicated the merit toward the Western Pure Land. In his daily life, he performed various meritorious deeds and strictly observed the precepts against killing while releasing captive creatures.

Following the legacy of Master Wang Shi, he had a daughter who married into the Taiyuan family; when she fell ill with consumption, he instructed her to recite the Buddha’s name, and she passed away peacefully.

More than a year later, Lady Ding fell ill with abdominal distension; she found it difficult even to turn over in bed. As her end approached, she summoned all her strength to rise and sit facing west.
She called for her family members to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra* and the Buddha’s name. After barely a hundred invocations, it appeared as though she were gazing intently at something.

When asked whether she had seen the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas, she nodded her head slightly. A short while later, both her voice and her breath ceased entirely. This occurred in the eighth year of the Daoguang era.

On the ninth day of the fifth month of this year, Gao Shizhen—whose courtesy name is Yansan—is a native of Qiantang. His ancestors resided in Meili, Shan-yin; therefore, he styled himself [accordingly].

The Daoist Master Meixi was fifty-one years old when he fell ill and entered the underworld to tour the various hells. There, an official of the netherworld addressed him, saying: "You must now return;
you must single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and single-mindedly practice good deeds. Then you will surely be able to escape from suffering. Shi Zhen recognized this [vision].
Three days later, he revived, and his illness was completely cured. He resolved his mind to recite the Buddha’s name and practiced various wholesome dharmas, turning his face toward the West.
He practiced this method himself and also taught it to others. In this way, twenty-five years passed until he reached the age of seventy-five.

Three days before his death, knowing that the time had come, he said, "Now I am free from suffering and affliction. He exhorted the people of the world, saying, "Practice and cultivate yourselves early."
"Do not leave behind any cause for regret. He passed away peacefully. This was during the twelfth month of the thirty-fifth year of the Qianlong era.
Ding Shiji (style name Ziyi), a student of the Yuanhe Academy, aged fifty, took refuge in the Dharma with Master Beidu Hai.
His name was Guangru. He diligently cultivated pure karma for ten years without weariness. In the winter of the twenty-fifth year of the Daoguang era, he fell ill.
Every night, he would invariably recite the Buddha’s name one thousand times, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* three times, and the *Vow Text* once.
One night, as he recited to the passage, "The pure light shines upon me," he suddenly smiled and said, "I now behold the Buddha’s pure light. Ten...

On the thirteenth day of the first month, at the hour of midnight, as his kinsmen sat in a circle before his bed, they suddenly smelled a wondrous fragrance drifting through the air and gradually filling the entire room.
They all marveled at this. On the following day, Shijie asked for a brush and composed two seven-character quatrains in the style of the *Lishi* (Seven-Verse) form;
however, the characters were blurred and indistinct, though the final line of one was recognizable: "When I have my will, I shall return home."
She saw only the six characters of the Buddha’s name. At night, she joined her palms, recited the Buddha’s name, and passed away at the age of sixty-one.
Lady Lu was a native of Suzhou.
She married Bao Xin’yu, a student at the Imperial Academy, and served her mother-in-law with filial piety. Once, while attending to her during an illness, she... [text ends]
As for her loosening of the belt [her renunciation of worldly ties], it has been for many months. Because her mind was simple and sincere, she was courageous in performing virtuous deeds.

Whenever she constructed bridges, repaired roads, gave away clothing, or released living beings, she always felt a sense of solemnity in her heart. Her ladyship would invariably assist and support her with all her might. In her youth, she once traveled across the sea to visit Putuo Shan;
after middle age, however, her feet never crossed the threshold of her home. For forty years, she has risen at dawn to recite sutras, dharanis, and the names of the Buddhas.

In the middle [of his life], there was not a single day of idleness. In the fourth month of the twenty-seventh year of the Daoguang era, he contracted a slight illness. He told his son and daughters-in-law:

"Last night in a dream, three people in ancient robes and caps invited me, saying that because my recitation of the Buddha's name has been so sincere, they will allow me to see the Buddha this very day.
At dawn on the eighth day, he faced west, recited the Buddha’s name, and passed away at the age of eighty-five.

Qiu Fengtai, whose courtesy name was Xingjie, was a grain-student (linsheng) from Changzhou. From his youth, he suffered from the ailment of hemoptysis. In the summer of that year, the illness flared up violently;
he suddenly took faith in the Buddha-vehicle and invited Master Jingmao to recite the Buddha’s name before his bed. His illness subsequently abated, and he withdrew behind closed doors.
He did not emerge from his state. He had read all the various texts concerning the Pure Land. In the summer of the twenty-ninth year of the Daoguang era, his illness flared up again;

yet he did not cease reciting the Buddha’s name. Sitting cross-legged with palms joined, he passed away. His father, Wei Luo, was a vice-juren who had long practiced virtuous deeds and cultivated the Pure Land path.
Before long, she also passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name.
As for the Qian family: her name was Lan-zhen. A native of Suzhou, she was naturally dignified and composed from childhood. She married Gu Gan as his wife. Later...
Because she was pregnant, she contracted a severe illness that became critical; half of her body grew cold and her consciousness became clouded and confused.

A close relative visited her and exhorted her husband to vow to abstain from killing and to recite the sacred name of Avalokiteśvara. He followed this advice. After three days, she broke into a sweat and her illness vanished as if lost.
From then on, the Qian family turned their hearts toward the pure practice; every night they burned incense and recited the name of the Great Being (Mahāsattva), even amidst strict [circumstances].

He did not cease his practice even during the extremes of cold and heat. In the winter of the twenty-eighth year of the Daoguang era, he contracted a coughing fit with blood, which gradually grew more severe.
It continued until the eighth day of the tenth month of the twenty-ninth year, when he suddenly said, "The sea of suffering is vast and boundless; I shall emerge from it in three days.
On the morning of the tenth day, he ordered that an incense altar be set up to the right of his bed and said, "Today, I am certain to depart."
He continued to recite the name of the Great Being (Mahāsattva) from his mouth. After a short while, he suddenly began to chant "Amitābha Buddha.

By the hour of Shen (5–7 p.m.), his voice gradually grew faint, and he passed away peacefully facing west. At dawn the following day, the crown of his head remained warm. He was twenty-nine years old.

Qian Wenbin, courtesy name Yangyu, was a native of Changzhou County in Suzhou. Every morning at dawn, he would silently practice the method of ten recitations and perform acts of goodness, all of which he kept secret.
He once spent a thousand pieces of gold to release various fish and birds. He had long suffered from the ailment of hemoptysis.
At the age of forty-one, his illness became severe. He invited Master Jingmao to take refuge in the Triple Gem. During his illness, he took joy in hearing the sound of chanting the Buddha’s name.
On the day before his death, he invited Master Lingjiu Fohai to his bedside; there, they made offerings to the Buddha, prepared seats, and he received the Bodhisattva precepts.
He left several monks behind to chant the Buddha’s name in rotation. At the hour of *buh* (the late afternoon) on the following day, he urgently ordered them to help him sit up.
He sat upright, gazed intently at the Buddha image, and passed away. This occurred on the twenty-fifth day of the second month in the twenty-eighth year of the Daoguang era.
By Qian Wencan.

Qian Wencan, whose Dharma name was Kongsang and courtesy name Anxuan, was the younger brother of Wenbin. In his early twenties, he encountered Wu Zongwei, who instructed him in the Pure Land practice.
He took refuge with Master Jianxin and received the Bodhisattva precepts from Master Yi of Lingjiu.

He maintained a lifelong vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha’s name for over twenty years. He once published the *Nianfo Jingce* (Exhortation to Mindfulness of the Buddha) and distributed it widely. Ling...
He solicited donations to construct sixteen-foot statues of the Three Holy Ones, but his funds were insufficient; Wencan assisted him in completing the project.

At Mount Yu, there was an ancient monastery where he likewise solicited funds to build three holy images, undertaking this entirely on his own. He also relied heavily on his efforts to cast a bronze bell for Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai.
Releasing living beings and aiding the poor became his regular practice every year. In the summer of the thirtieth year of the Daoguang era, he suffered from dysentery.
He sent someone to Mount Yu to invite his dharma friend Zhang Yuanqi. He said, "I and you are friends in life and death.

My illness is critical; I beg you to assist me for a while. Yuanqi replied, "I agree. Day after day they recited the Buddha's name together. Whenever [Wencan] became drowsy or wished to sleep, Yuanqi would urge him on.
Later, when Yuanqi wished to return home, Wencan said, "During these four days, I have been able to do without..."
"I am ill. I cannot wait beyond this. Yuanqi followed his instructions. When he returned four days later, [Wenchao's] stupor had intensified even further.
Yuanqi reported this to Quanchu (the account appears in the *Jingtu shengxian lu qianbian*). Wenchao wept profusely and, with great vigor, began to recite the Buddha’s name.
From the hour of Wei until Hai, his consciousness suddenly became clear; he continued throughout the night.
He was free from weariness. As dawn approached, he formed his hands into the shape of a lotus and showed them to Zhang, then passed away lying on his right side.
This was the fourth day of the seventh month. His final instruction was that no meat or wine should be used during the funeral rites. He was forty-three years old.
Dingyi Dingyi.
It is not clear from whence he originated. In his middle years, he left the household life and diligently upheld the precepts. He presided over Longqing Temple on Mount Jia in Danyang.
In the first year of the Tongzhi era, he sought refuge at Baoyan Temple by the Chu River, where he promoted the Lotus School and led the assembly.

He practiced the recitation of the Buddha’s name with such pure and uninterrupted devotion that he chanted the Buddha’s name fifty thousand times daily. He performed the Pure Repentance twice each day, never failing even amidst the extremes of cold and heat.

The fourfold assembly took refuge in his heart and all held the Elder of Mount Jia in the highest esteem. On the first day of the first month of the year Yichou, he announced in advance the date of his passing.
Each day he drank only two cups of clear water. On the morning of the seventh day, having completed the Liturgy of the Pure Land, he sat in the full lotus posture.
He sat upright facing west and passed away. Neighbors smelled the fragrance of lotus flowers, which did not dissipate for some time.
Mingzhou, Mingzhou—son of the Mao family of Qinyou—followed Guanyin Jingquan at a young age to receive the tonsure. At the age of eighteen, he received full ordination.
At Anle Temple in Linze, he made it his practice to respond to the needs of others. Later, he encountered Master Yongqing, who transmitted to him the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.

He subsequently resolved to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name. He later traveled back and forth to Qintang, where he daily investigated the profound meanings of the teachings; his faith grew ever more firm.

He constantly led the assembly in reciting the Buddha’s name; even when the candles were exhausted and the incense had burned away, he would still lament before the Buddha, vowing to be swiftly reborn in Sukhāvatī to benefit and deliver all sentient beings.
Consequently, those far and near turned their hearts toward him; even those of the icchantika class bowed their heads in refuge.
In the third month of the Yichou year of the Tongzhi era, he took his leave of his friends and acquaintances. On the first day of the fifth month, he manifested illness;

at dawn on the twelfth day, he performed prostrations before the Buddha and entered his coffin. He sat with the assembly reciting the name of the Buddha for four fixed incense sticks; by noon, his voice gradually grew faint.

Looking back, how swiftly time has passed! Qinyou is a secluded place by the lakeshore; yet within the past twenty years, the Lotus School has flourished to the point that its teachings are chanted from every household.
This is surely because Master Zhou initiated this movement.

Wang Shanqing, courtesy name Langxian, style name Faru, was a native of Renhe in Zhejiang. Orphaned at a young age, he followed his mother, Lady Zhuang, to live with his maternal relatives for his education.
He was exceptionally filial and possessed great intelligence. Just as he reached the age of thirteen, he entered the Confucian academy (*páng-gōng*). When his mother...

He passed away. His funeral rites were conducted according to the full requirements of propriety. He had betrothed himself to a lady of the Zhu family but had not yet married when he encountered the rebellion of the Yue-pi (Taiping Rebels).
Left all alone, he fled to Lusi Market in Jiangbei, where he met Xu Lingxu of Qingxiu from his own village, who invited him to serve as a private tutor.
He had long harbored the aspiration for transcendence. Upon meeting the lay practitioner Xu from the West, he was instructed in the dharma-gate of recitation.

Thereupon, he applied himself with earnest devotion to the inner scriptures; the meanings of all the sutras passed before his eyes without omission. When Xu returned to Zhejiang, he moved to the Tripitaka Hall in Yangzhou.
For over ten years, he maintained a vegetarian diet, frequently sitting in meditation, and kept few social ties. Whenever anyone came to seek the Way from him, [he would instruct them].

There was no one to whom he did not devote his heart in guiding and instructing them. His physical constitution was naturally frail; through the exhaustion of constant study and meditation, he frequently suffered from dizziness and coughing.
Nevertheless, he remained tireless in his mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). In the intercalary month of the ninth year of the Tongzhi era, his illness became critical.

He gathered his friends and said, "The realm of the West is excellent; on the twenty-third day, I shall depart for good. When that date arrived, he passed away as expected, his countenance unchanged. Afterward—
When the day for the enshrouding arrived, he stroked the crown of his head; his breath was still warm. He was forty-two years old at the time.
His works, including the *Zanglong ji*, the *Jianzhu ji*, the *Tiantai Zong Sijiao Duanzheng Tu Song*, and one hundred poems composed during his illness, have been circulated in the world.
Jingbo Jingbo, a native of Caoyan Village, was twenty years old when he received the tonsure at Yiqian Temple. He devoted himself single-mindedly to the Pure Land teachings.
After receiving the precepts, he traveled between Taining Temple in Changzhou, Gaomin Temple in Yangzhou, and the Tripitaka Library Temple. His temperament was serene and composed.
Throughout his life, he remained unchanged. Furthermore, he was able to practice mindfulness of the Buddha without slackening, constantly performing seven-day cycles of prostrations (*buddha-pūjā*).

He secluded his mind and stilled his thoughts; few people were able to emulate him. He subsequently went to Mount Jinshan, where for several years he resided in a tower, his feet never crossing its threshold.

Suddenly one day, having bathed and changed his robes, he personally visited the abbot’s quarters to bid farewell, saying, "Seven days from now, I shall return to the West. Indeed, in the tenth year of the Tongzhi era...
On the tenth day of the fourth month in the third year, without any illness or suffering, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture reciting the Buddha’s name.
This truly demonstrates that there is neither coming nor staying. He was eighty-two years old.
Ye-te-mu Tai-furen, Ye-te-mu Tai-furen.
Her Dharma name was Rennyū. She was a member of the Manchu Ching-hung Banner. She was diligent, frugal, benevolent, and compassionate.
Her affection for her clan was profound, and her kindness extended to her relatives and associates. She was diligent and tireless in supporting her husband and instructing her children;
thus, when the two gentlemen, Tong-Azha and Fen-A, served as local magistrates, they achieved distinguished reputations in their governance, upholding their mother’s instructions.

The Great Lady had observed the vegetarian fast since middle age and devoted herself to the pure practices of the Dharma. She maintained a daily fixed regimen, reciting the Buddha’s name two [thousand times].
For over twenty years, through countless cycles of winter and summer, she remained steadfast.

In the first year of the Guangxu era, at the age of sixty-two, her spirit and vitality suddenly showed no sign of decline after the full moon of the winter month. She said to her family members, "I see several Buddha images."

The children of the spring—both boys and girls—came forth in unison, holding banners and streamers, to welcome me. I had already determined that on the twenty-seventh day at noon, I would be reborn in the Western Land.

Consequently, I distributed my stored clothing and ornaments among my daughters-in-law and other women, instructing them all to maintain their integrity while living in this world and to take skillful means as their foundation.
Having no other words to say, when the appointed time arrived, I urged everyone to close the doors.
The family members knelt in a circle and recited the Buddha’s name. He then joined his palms, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away while clearly proclaiming the Buddha’s name.
Yu Shengxing—his Dharma name was Jing’a—was a native of Ganquan in Yangzhou. From youth, he had been refined in the study of antiquities and subsequently made it his vocation.

He provided for his livelihood. When his karmic ties with his family were exhausted, he remained solitary and alone. In the year of the Water Ox (1865), he heard that a Buddha-recitation hall had been opened at the Tripitaka Library where spiritual friends gathered like clouds.
Upon hearing their voices, he looked up in admiration, began to recite the Buddha’s name, adopted a vegetarian diet, took refuge, and entered the monastery.

He served to protect and maintain the hall, making the release of living beings and the seven-day Buddha-recitation retreat his primary tasks. Throughout the entire year, he never showed a trace of indolence. His radiance—

In the winter of the year Yi-hai (1795), he suddenly contracted a slight illness. His mindfulness of the Buddha became even more earnest. On New Year’s Eve, he addressed the assembly, saying, "Quickly prepare incense and flowers for an offering to the Buddha;

I am about to pass away. When his strength had become frail and feeble, he firmly instructed his attendants and the virtuous assembly to assist him in reciting the Buddha's name, and he passed into nirvana at the age of sixty-nine.
Dharma Master Yufeng, whose courtesy name was Guku and who was also known as Liànxi (Devoted to the West), set his will upon the Pure Land.

A native of Guangxin in Jiangxi, he entered the monastic order at the age of ten or so at Puning Temple. Possessing spiritual roots cultivated in past lives, he immediately attained full understanding upon first reading various Mahāyāna sūtras.

The general meaning is as follows: Having received full ordination, he resided at Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai, where he resolved to follow the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*. He joined the assembly to practice Chan meditation and exerted himself to investigate the fundamental tenets of the school.

Suddenly, upon hearing the sound of a bell, he attained a sudden awakening. Later, while reading Ouqi’s *Commentary on the Perfect Middle*, he found it to be in perfect accord with his own mind, which increased his Dharma-joy.
Thereupon, he established firm vows to strictly uphold the precepts and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name.

He sought rebirth in the Pure Land, practicing for himself and transforming others with singular sincerity and earnestness. Among both monastics and laity, those who were transformed by him were very numerous.
He revealed the suffering of birth and death to later students; his words were so piercing that those who heard them shed tears. He taught people to recite the Buddha’s name.

One should have a fixed daily practice of reciting the Name while counting the repetitions—whether ten thousand, twenty thousand, or even one hundred thousand—according to one’s mental capacity, without interruption, making it a lifelong commitment.
By practicing in this way without regressing, one will certainly be born in the Pure Land after death;
this is a method already verified by those who came before, and it may be trusted without doubt. Furthermore, he composed many treatises to elucidate [this teaching].

He propagated the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, which is easy to practice and easy to accomplish, its merit surpassing all other practices. If one is willing to follow it, one will certainly not be deceived.
Furthermore, he carved and printed Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas, and engraved the precious scriptures of Amitābha upon stone, circulating the True Dharma to repay the Buddha’s kindness.
His various other sublime deeds are too numerous to describe in full. In the fifteenth year of the Guangxu era, at Mingzhou...
The monk Jingguo of Xifang Temple invited him to reside at Xifang Temple; as the temple’s name accorded with his original vow, he settled there permanently.
From the time he first resolved his mind until his death, the Master daily recited the Buddha’s name sixty thousand times, dedicating the merit twice a day.

Without ceasing through cold or heat, he maintained this as his perpetual daily practice. On the sixth day of the seventh month in the eighteenth year of the Guangxu era, after his midday meal, he felt a slight distension in his abdomen.
The following day, Jingguo invited a physician to examine him; the physician stated that his pulse was completely absent and that there was no need for medicine.
Yet the Master sat in the lotus posture facing west, reciting the Buddha’s name without uttering any other words. His spirit remained clear and robust, surpassing [his usual state].
During his usual state, physicians marveled at it as something rare. Jingguo said, "May I request the assembly of masters to recite the Buddha's name to assist him?
The master consented. Thereupon, he invited eight monks to kneel facing west and chant the sacred name of Amitābha for the duration of one incense stick.
Just as the hour of Shen arrived, he saw the master join his palms and recite the Buddha’s name with great vigor several hundred times, appearing serene and joyful.

The account continues: on the ninth day, when he was placed in the sarcophagus, his facial complexion remained moist and lustrous, and the crown of his head was still warm. On the full moon day of the second month of the following year, his body was cremated.
Several hundred monastics and laypeople accompanied him as he was escorted away. Once the fire had been ignited, the door of the sarcophagus opened first;

there, the Master was seen sitting cross-legged, as solemn and lifelike as if he were alive. As the fierce flames grew intense, the multitude saw ten Buddhas manifest upon the crown of his head, with two [figures] in each hand.

A single image of the Buddha appeared; this was because during his lifetime, the Master had once burned ten incense sticks upon his crown as an offering to the Buddhas of the ten directions, and had burned one finger from each hand—one for Śākyamuni Buddha and one for Amitābha.

Thus, at the time of his cremation, images of the Buddhas manifested from his crown and hands. This was truly the result of his sincere devotion—a rare and wondrous omen. How extraordinary! *Ataḥi shēng* (Alas! His Life)
He shall become a leader of the Pure Land; that he will attain rebirth in the supreme grade after his death is beyond doubt.

Previously, the three Grand Historians Shen, Zhu, and Wu sought instruction from the Master and praised his spiritual practice and conduct most highly, declaring him to be truly a bridge and raft for the degenerate age, and so forth.
Yuandeng, whose courtesy name was Sisi’an, was the son of the Xie family of Qiantang in Hangzhou. In his youth, he studied Confucianism as a scholar-official student.

Realizing that the world is impermanent, he turned his heart toward the Triple Gem. He traveled extensively to consult and question masters of both the doctrinal and Chan schools. Later, he studied under Dharma Master Yufeng.
He was instructed that for those seeking liberation from suffering, the single method of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) is the most easily accomplished.

He subsequently resolved to maintain a daily fixed practice of reciting the Buddha’s name sixty thousand times. All the meritorious deeds he performed throughout his life were dedicated toward rebirth in the Pure Land.
In the *Ren-shen* year of the Tongzhi era, he received the five precepts at Haichao Temple. Furthermore, deeply weary of worldly toil, he sought early liberation.

In the ninth year of the Guangxu era, he entrusted his household affairs to his two sons and went directly to Huguo Temple west of the prefecture to take refuge with the monk Jingfeng and enter the monastic order.
That winter, he received full ordination at Zhiyuan Temple in Xiaoshan and returned once more to Huguo Temple, where he devoted himself single-mindedly to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism.
After laboring diligently for a long time, he suddenly fell ill; although he underwent medical treatment, he soon recovered.
Shortly after she departed, her two sons, longing for her, brought her home to care for her. They set aside a separate room specifically as a place for her to practice *śubha* (purity).

In the autumn of the fifteenth year of the Guangxu era, she suddenly fell ill with dysentery; though medical treatment proved ineffective, her appetite diminished yet her recitation of the Buddha’s name became even more earnest.
On the tenth day of the ninth month, she suddenly said to her son, "I am going to be reborn in the Pure Land."

When the appointed time arrived, he invited monks to his home to perform a seven-day Buddha-recitation retreat (*buddha-śīti*) to assist him in his journey to the West. He himself fixed the start for the twelfth day.
On the seventh day, he said to Seng Langfeng, "There are still seven days until the fifteenth. Then, taking the hand of Seng Tingshan, he said:
"I have stayed for only three days; I must depart. On the seventeenth day, during the fourth watch, he asked what time it was. His son replied, "It is the hour of the Ox (the second watch).
He said, "The hour of the Ox belongs to the eighteenth day. This 'zi' (the eleventh watch) is the time of my rebirth. You should invite the masters to recite the Buddha's name to assist me.
Thereupon, he joined the assembly in reciting the Buddha's name. After approximately one and a half incense sticks had passed, he suddenly closed his eyes and passed away.
After a long silence, he suddenly opened his eyes, joined his palms, and addressed the assembly with words of gratitude, saying:
"I have personally reached the Western Land and directly beheld Amitābha Buddha and the two Great Beings. I am deeply indebted for the Buddha’s compassion, which bestowed upon me pure robes.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva sprinkled water upon the crown of my head. I also saw Master Lianchi preaching the Dharma for the assembly, and I beheld the seven treasures."
Within the pond, amidst the various jewel lotuses, was my place of birth. Relying upon the Buddha’s compassion, he commanded me to return and inform everyone:
"I have already attained rebirth in the Pure Land. I exhort you all to focus single-mindedly on the recitation of the Buddha's name;

we shall meet again in the Pure Land on another day. He then requested pure water, drank it three times, and lay down in an auspicious manner. He recited the Buddha’s name several dozen times before passing away.
However, he passed away. The following day, when his body was placed in the coffin, his crown remained warm to the touch.
Within the city of Hangzhou, there have certainly not been a lack of people over the past several decades who, through diligent recitation of the Buddha’s name, attained rebirth in the Pure Land;
such cases are clear and manifest, providing undeniable evidence. Yet, Master Deng alone is truly exceptional. Alas! Were it not for his long-standing [merit]...
Only those endowed with spiritual roots could have achieved such a thing. I have recorded this to serve as an exhortation for those who practice the Pure Land path.
Xie Chunhua, surnamed Xie, was a native of Qiantang in Hangzhou. He followed the trade of selling clothing; his natural disposition was gentle and upright, and he never quarreled with others.
He was profoundly filial toward his parents and never once caused them displeasure. Whenever he encountered virtuous deeds, he would assist with all his might;

however, as for the practice of vegetarianism and the recitation of the Buddha’s name, he was unable to carry these out. In the tenth year of the Guangxu era, he suddenly contracted a disease of intestinal swelling caused by parasites. Neither medical treatment nor prayers proved effective.
He was merely groaning as he awaited the end of his life. His cousin, the layman Zhu Jinbo, had long been devoted to the Buddha-dharma;

having studied under various masters, he had gained much insight into the essential principles of the Chan school. One day, he came to Chunhua and said, "Observing the suffering from your illness, it is clearly the result of karmic obstacles from past lives.
If you do not establish great vows for wholesome merit and practice the recitation of the Buddha's name along with repentance," [the illness will not be resolved].

Fearing that it would be difficult to eliminate [the karmic obstacles], Chunhua nodded in agreement and then made a vow: for the rest of her life, she would abstain from killing, release captive animals, and recite the Buddha’s name with a sincere heart.
Once the vow was established, Master Zhu instructed her to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha together for a period of forty-nine days.
That evening, she dreamed of a monk giving her a medicinal pill and telling her to swallow it; upon waking, she felt a rumbling movement within her abdomen.
He descended several times in succession; immediately his body was at ease, and within three days his illness was completely cured.

From then on, his faith became earnest and sincere, and he recited the Buddha’s name without interruption. Whenever there was a Buddhist assembly, he never failed to participate in person. This continued until the fifteenth year of the Guangxu era.
In early summer, he was briefly afflicted by a slight illness; while his appetite for food and drink diminished, his mindfulness of the Buddha became even more earnest.

On the twenty-sixth day of the fourth month, he personally beheld the Three Holy Ones of the Western Paradise within a dream. Knowing this to be an omen of rebirth there, he informed all his relatives and friends.
He was about to be born in the Pure Land. The layman Yao Mingzhai said to him, "On the twenty-eighth day, I shall depart for the West;
you should come to recite the Buddha's name to assist me. [The master] replied, "On the twenty-eighth, I will have no leisure and cannot come.

He asked again, "Would the twenty-ninth be possible? [The master] replied, "On the twenty-ninth as well, I will have no leisure. [Yao] spoke once more, "If that is the case, then surely it must be on the first day of the fifth month."

When asked how he would depart, he replied, "On the first day, it is appropriate to come and see me off. On the appointed day, he bathed, changed his clothes, and sat facing west in a dignified posture.
He said to his sons, "If you possess a filial heart, recite the Buddha’s name to assist me; do not weep or wail.

Soon after, his virtuous friends gathered together, and for about half an incense stick's duration, they all chanted the Buddha’s name. Then, raising his hands in palms-joined reverence, he offered his thanks.
The assembly [practiced] the aids to the Path. He looked up at the sky; as if seeing something, he joined his palms toward the sky, smiled, and passed away.
After his death, the assembly smelled a wondrous fragrance that did not dissipate for several days. This was truly a rare occurrence.
